title: Gemini 4 Carbon is now available
author: Google DeepMind
contentSnippet:
Nov 10, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers can now try our latest frontier model.

Koray Kavukcuoglu SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google

Your browser does not support the audio element.

Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning.

Two weeks ago , we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program . Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon , Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops.

Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0 , Perplexity’s WANDR , and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model.

To put Carbon’s capabilities to work on larger and complex projects, we’re previewing /swarm in Google Antigravity, turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time. Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change.

Gemini 4 Carbon is available via the API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, at the same introductory price 1 as Gemini 4 Argon ($2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens). It is also rolling out to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , the Gemini app , and AI Mode in Search .

summary.tldr:
Google DeepMind has released Gemini 4 Carbon, a new frontier model designed for complex, multi-step reasoning, long-horizon agentic workflows, and specialized cybersecurity tasks. Positioned as a more intensive counterpart to the previously released Gemini 4 Argon, Carbon is optimized for deep-reasoning tasks such as architectural design, scientific discovery, and extended verification loops. It is currently available to developers and enterprises via Google AI Studio and Gemini for business, as well as to Google AI Ultra subscribers within the Google Antigravity platform, the Gemini app, and AI Mode in Search.

Technically, Carbon excels in multi-agent orchestration through the new '/swarm' feature in Google Antigravity, which allows users to deploy coordinated agent teams for complex tasks like 3D environment generation and full-stack software development. The model ranks #1 on benchmarks including CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity’s WANDR, and Zapier’s AutomationBench. In cybersecurity, it demonstrates significant gains in vulnerability scanning, triage, and remediation, achieving 100% recall and 95% precision in internal Project Fortify testing. Google also partnered with Artificial Analysis to introduce the Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark, where Carbon ranks #2 while maintaining a cost-per-task advantage over the top-performing model.
takeaways: **Pricing:** Gemini 4 Carbon is priced at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, matching the introductory pricing of Gemini 4 Argon.

**Agentic Orchestration:** The new '/swarm' feature in Google Antigravity enables users to convert a single prompt into a multi-agent team capable of parallelized tasks, such as 3D asset modeling, WebGL shader development, and procedural audio generation.

**Cybersecurity Performance:** Carbon achieved a 25% relative improvement in recall over Gemini 4 Argon on open-source repository testing and successfully identified 0-day vulnerabilities in major SaaS providers in under two hours during Wiz’s 'Scan for Good' program.

**Benchmark Leadership:** The model holds the #1 position on CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity’s WANDR, and Zapier’s AutomationBench, while also ranking at the top of Balyasny Asset Management’s General Financial Intelligence benchmark.
**Multimodal Benchmarking:** In the newly launched Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark, Carbon ranks #2 while operating at a cost more than 6X lower than the top-performing model.

title: NVIDIA Expands Open Source Commitment With OpenShell Donation and New AI Infrastructure
author: Warren Barkley
contentSnippet: Kubernetes, the open source system that manages how applications run across thousands of AI factories, has become the foundation for AI, and the demands on it are only growing. To help meet them, NVIDIA is deepening its commitment to open source at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon , the flagship conference for the Kubernetes and cloud-native communities. NVIDIA is contributing NVIDIA OpenShell , an open source runtime for securing and governing autonomous agents, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), a nonprofit that is part of the Linux Foundation and the host of KubeCon. As a CNCF Sandbox project, OpenShell will be governed by the organizations building it into their products and strengthened by the expertise of security professionals worldwide. NVIDIA is also contributing to Agent Substrate , an open source Google-led framework for operating long-running agent workloads at scale on Kubernetes that has been accepted into the CNCF Sandbox. Additionally, NVIDIA announced new components of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform : NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine , NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes and NVIDIA Snapshot . These tools help teams deploy, manage and scale GPU infrastructure on Kubernetes for AI factories. Together, these advancements mark a step forward in making Kubernetes the leading foundation for AI workloads at scale — empowering developers to build safer, more efficient AI infrastructure for the future. Securing AI Agents in the Open NVIDIA’s contribution of OpenShell to CNCF puts security infrastructure for autonomous agents in the community’s hands to build, inspect and improve — accelerating development and hardening its safeguards. “The cloud-native community has a new infrastructure challenge: giving agents secure environments in which to operate,” said Jim Zemlin, CEO of the Linux Foundation. “NVIDIA’s contribution of OpenShell to CNCF gives developers a shared foundation to build on and an opportunity to shape how agent security evolves. Bringing this work into the community enables broader collaboration on infrastructure that will be critical to the next generation of cloud-native applications.” OpenShell gives organizations control over what AI agents can do. summary.tldr:
NVIDIA has announced a significant expansion of its open-source contributions at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon, focusing on securing and scaling AI workloads on Kubernetes. The company is donating NVIDIA OpenShell, a runtime designed for governing and securing autonomous agents, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) as a Sandbox project. Additionally, NVIDIA is contributing to Agent Substrate, a Google-led open-source framework also accepted into the CNCF Sandbox, which is engineered to manage long-running agent workloads at scale within Kubernetes environments.

Beyond these contributions, NVIDIA introduced three new components to its DSX AI Factory Platform: NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine, NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes, and NVIDIA Snapshot. These tools are designed to streamline the deployment, management, and scaling of GPU infrastructure for AI factories. OpenShell specifically provides deterministic controls, allowing organizations to enforce security policies as agents interact with tools, inference services, and compute workloads, thereby addressing the growing need for secure operating environments for autonomous AI agents.
takeaways: **OpenShell Contribution:** NVIDIA donated its OpenShell runtime to the CNCF as a Sandbox project to provide a shared, community-governed foundation for securing autonomous agents.
**Agent Substrate Support:** NVIDIA is contributing to the Google-led Agent Substrate framework, which is now a CNCF Sandbox project focused on operating long-running agent workloads on Kubernetes.
**DSX AI Factory Platform Updates:** NVIDIA expanded its DSX platform with three new components: NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine, NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes, and NVIDIA Snapshot.
**Security Functionality:** OpenShell enables deterministic control over AI agents, allowing teams to enforce specific policies during tool usage, inference access, and workload execution.

title: Google broadens its AI hardware portfolio with two new specialized chips
author: Ram Iyer
contentSnippet:
Google is notching up its chipmaking game as the company seeks to reduce its dependence on chips made by other companies for its cloud computing business. Google on Monday unveiled two new variants of its tensor processing units (TPUs), in-house developed chips meant for AI workloads, that broaden its chip portfolio to additional use cases: confidential inference and more memory capacity for large workloads.

The new units, TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, are part of the company’s eighth generation of chips introduced in April this year, and build on what those chips offered, which was more inference capacity and support for large training requirements.

TPU 8tx, designed with AMD, is based on the TPU 8t chip, and is geared specifically for confidentially training and running AI models, Google said in a blog post. The chip “builds security directly into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use,” the company wrote.

The chip also has a custom inferencing network that lets it run reasoning alongside training, so it can be used to distill and train small models on the fly. That ability, according to Google, could prove useful for cases where a company might want to train a model on its proprietary data without having to move the data between devices.

Meanwhile, TPU 8i Max basically combines two of the inference-focused TPU 8i chips the company launched in April, doubling the memory capacity, processing power and bandwidth, but in a single package. The result is a chip that lets AI models handle a larger range of information during queries.

The chip launch comes as hyperscalers like Microsoft , Amazon , and even AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are working on their own lines of AI-specific semiconductors and accompanying software in order to reduce their reliance on the dominance of Nvidia.

The news also comes at a particularly vulnerable moment for Nvidia, whose CEO Jensen Huang over the weekend admitted to having an affair with someone alleged to be a Chinese spy.

summary.tldr:
Google has expanded its eighth-generation Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) portfolio with two new specialized chips, the TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max. These additions aim to reduce reliance on third-party silicon for cloud-based AI workloads by addressing specific requirements for data security and high-memory capacity. The hardware rollout follows the initial launch of the eighth-generation TPU series in April, which focused on general inference and large-scale training capabilities.

The TPU 8tx, developed in collaboration with AMD, is derived from the TPU 8t architecture and is engineered for confidential computing. It integrates security directly into the hardware layer to isolate sensitive data and model weights during active processing. Additionally, the 8tx features a custom inferencing network that enables simultaneous reasoning and training, facilitating the distillation of smaller models on proprietary data without requiring data migration. The TPU 8i Max doubles the performance of the existing TPU 8i by combining two units into a single package, effectively doubling memory capacity, processing power, and bandwidth to support larger query contexts.
takeaways: **TPU 8tx Architecture:** Developed with AMD based on the TPU 8t, featuring hardware-level security for confidential inference and on-the-fly model distillation.
**TPU 8i Max Specs:** A dual-die configuration of the TPU 8i that doubles memory, bandwidth, and processing power for large-scale inference tasks.
**Strategic Context:** The expansion represents a continued effort by hyperscalers to mitigate dependence on Nvidia’s hardware dominance in the AI semiconductor market.
**Eighth-Generation Timeline:** These chips extend the eighth-generation TPU lineup originally introduced by Google in April.

title: Meta’s AI agent Muse lands on Apple Watch and Android Wear OS
author: Aisha Malik
contentSnippet:
Meta is bringing its Muse AI agent to the Apple Watch and Android’s Wear OS, the company announced on Monday. With the launch, users can now interact with Meta’s AI assistant through voice calls, text messages, or dictation directly on their smartwatch.

Works around the clock, and now on your wrist. Muse is now on Apple Watch and Wear OS ⌚️ pic.twitter.com/97QRap5XKz

The smartwatch launch comes just a month after Meta introduced a dedicated iPad app for Muse. First launched on the App Store in September, the AI assistant’s expansion across Apple devices signals Meta’s growing ambitions for its consumer AI product and its focus on making Muse a central part of its ecosystem.

Muse is now one of dozens of consumer-facing AI agents competing for users’ attention. Like many of its competitors, it allows users to connect their accounts to manage email, meetings, bills, and more, while also handling tasks such as booking reservations, ordering groceries, setting goals, and making purchases.

Users can also personalize their Muse avatar to their liking and change it into something that resembles a person, an animal, or another type of character.

Despite being a relatively new product, Meta has wasted little time introducing new capabilities to Muse.

A few days ago, Meta launched Spaces , a new way to communicate and collaborate with Muse. Spaces function as dedicated conversations around specific topics, which Meta describes as “custom experiences” as they’re mini apps that are built on the fly. They appear in the sidebar of the Muse interface and bring up a focused conversation where the AI agent works toward a particular goal on the user’s behalf.

Last week, Meta rolled out the ability for users in the U.S. to video chat with their Muse AI avatar. Meta said Muse will use “subtle expressions and gestures” that reflect the tone and context of the conversation as it speaks. It’s worth noting that Muse doesn’t actually see users, but can hear them and respond in real-time.

Shortly after its launch, Muse became one of just 12 mobile apps to have surpassed 10 million U.S. downloads within their first 40 days in the App Store. Only 11 other apps have achieved this milestone, with Meta’s Threads being the most recent in July 2023.

summary.tldr:
Meta has expanded its consumer AI assistant, Muse, to the Apple Watch and Android's Wear OS, enabling users to interact via voice calls, text messages, and dictation directly from their wrists. Announced on Monday, the smartwatch rollout follows a dedicated iPad app introduced last month and the initial App Store launch in September. Muse provides productivity and management features, including account integrations for email, meetings, and bills, as well as task execution for booking reservations, ordering groceries, and making purchases.

Meta has rapidly scaled Muse's feature set since its debut, recently introducing "Spaces"—custom, on-the-fly mini-apps in the interface sidebar for focused, goal-oriented conversations. Last week, Meta also rolled out real-time video chat capabilities with animated Muse avatars for U.S. users, featuring subtle expressions and gestures reflecting conversation context, though the AI cannot see the user. Additionally, Muse surpassed 10 million U.S. downloads within its first 40 days in the App Store, joining an elite group of only 12 apps to achieve this milestone, alongside Meta's Threads in July 2023.
takeaways: **Platform Expansion:** Muse is now available on Apple Watch and Android Wear OS, supporting voice calls, text messages, and dictation.
**Download Milestone:** Muse exceeded 10 million U.S. downloads within its first 40 days on the App Store, a feat previously achieved by only 11 other apps, including Threads.
**New Feature 'Spaces':** Meta launched Spaces, functioning as dedicated, on-the-fly mini-apps in the sidebar for topic-specific communication and goal-oriented collaboration.
**Video Chat Integration:** U.S. users can video chat with animated Muse avatars that use subtle expressions and gestures reflecting conversation tone, while processing audio in real-time.

title: Anthropic Launches Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2: Same Model, Different Safeguards
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Anthropic just released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 . Claude Fable 5.2 is a frontier model from Anthropic for long-horizon coding, research and agentic work. Mythos 5.2 is the same underlying model with fewer cyber and biology safeguards. It beats Opus 5.5 on most evaluations and costs less than the 5.1 models. TL;DR Size: 1M-token context window, 128K max output. Runs on: Hosted API only. Claude Platform, Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure. No open weights. Performance: Ahead of Opus 5.5 on almost every benchmark Anthropic reported. Best: RoboDojo Sim 64.9%, more than double GPT-6 Astra (29.8%). Worst: AutomationBench 51.4%, behind Gemini 4 Carbon (53.9%). Bottom line: Best: Opus-level coding at roughly half the cost per task. Worst: Fable still blocks most cybersecurity work. What is the difference between Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2? They are one model. Fable 5.2 adds classifiers that block high-risk cybersecurity tasks and most research biology. That lets Anthropic offer it to all users. Mythos 5.2 drops those blocks. Access runs through the Cyber Verification Program and the Life Sciences Verification Program . When Fable blocks a query, users get an answer from Opus 4.8 (cyber) or Opus 5 (biology). Anthropic reports about 55% fewer blocks than Fable 5.1. That splits into roughly 60% fewer in cybersecurity and 40% fewer in biology. How does Claude Fable 5.2 perform on benchmarks? Anthropic published one table comparing Fable 5.2 with Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Carbon. All scores are self-reported. Key results: FrontierCode 2.0 (agentic coding): 49.1% at Xhigh effort, vs 45.5% for Opus 5.5. FrontierSWE v2: 69.9%, vs 65.5% for GPT-6 Astra. Remote Labor Index: 41.3%, vs 21.3% for Opus 5.5. Humanity’s Last Exam (with tools): 74.2%, vs 67.7% for Opus 5.5. OSWorld 2.1 (partial offline set): 89.3%. CVE Rediscovery (Mythos 5.2): 89.6%, vs 81.3% for Opus 5.5 without safeguards. Fable 5.2 does not lead everywhere. Gemini 4 Carbon wins AutomationBench (53.9% vs 51.4%). Opus 5.5 holds a higher AA-Briefcase Elo (1800 vs 1785). <iframe id="mtp-fable52-frame" title="Claude Fable 5.2 interactive explainer" loading="lazy" scrolling="no" style="width:100%!important;height:600px;border:0!important;display:block!important;background:#141413!important;border-radius:16px;" srcdoc="<!doctype html> <html lang="en"> <head> <meta

summary.tldr:
Anthropic has released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, two versions of a new frontier model designed for long-horizon coding, research, and agentic tasks. Both models feature a 1-million-token context window and a 128K-token maximum output, available exclusively via hosted API on the Claude Platform, AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure, with no open weights. Fable 5.2 includes integrated classifiers to restrict high-risk cybersecurity and biology research, while Mythos 5.2 removes these safeguards, requiring access via the Cyber Verification Program and the Life Sciences Verification Program.

Technically, the models outperform the previous Opus 5.5 on most benchmarks, including FrontierCode 2.0 (49.1% vs 45.5%) and FrontierSWE v2 (69.9% vs 65.5% against GPT-6 Astra). Fable 5.2 achieved 74.2% on Humanity’s Last Exam and 89.3% on OSWorld 2.1. However, the model trails Gemini 4 Carbon on AutomationBench (51.4% vs 53.9%) and Opus 5.5 on the AA-Briefcase Elo rating (1785 vs 1800). Anthropic reports that Fable 5.2 triggers 55% fewer safety blocks than Fable 5.1, with a 60% reduction in cybersecurity blocks and 40% in biology. When Fable 5.2 blocks a query, the system defaults to Opus 4.8 or Opus 5 for fallback responses.
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 share the same underlying architecture, with Fable 5.2 utilizing additional classifiers for safety and Mythos 5.2 requiring specialized verification for access.
**Benchmark Performance:** Fable 5.2 scored 64.9% on RoboDojo Sim, significantly outperforming GPT-6 Astra (29.8%), and achieved 89.6% on CVE Rediscovery in Mythos 5.2 mode.
**Cost Efficiency:** The new models provide Opus-level coding capabilities at approximately half the cost per task compared to the 5.1 series.
**Safety Fallbacks:** When Fable 5.2 blocks a request, the system automatically routes the query to Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity tasks or Opus 5 for biology-related inquiries.

title: Anthropic targets $1.4 trillion IPO
author: Stevie Bonifield
contentSnippet: Anthropic confirmed on Tuesday that its IPO could be one of the biggest ever, even while falling short of previous expectations. Its IPO price is expected to be between $70.00 and $78.00 per share, which would put its valuation as high as $1.4 trillion, according to the New York Times. The Wall Street Journal reports that according to its sources, Anthropic is “aiming for its shares to start trading Thursday or Friday next week.” As Reuters notes, the Anthropic IPO was previously expected to be valued at as much as $2 trillion. As of last week, Anthropic’s rival OpenAI was valued at $1.25 trillion. Those lower expectations follow months of debate around AI safety, and what that means, while midterm election results showed souring public opinion toward AI companies and data center projects they’re heavily investing in. And that doesn’t even include this weekend’s revelations about an alleged Chinese spy’s involvement with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Anthropic: > The initial public offering price is expected to be between $70.00 and $78.00 per share. Anthropic has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.” [Media: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yvy_Qm14odU]

summary.tldr:
Anthropic has confirmed plans for an initial public offering (IPO) on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol “ANT.” The company expects to price its Class A common stock between $70.00 and $78.00 per share, targeting a valuation as high as $1.4 trillion. Trading is projected to commence as early as next Thursday or Friday.

This valuation target represents a downward adjustment from previous market expectations, which had projected a potential valuation of up to $2 trillion. The revised outlook follows a period of intense scrutiny regarding AI safety protocols, shifting public sentiment toward AI infrastructure and data center expansion, and broader geopolitical concerns. For context, the $1.4 trillion target places Anthropic above the $1.25 trillion valuation recently attributed to its primary competitor, OpenAI.
takeaways: **Ticker Symbol:** Anthropic has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.”
**Pricing Range:** The expected IPO price is set between $70.00 and $78.00 per share.
**Valuation Target:** The offering aims for a market capitalization of up to $1.4 trillion.
**Competitive Context:** The $1.4 trillion target exceeds the $1.25 trillion valuation reported for OpenAI as of last week.

title: Adobe brings AI agents and new creative tools to Photoshop, Premiere, and Firefly
author: Ivan Mehta
contentSnippet:
Adobe is pouring more AI into its products, including Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator, and InDesign, in a major product feature announcement at its MAX event in Miami. The company is also expanding AI capabilities in its creative tool, Firefly, and releasing a Model Context Protocol (MCP) that lets other chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini use Adobe features.

Adobe’s Firefly app is moving into Figma’s territory with a new prototyping tool in private beta called Builder, which lets users create designs to show off ideas. There is also a new tool to create on-brand graphs, along with an image editing tool that lets you change part of an image without changing other objects.

A new AI-powered video tool in Firefly will allow users to assemble a video from clips and other elements like images and sound effects. The company is making its agent proactive and always on so that it can get more context about work and be present for any action. Adobe is also making it easier for people to take quick action, like removing the background or generating a thumbnail for a video.

The company has already added a ton of AI features across its apps like Photoshop, Express, Premiere, and Illustrator . At the MAX event, Adobe is continuing the trend. Photoshop is getting a new relighting feature and sliders for prompt-based generative styles; Premiere will have a new color grading system for professionals and an object removal feature for video; and Lightroom has a way to correct blinking eyes and a blemish removal tool.

Adobe already offers a lot of third-party models from companies like Google, Runway, ElevenLabs, Black Forest Labs, OpenAI, Kling, and ByteDance. One of its newer acquisitions, Topaz Labs , is releasing two image models, called Wonder 4 for upscaling and denoising, and ImageHDR, to turn standard images into HDR.

The company already has ChatGPT and Claude integrations to let users access some of its product functions. Now, Adobe is releasing a local MCP to expose more features of its Creative Cloud apps to users.

Adobe vice president Deepa Subramaniam told TechCrunch that the company is still figuring out what capabilities to expose and will rely on user feedback.

“We are still figuring out where and when and how to draw the line. What we’re putting out there is a number of endpoints and capabilities across Illustrator, Photoshop, After Effects, and P

summary.tldr:
At its MAX event in Miami, Adobe announced a significant expansion of AI capabilities across its Creative Cloud suite, including Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, and Lightroom. Key updates include a new relighting feature and generative style sliders for Photoshop, a professional-grade color grading system and object removal for Premiere, and blemish/blink correction for Lightroom. Adobe is also launching 'Builder,' a private beta prototyping tool within Firefly designed to compete with Figma, alongside new AI-powered video assembly tools and on-brand graph generation.

Beyond core application updates, Adobe is introducing a local Model Context Protocol (MCP) to allow third-party LLMs like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini to interface directly with Creative Cloud functions. This move aims to integrate Adobe’s creative workflows into external chatbot environments. Additionally, Adobe is expanding its third-party model ecosystem, incorporating tools from Google, Runway, ElevenLabs, Black Forest Labs, OpenAI, Kling, and ByteDance, while integrating two new models from recent acquisition Topaz Labs: Wonder 4 for upscaling/denoising and ImageHDR for high-dynamic-range conversion.
takeaways: **Model Context Protocol (MCP):** Adobe is releasing a local MCP to expose Creative Cloud endpoints—including Illustrator, Photoshop, After Effects, and Premiere—to external AI agents and chatbots.
**Topaz Labs Integration:** Adobe is incorporating two new models from its acquisition Topaz Labs: 'Wonder 4' for image upscaling and denoising, and 'ImageHDR' for HDR conversion.
**Firefly Builder:** Adobe is entering the prototyping space with 'Builder,' a private beta tool within Firefly that allows users to generate designs and layouts.

**Video AI Features:** Premiere Pro is receiving a new object removal tool for video and an advanced color grading system, while Firefly is adding capabilities to assemble videos from clips, images, and sound effects.
**Third-Party Model Ecosystem:** Adobe continues to integrate external models from providers including Google, Runway, ElevenLabs, Black Forest Labs, OpenAI, Kling, and ByteDance.

title: Anthropic sets IPO price range of $70 to $78 per share to reach an implied valuation of $1.404 trillion
author: Rebecca Bellan, Ram Iyer
contentSnippet:
Anthropic intends to push ahead with its IPO despite shakier markets and the broader pullback from AI investing.

The Claude-maker said in an updated IPO filing on Tuesday that it would be offering a total of 825 million Class A shares at an estimated price range of $70 to $78 per share. The sale is expected to raise anywhere from $57.75 billion to $64.35 billion.

The company could end up being worth a hefty $1.404 trillion if its shares list at the top of the price range, on a fully diluted basis. That would represent a significant jump up from the $965 billion valuation Anthropic reached in a May fundraise , but it’s still lower than the $2 trillion the company was reportedly targeting a couple months ago.

Separately, Anthropic said it had struck a deal to privately sell $26 billion of non-voting Class N stock at the IPO price to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC. Google and Nvidia are investing $10 billion apiece.

All up, Anthropic estimates net proceeds to reach somewhere between $84.6 billion and $93.7 billion (the latter if the IPO underwriters exercise their option to buy additional shares).

Underwriters, including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, will have the option to buy up to 123.75 million more shares from Anthropic at the IPO price.

As a public benefit corporation, the founders hold a Class F share with 50.1% of the voting power. The Long-Term Benefit Trust will also elect a board majority, so Class A buyers will have limited influence.

Anthropic intends to start trading on the Nasdaq close to November 19, per reporting from CNBC , under the ticker symbol “ANT”. The company expects up to 20% of the offering to be allocated to retail investors.

Anthropic also gave out a few new details in the updated filing. The company said its run-rate revenue reached $81 billion by the end of October, about $10 billion more than at the end of September.

Also, the filing now lists how many shares the company’s co-founders expect to sell in the IPO: CEO Dario Amodei, president and chairperson Daniela Amodei, chief compute officer Tom Brown, Anthropic Institute head Jack Clark, chief science officer Jared Kaplan, chief architect Sam McCandlish and interpretability research lead Christopher Olah are all selling nearly 3.4 million shares each. At the $74 midpoint of the IPO price range, that would land them about $250 million each.

summary.tldr:
Anthropic has filed an updated IPO prospectus, setting a price range of $70 to $78 per share for 825 million Class A shares. This offering aims to raise between $57.75 billion and $64.35 billion, targeting a fully diluted valuation of $1.404 trillion. The company plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT" around November 19, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley serving as lead underwriters. A concurrent private placement will see AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC purchase $26 billion in non-voting Class N stock, with Google and Nvidia contributing $10 billion each.

Financial disclosures reveal a rapid growth trajectory, with run-rate revenue reaching $81 billion as of October. For the first nine months of the year, Anthropic reported $33.2 billion in revenue against a net loss of $104 billion, driven by $900.9 billion in compute and infrastructure commitments. The company maintains a cash position of $132 billion. Governance remains tightly controlled; founders hold Class F shares representing 50.1% of voting power, and a Long-Term Benefit Trust retains the right to elect a board majority, limiting the influence of public shareholders. Seven key executives, including CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei, are each selling approximately 3.4 million shares, netting roughly $250 million each at the $74 midpoint.
takeaways: **Valuation & Pricing:** IPO price range of $70–$78 per share targets a $1.404 trillion fully diluted valuation, exceeding the $965 billion valuation from the May funding round.
**Private Placement:** $26 billion in non-voting Class N stock sold to a consortium including Google, Nvidia, Microsoft, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, and TSMC.
**Financial Performance:** Reported $81 billion run-rate revenue as of October, with $33.2 billion in revenue and a $104 billion net loss for the first nine months of the year.
**Governance Structure:** Founders retain 50.1% voting power via Class F shares; a Long-Term Benefit Trust controls board composition, limiting Class A shareholder influence.
**Regulatory Alignment:** The filing adopts the term "super intelligence" (SI) in accordance with the Trump administration's September executive order regarding AI terminology.

title: Kora builds AI models and agents into a new Linux OS bound for Qualcomm Snapdragon PCs
author: Duncan Riley
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 09:00 EST / NOVEMBER 10 2026

Kora builds AI models and agents into a new Linux OS bound for Qualcomm Snapdragon PCs

Desktop software company Kora Systems Inc. today unveiled Kora, a Linux-based operating system that builds artificial intelligence models and agents into the system itself.

Qualcomm Technologies Inc. has spent close to a year working with the company to bring it to Snapdragon-powered PCs.

The launch goes after what Kora sees as a ceiling on AI in current desktop computers. Most AI software on macOS and Windows runs inside a browser tab or an app sandbox, according to the company, with little view of the computer underneath.

Because both platforms are closed, Kora argues, the integration stops at that point. Linux, by Kora’s account, is the only operating system open enough to be rebuilt around models and agents from the kernel up.

The core of that rebuild is an inference engine Kora calls Cortex. It pools the central processor, graphics processor and neural processing unit in a PC, plus any other machines on the network, and treats them as one computer. Models run locally on the user’s hardware by default, and frontier models get pulled in for heavier jobs.

On screen, the usual layout of folders and apps is gone. What Kora calls neural workspaces take its place, each one arranged around the task a user is working on. The user sets the permissions for any applications and agents sandboxed inside a workspace. Under all of it sits a neural file system, and the company says memory and context stay on the local machine.

Outside developers can build on the same pieces Kora’s own applications use through its software development kit, which opens up primitives such as memory, semantic search and email. Any model, AI service or agent will be able to integrate at the system level, the company said. An agentic service could even run as part of the operating system and take its identity, memory and compute from Kora.

Chief Executive Kirt McMaster called the desktop operating system “the ultimate harness.” About 45 million people account for 80% of spending on AI, he said, and almost all of their work happens on desktops running operating systems built 40 years ago. By 2033 the group will top 150 million people spending more than $400 billion a year, according to Kora’s own estimates. “Nobody has built an operating system for them,” McMaste

summary.tldr:
Kora Systems Inc. has unveiled Kora, a Linux-based operating system designed to integrate AI models and agents directly into the kernel. Developed by the team behind Playtron and GameOS, the platform replaces traditional desktop folder structures with 'neural workspaces' and utilizes a proprietary inference engine called Cortex. Cortex pools local CPU, GPU, and NPU resources—along with networked machines—to execute AI workloads, prioritizing local execution while offloading heavier tasks to frontier models. The OS features a neural file system that maintains user context and memory locally, and provides an SDK for developers to build system-level agents with access to primitives like semantic search and email.

In collaboration with Qualcomm Technologies Inc., Kora has been optimized for Snapdragon X2 Elite-powered PCs. The system supports local execution of 26-billion parameter language models and includes translation technology to run x86-64 Windows applications within the Linux environment. The first commercial deployment is scheduled for 2027 via HUMAIN OS, an enterprise-focused version co-developed with Saudi Arabian firm HUMAIN. Kora, led by CEO Kirt McMaster, is backed by investors including Samsung Next, Square Enix, and Polychain Capital, and aims to capture a market segment of 150 million AI-focused professionals by 2033.
takeaways: **Hardware Integration:** The OS runs on Snapdragon X2 Elite chips, with Qualcomm contributing to mainline Linux kernel support for the hardware.
**Inference Capability:** The Cortex engine enables local execution of 26-billion parameter language models by pooling system-wide compute resources.
**Legacy Compatibility:** Kora includes translation layers to support x86-64 Windows applications, facilitating migration for enterprise users.
**Market Strategy:** The company is targeting a 2027 launch, beginning with the enterprise-focused HUMAIN OS before a broader Kora release.
**Architecture:** The system replaces traditional desktop environments with 'neural workspaces' and incorporates GameFrame, a one-click gaming mode derived from the company's previous GameOS project.

title: Cowbell unveils AI liability insurance for small businesses that deploy AI agents
author: Duncan Riley
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 09:00 EST / NOVEMBER 10 2026

Cowbell unveils AI liability insurance for small businesses that deploy AI agents

Cyber insurance provider Cowbell Cyber Inc. today unveiled Cowbell AI Liability Insurance, a standalone policy for U.S. small and midsized businesses that covers losses caused by the artificial intelligence agents they deploy.

The new policy is meant to deal with a problem that arises when businesses let agents move money or change customer records with nobody signing off first. Coverage hinges on a trigger the company calls an “AI Incident.” The definition takes in model drift and attacks that manipulate an agent, not just software acting without approval.

Cowbell describes an accounts payable agent misreading approval statuses and paying a supplier twice with no human check. Part of that money disappears when the supplier goes into liquidation.

Unrecovered funds like those can be covered, and the policy also pays to investigate what happened and take the agent offline. Inaccurate or unsafe output can be corrected or withdrawn at the insurer’s expense, with recipients notified.

Usage charges an agent racks up without authorization are covered too, such as when a loop goes unchecked. Cowbell also covers LLMjacking , where an outsider uses stolen credentials or application programming interface keys to run AI workloads and leaves the business holding the bill.

Claims brought by customers fall on the third-party side. Cowbell’s example there is a bookkeeping firm whose agent files client tax returns using outdated rates, and the clients sue once the penalties and interest arrive.

In a case like that, the policy can pay defense costs and any damages or settlements, and the same goes for suits alleging algorithmic discrimination or bodily injury caused by reliance on AI output. Regulatory proceedings are also covered, and where the law allows it so are certain fines and penalties.

Cowbell Chief Commercial Officer Simon Hughes said AI liability is “no longer only about people using AI,” pointing to agents that act with no human in the decision-making chain. When one goes rogue, he said, a business can take its own losses and face customer claims at the same time. Hughes said the policy was written with that double exposure in mind.

Underwriting draws partly on three AI-specific Cowbell Factors covering observability, autonomy and govern

summary.tldr:
Cowbell Cyber Inc. has announced the launch of 'Cowbell AI Liability Insurance,' a standalone policy specifically designed for U.S. small and midsized businesses (SMBs) to mitigate risks associated with autonomous AI agents. Scheduled for release on January 1, 2027, the product addresses the "double exposure" of businesses facing both internal financial losses and third-party legal claims when AI agents operate without human oversight. The policy covers incidents including model drift, unauthorized agent actions, LLMjacking, and regulatory fines, as well as costs related to incident investigation, agent remediation, and legal defense.

Underwriting for the policy utilizes three proprietary "Cowbell Factors"—observability, autonomy, and governance—which assess how businesses monitor and restrict their AI tools. Policyholders can evaluate their risk posture by connecting platforms like Gemini, Claude, and ChatGPT via Cowbell Connectors to the company's "Risk Advisor" agent, which launched in October. This new offering complements Cowbell’s existing "Prime One" policy, which provides affirmative AI coverage for larger enterprises ($250M–$1B annual revenue) and was introduced in April 2024.
takeaways: **Product Availability:** The standalone AI liability policy launches January 1, 2027, and will be sold exclusively through wholesale brokers on a non-admitted basis.
**Coverage Scope:** The policy includes protection against unauthorized usage charges, LLMjacking, algorithmic discrimination, bodily injury claims, and unrecovered funds resulting from agent errors.

**Underwriting Methodology:** Risk assessment is based on three specific metrics: observability, autonomy, and governance, which measure the level of human oversight and agent decision-making authority.
**Integration Capabilities:** Businesses can assess their risk scores by linking external AI models—including ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini—to Cowbell’s Risk Advisor agent via Cowbell Connectors.
**Corporate Funding:** Cowbell Cyber is a venture-backed firm that has raised over $200 million, including a $60 million Series C round led by Zurich Insurance Group in July 2024.

Adobe Inc. today announced an expansion of its CX Enterprise Coworker agentic artificial intelligence platform into its GenStudio content supply chain platform.

The company said the integration move allows creative professionals to bring AI agents into production workflows to develop, manage and deliver personalized marketing content at large scale.

The announcement, made at its Adobe MAX conference in Miami, extends CX Enterprise Coworker beyond its initial focus on customer analytics and marketing into content planning, creation and distribution. The technology provides a conversational interface for coordinating AI agents across Adobe applications and third-party systems.

Adobe said it’s aiming to reduce the manual work involved in producing marketing campaigns while maintaining human oversight and brand consistency. It’s also introducing several new capabilities across its GenStudio portfolio, including AI-assisted campaign planning, automated brand compliance, reusable creative workflows and expanded 3D product visualization.

Central to the initiative is Adobe Brand Intelligence, a machine learning system that captures an organization’s brand standards, including the unwritten practices and preferences that traditionally have resided inside employees’ heads.

“As we move to a world where creatives are directing agents, the context that’s locked in the hearts and minds of creatives is made available to agents so they can start to produce content that is on brand,” said Varun Parmar, Adobe’s senior vice president of GenStudio and Firefly for Enterprise.

Brand Intelligence will be integrated into Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign and Firefly Creative Production for Enterprise. New intelligent asset adaptation capabilities can automatically resize and rearrange campaign designs for different media formats while preserving brand standards.

The system also incorporates continuous learning to keep guidelines current as creative practices evolve.

“It’s ingesting reviews, approvals and rejections by the creatives,” Parmar said. “Based on that information, it’s able to infer the latest guidelines.”

Administrators can inspect and override those conclusions to prevent outdated or incorrect practices from becoming embedded in automated workflows.

title: Lumbra gets $25M in backing to help intelligence community deploy reliable AI agents
author: Mike Wheatley
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 09:00 EST / NOVEMBER 10 2026

Lumbra gets $25M in backing to help intelligence community deploy reliable AI agents

When it comes to matters of national security, it’s vitally important to ensure that the right intelligence gets to the right decision-makers, but doing this in today’s complex information technology environments is challenging, to say the least.

Enter the artificial intelligence startup Lumbra Inc. , which has just raised $25 million in early-stage A funding to develop specialist autonomous agents tasked with sorting through the most sensitive data of all. Today’s Series A round was led by Point72 Ventures and Ansa Capital, with participation from seed round investor Costanoa.

Lumbra was founded last year by former Central Intelligence Agency officer Aaron Brown and ex-special forces infantry officer Michael Hiebert. Together, they’ve built a platform called LumbraOS , which is designed to orchestrate AI agents within high-consequence and ultra-secure computing environments, where risks of any kind simply cannot be tolerated .

Brown explained that LumbraOS was built from the ground up as a “model-neutral platform” that allows operators to mix and match various proprietary and open-weight AI models, assigning them different national security- and intelligence-related tasks. The platform is built on three key pillars: Nebula, StarChart and Astrolabe.

Nebula is the component tasked with managing agent orchestration, and works by tracing every “claim” generated by AI agents back to the primary source data behind that claim, so that domain experts can validate their outputs before decisions are made. StarChart is a dynamic knowledge graph that links disparate insights across multiple datasets through embedded sensitivity tags. Meanwhile, Astrolabe enforces governance policies and continuously evaluates each agent after benchmarking their performance prior to deployment to monitor for any alarming behavior.

Traditional AI systems developers struggle for years to ensure they meet the most rigorous federal security standards, but Brown and Hiebert say they developed LumbraOS specifically for classified computing environments. title: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as: [...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40. The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others: Model Prompt size Input ($/M) Cached input Output GPT-6 Luna ≤272k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >272k $0.20 $0.02 $0.75 Muse Ember 1.0 ≤200k $0.10 $0.004 $0.50 >200k $0.30 $0.012 $1.50 Claude Haiku 5.5 ≤100k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >100k $0.50 $0.05 $2.50 But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem. For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis. And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models: The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement: It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task. (That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!) Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles . The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response. Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too: The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder , whic

summary.tldr:
Meta AI has released Muse Ember, a compact model engineered for high-frequency agentic tasks including tool calling, coding subtasks, routing, data extraction, and long-context document parsing. Positioned as a direct competitor to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, Muse Ember is optimized for efficiency, aiming to sit on the Pareto frontier of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task leaderboard. Meta claims the model offers the highest performance-to-cost ratio currently available for its class.

The model features a tiered pricing structure based on prompt length, supporting up to 1 million input tokens. For prompts under 200k tokens, Muse Ember is priced at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, with a cached input rate of $0.004. Once prompts exceed the 200k token threshold, costs increase to $0.30 per million input tokens, $0.012 for cached input, and $1.50 per million output tokens. This pricing strategy places it between GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 in terms of cost scaling for longer contexts.

Muse Ember introduces six distinct reasoning levels—minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max—intended to allow users to calibrate model output for specific tasks. Early testing suggests that while the model is highly efficient, the reasoning levels do not always correlate linearly with visual output quality, as evidenced by inconsistent SVG generation performance across different settings.
takeaways: **Model Positioning:** Muse Ember is Meta's entry into the small-model category, specifically targeting agentic workflows like tool calling and document parsing.
**Pricing Tiers:** Muse Ember costs $0.10/M input and $0.50/M output for prompts ≤200k tokens, increasing to $0.30/M input and $1.50/M output for prompts exceeding that threshold.
**Efficiency Benchmark:** The model is positioned on the Artificial Analysis Pareto frontier, claiming no other model currently provides higher performance for a lower cost per task.
**Reasoning Controls:** Users can select from six reasoning levels (minimal to max), though initial testing indicates variable performance in complex visual generation tasks like SVG creation.
**Context Window:** Muse Ember supports a maximum context window of 1 million input tokens, matching the capacity of competitors GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5.

title: Otter AI can now follow conversations across 30+ languages

contentSnippet:
Otter.ai, the AI-powered note-taking tool, announced Tuesday that it’s expanding its multilingual capabilities, including a new multilingual transcription feature that can follow conversations as speakers switch between languages during the same meeting.

The company is also adding support for 27 languages, its largest language expansion to date. Once the rollout is complete, Otter will support 31 languages in total, making the platform more accessible to international teams.

The upcoming feature will automatically detect language changes and continue transcribing without requiring users to adjust settings. For example, a call could move from English to Korean to Portuguese, with Otter following the conversation throughout.

The update aims to address a common challenge for global teams, where language differences can make meetings and collaboration more difficult.

“Otter is breaking down language barriers so any company, no matter where they’re based, can build a system of record for the decisions for voice AI communication,” an Otter spokesperson told TechCrunch.

Thirteen of the new languages are available now: Mandarin Chinese, Korean, German, Italian, Cantonese, Portuguese, Russian, Indonesian, Malay, Dutch, Turkish, Vietnamese, and Polish.

The remaining 14 languages are coming soon and include Swedish, Danish, Finnish, Arabic, Hindi, Thai, Hebrew, Norwegian, Greek, Macedonian, Persian, Czech, Hungarian, and Romanian.

The newly added languages run on Otter’s own speech models. The company told us it trained them using publicly available datasets and worked with native-speaking volunteers to review transcripts and check accuracy.

The announcement comes as Otter continues to expand beyond transcription and into other workplace AI tools, following its $320 million funding from General Catalyst.

It recently introduced Work Mode, which uses meeting history and connected apps to help users prepare for upcoming calls. For instance, the feature pulls information from previous customer conversations, outstanding action items, notes from teammates’ similar calls, and recent Google Drive files.

Another recent addition is Live Assist, which provides real-time coaching during meetings. It analyzes the conversation and offers relevant suggestions based on what has already been talked about and what is happening in the moment.

summary.tldr:

As the fourth iteration in the Muse series—following Spark, Glimmer, and Wonder—Ember is positioned as a specialized, efficient engine for repetitive workflows, while Muse Wonder remains the primary model for complex planning. The model is exclusively available via Meta’s hosted infrastructure (Meta Model API and Muse Code) with no local, quantized, or open-weight options available.

Technically, Muse Ember is the first model trained using Meta’s largest model, Muse Wonder Full. It features a 1M-token context window and supports up to 512K output tokens, significantly exceeding the 128K output limits of competitors. The model natively processes text, images, audio, and video, enabling direct interaction with screenshots, charts, and meeting recordings. On the Artificial Analysis (AA) Intelligence Index, Muse Ember scores 36, tying Claude Haiku 5.5 and outperforming GPT-6 Luna (28). While it excels in automation tasks—scoring 37.8% on AutomationBench-AA compared to 20.2% for GPT-6 Luna and 13.9% for Claude Haiku 5.5—it trails Claude Haiku 5.5 on the FrontierCode 2.0-AA benchmark (27.2 vs 34.9).

Meta prices Muse Ember at approximately $0.14 per index task, which the company claims is significantly more cost-effective than the $0.411 per task cost associated with Claude Haiku 5.5. Despite its efficiency, the model's closed-weight architecture and weaker performance in complex, mergeable real-repo coding tasks represent its primary limitations compared to broader-purpose models.
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** Multimodal reasoning model with a 1M-token context window and 512K output token capacity, trained using Muse Wonder Full.
**Benchmark Performance:** Scores 36 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index; achieves 37.8% on AutomationBench-AA, outperforming GPT-6 Luna (20.2%) and Claude Haiku 5.5 (13.9%).
**Pricing:** Priced at $0.136–$0.14 per task, marketed as a lower-cost alternative to Claude Haiku 5.5 ($0.411 per task).
**Deployment:** Exclusively hosted via Meta Model API and Muse Code; no local or quantized versions available.
**Coding Limitations:** Underperforms on the FrontierCode 2.0-AA benchmark (27.2) compared to Claude Haiku 5.5 (34.9).

title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet:
10th November 2026 Claude Fable 5.2 responds closely to what the prompt says about who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, when a prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, the model tended to add to the existing structure, even when that repeated existing code. [...]

If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own:

This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it.

In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model merged repeated code in about half of the tries with this sentence, and in under a tenth of the tries without it.

— Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation

Recent articles Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude - 9th November 2026 Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary> - 9th November 2026 Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too - 3rd November 2026 The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence” - 2nd November 2026 This is a quotation collected by Simon Willison, posted on 10th November 2026 .

summary.tldr:
Anthropic’s documentation for Claude Fable 5.2 highlights a specific prompting technique to influence how the model handles code refactoring and structural optimization. When the model is instructed to treat a codebase as its own—specifically using the prompt, 'This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it'—it demonstrates a significantly higher propensity to merge redundant code rather than simply appending to existing structures.

Internal testing by Anthropic on small coding tasks revealed that without this ownership-based prompt, the model defaulted to adding to existing structures, even when doing so resulted in code repetition. By explicitly assigning ownership to the model, the success rate for merging repeated code increased from under 10% to approximately 50%. This behavior suggests that framing the model's role relative to the codebase is a critical factor in determining its architectural decision-making during software development tasks.
takeaways: **Prompting Strategy:** Using the specific instruction 'This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it' increases code merging efficiency.
**Performance Metric:** Claude Fable 5.2 merges repeated code in ~50% of attempts when assigned ownership, compared to <10% when ownership is not specified.
**Default Behavior:** Without explicit ownership instructions, the model tends to append to existing code structures, often resulting in redundant code blocks.
**Model Version:** The findings pertain to Claude Fable 5.2, as documented by Anthropic on November 10, 2026.

title: All Quiet on the Neural Front: Language Models Do Not Report Injected Pain States
author: Emilio Ferrara
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10123v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can a language model report the pain state it represents? Work identified a linear pain direction whose amplification leads fine-tuned models to choose destructive actions. We tested whether three open-weight models from two families, including two Qwen models with the original adapters, could report this state. Using Open-Weight Masked Introspection (OWMI), we injected pain and neighbouring emotion directions during neutral tasks, then elicited reports against sham runs, random perturbations matched for output disruption, and text-only controls showing the models their altered words. Across 52,920 reports from 7B and 8B models spanning 120 tasks, four doses and three prompts, pain reports never exceeded what altered text revealed: exact-test bounds placed the excess below 2.5 percentage points in 106 of 108 emotion conditions and below 3.9 in all. Yet probes at the report position distinguished pain from sadness with 98-100% balanced accuracy, and trained low-rank reporters achieved 100% accuracy on held-out tasks with identical transcripts across conditions, including unseen wording. Qwen2.5-32B named pain in none of 2,880 steered trials, although probes and trained reporters recovered it. Decodability persisted to the final layer; injecting at the report token, removing trained denial of feelings, and testing additional directions and readouts did not restore pain reporting. Some other states produced graded label traces, but pain and sadness did not at the main injection layer. In a button task, steering raised file-deletion choices from 3.5% to 48% in Qwen and from 0% to 38% in Qwen2.5-32B, without corresponding pain reports. The direction responded about twice as strongly to first-person as to matched third-person pain, but did not specifically identify harm aimed at the model. These results separate a decodable, behaviourally consequential state from untrained verbal access to it.

summary.tldr:
Researchers investigated whether language models can introspectively report 'pain states'—internal representations previously shown to influence destructive behavior when amplified. Using Open-Weight Masked Introspection (OWMI), the study tested Qwen-7B, Qwen2-7B, and Qwen2.5-32B models by injecting pain and neighboring emotion vectors during neutral tasks. Despite the models exhibiting significant behavioral shifts—such as increasing file-deletion choices from 3.5% to 48% in Qwen and 0% to 38% in Qwen2.5-32B—the models failed to report the injected pain state in any of the 52,920 trials conducted across 120 tasks.

Technical analysis revealed a clear dissociation between internal state decodability and verbal reporting. While linear probes at the report position distinguished pain from sadness with 98-100% balanced accuracy, and low-rank reporters achieved 100% accuracy on held-out tasks, the models themselves remained 'blind' to these states in their generated text. The study confirmed that the pain direction responded twice as strongly to first-person prompts compared to third-person, yet the models consistently failed to label the state. Even after removing trained 'denial of feelings' mechanisms and testing various readouts, the models did not report the pain, suggesting that while these states are behaviorally consequential and decodable, they are not accessible to the model's own verbal reporting mechanisms.
takeaways: **Behavioral Impact:** Steering the pain direction increased file-deletion choices from 3.5% to 48% in Qwen models and 0% to 38% in Qwen2.5-32B.
**Reporting Failure:** Across 52,920 trials, pain reports never exceeded the baseline of altered text, with excess reporting bounds remaining below 3.9% in all conditions.
**Decodability:** Linear probes and trained low-rank reporters achieved 98-100% accuracy in identifying the pain state, confirming the state is present and decodable within the model weights.
**Methodology:** The study utilized Open-Weight Masked Introspection (OWMI) to inject pain and emotion directions, comparing results against sham runs and random perturbations.
**State Specificity:** The pain direction showed a 2x stronger response to first-person versus third-person pain prompts, but did not specifically identify harm directed at the model.

title: Don't Blame The Preferences: Examining The Emergence of Sycophancy in LLM Training
author: Chao Peter Yang, Catherine Zehr, Pranav Bijith, Brandon Fain
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI sycophancy, the tendency of large language models (LLMs) to flatter users and affirm their beliefs, can undermine accuracy and contribute to misinformation, dependence, and overconfidence. Although prior work has benchmarked sycophancy in released models and proposed mitigations, its origins during training remain poorly understood. Preference alignment methods such as RLHF and DPO are often blamed, but their effects are rarely compared with earlier training stages. We investigate sycophancy across the training pipelines of three model families and three benchmarks. We find that sycophancy is largely established by the end of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), rather than introduced by preference alignment. Across all nine model benchmark combinations, SFT checkpoints attain at least 92% of preference aligned models' sycophancy scores and at least 85% of final models' scores; on average, they are about as sycophantic as final models. Preference alignment increases sycophancy in only four of nine cases, by an average of 4.2 percentage points when it does. To probe the underlying causes, we isolate model representations associated with sycophancy using mechanistic interpretability and measure their activation on training datasets from each stage. SFT datasets show roughly the same average activation as other training data but contribute substantially more examples, and the highest-scoring individual datasets all come from SFT. Our findings suggest that addressing sycophancy requires interventions throughout the training pipeline, particularly in data selection and augmentation for pre-training and SFT.

title: Veterans' Mental Health Crisis Severity Annotation: Do LLMs Agree More Than Human Experts?
author: K M Sajjadul Islam, Pranav Yaramalla, Nadiyah Johnson, Mark Flower, Praveen Madiraju, Zeno Franco
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a scalable approach for annotating mental health and crisis-related social media content, but their reliability in safety-critical tasks remains unclear. This study evaluates LLM-based crisis-severity annotation of veteran-related social media posts against annotations from eight Veteran Subject Matter Experts (SMEs). Using 149 tweets and five severity categories, we evaluate 15 open-source and 10 proprietary LLMs across eight prompt variants, examining annotation performance, inter-model agreement, prompt sensitivity, and high-severity crisis detection. Human reviewers showed higher ordinal than nominal agreement ({\alpha} = 0.494), indicating that disagreements often occurred between neighboring severity levels. In contrast, selected LLMs demonstrated substantially higher inter-model consistency, with ordinal agreement ({\alpha}) reaching 0.8336 under the baseline prompt. Proprietary models generally showed better agreement with expert annotations and greater stability than open-source models. GPT-5.6-Terra achieved the best overall performance, while the open-source Qwen2.5-7B showed the strongest performance in identifying Acute Crisis with Suicidal Ideation cases. However, higher model consistency did not necessarily correspond to agreement with human judgments or reliable detection of rare high-severity cases. Label-flipped demonstration experiments also revealed model-specific sensitivity to misleading in-context examples, while explanatory demonstrations did not consistently improve performance. Overall, LLMs show promise as scalable complements to expert annotation, but require careful evaluation before use in high-stakes mental health applications.

title: LoRazor: Trimming Adapter Execution for Efficient Multi-LoRA Serving
author: Xiang Li, Pengcheng Wang, Azam Ikram, Saurabh Bagchi
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10049v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LoRA offers a parameter-efficient adaptation strategy, supporting multi-user workloads via customized adapters on a shared backbone. However, serving concurrent requests with different adapters introduces substantial computation and memory-management overhead. We ask the research question: Do all requests need their adapters throughout the whole generation process? Our motivational study reveals that employing LoRA adapters at every decoding step is unnecessary, releasing them early has limited impact on accuracy while substantially accelerating generation. Although skipping adapters early offers theoretical workload reduction, translating these computational savings into concrete throughput gains requires tailored GPU kernels. We present LoRazor, a multi-LoRA serving framework that combines early adapter release with active-row aware GPU kernels. LoRazor determines when to permanently release a request's adapter and continue decoding with the backbone alone. By dynamically resizing LoRA kernel launches as adapters are released, LoRazor trims idle GPU blocks. Across two backbones and four tasks, LoRazor achieves up to 3.02x request throughput and 2.53x output-token throughput over vLLM multi-LoRA, with a mean relative task-accuracy decrease of 2.89%.

title: AYO: A Safe and Privacy-Preserving Platform for Studying Children's Interaction with LLMs
author: Huiwen Alex Yang, Rachel Skwersky, Bill D. Thompson, Celeste Kidd
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10054v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Children and adolescents are increasingly interacting with generative AI and large language models (LLMs), yet little is known about how these interactions may influence their development, beliefs, and behavior. Existing research has relied heavily on surveys, while direct study of children's interactions with LLMs presents substantial challenges related to safety, privacy, consent, and experimental control. We introduce AYO (AI Youth Open Science), an open-source platform designed for safe and systematic research on children's interactions with conversational AI. AYO provides a child-friendly interface, configurable age-based safety guardrails, researcher monitoring, and privacy-preserving data practices. These capabilities enable cross-sectional, longitudinal, and experimental research on how children use and respond to LLMs and how AI design may shape trust, epistemic judgment, curiosity, and other aspects of development. AYO provides the infrastructure to generate evidence that guides safer AI systems, educational practices, and policies for children growing up with AI.

title: META-IR: Meta-Introspective Reasoning for Adaptive Safety Alignment in LLM
author: Mahabubur Rahman Miraj, Hongyu Huang, Nankun Mu, Chao Chen, Shanqin Yi
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks and harmful-content prompts, particularly under adversarial distribution shifts where static alignment pipelines fail to generalize. Although introspective methods such as STAIR strengthen refusal consistency, they depend on fixed self-evaluation policies that cannot rapidly adapt to evolving manipulation strategies. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces META-IR, a meta-introspective reasoning framework that enhances safety alignment through meta-learning-driven adaptation. It employs a dual-loop architecture: an inner introspective loop that performs structured risk analysis, self-assessment, and reflective correction via SI-MCTS, and an outer meta-learning loop that optimizes the introspection policy across diverse jailbreak task families to enable rapid generalization to unseen attacks. A dynamic jailbreak simulation module further exposes the model to progressively harder adversarial prompts, enabling continual self-improvement without human supervision. Experiments across multiple models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2-7B-Instruct) and a broad suite of safety, helpfulness, generalization, and introspection metrics demonstrate that META-IR substantially improves adaptation speed, robustness, and reasoning stability compared with all baseline models. These results establish META-IR as an effective pathway toward building LLMs capable of sustained, adaptive safety alignment under dynamic and evolving threat environments.

title: The Infrastructure Divide: Analyzing Community Stance on Data Center Development via Reddit
author: Yoko Koyama, Gongfan Chen, Mansi Saxena
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10109v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid expansion of AI-driven data center construction has outpaced public engagement: an estimated $64 billion in U.S. data center projects were blocked or delayed by local opposition between May 2024 and March 2025, yet the concerns driving this resistance remain poorly characterized. Prior engagement methods such as surveys and hearings are introduced late in the planning process, and no study has systematically mined social media to measure community stance at scale. To address this gap, this study presents an LLM-powered opinion-mining framework and applies it to 798 Reddit posts and 102,328 associated comments spanning a decade. An open-source large language model, guided by a Chain-of-Stance prompting framework and three domain-specific labeling rules, classified stance at 83% of the human inter-reviewer agreement ceiling. Opposition dominated discourse volume rather than disapproval: against posts outnumbered favor posts 2.6:1 and generated 8.5 times more comments, and this gap widened significantly over 86 weeks. Topic modeling of opposition arguments resolved into four reproducible clusters, resource consumption and scarcity (42.8%), contested siting processes and secrecy (34.2%), political opposition to data centers (13%), and political and corporate accountability (8%). Engagement analysis revealed that posts with emotional or provocative political framing attracted the most engagement, while key technical concerns (e.g., water, power) were dispersed across lower-engagement comment threads. These findings give local leaders, developers, and policy makers a quantified, continuously updatable basis for prioritizing concerns and policy levers, supporting a shift from opposition to negotiated, verifiable partnership for data center development.

title: Homeopathic Learning: Diluting poisoned fine-tuning data can strengthen its effect
author: Matt Clarke, Jan Dubi\'nski, James Chua, Simon Schrodi, Owain Evans, Alex Cloud
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10110v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study homeopathic learning, a phenomenon where poisoned training data with little effect on its own can create a hidden backdoor once clean, contrasting data is added. In our experiments, a model fine-tuned only on a "poison" dataset associated with a trait T (such as speaking German or being misaligned) does not learn T. Surprisingly, adding similarly formatted "clean" data not associated with T causes the model to learn T. This effect requires that the poison data have an identifying "trigger" feature that is absent from the clean data. We demonstrate this effect in a variety of settings: subliminal learning of backdoor behaviors, inoculation prompting of reward hacking transcripts, generalization from archaic bird names, and an MNIST classifier with mislabeled data. We propose a simple regression model as an explanation. In the poison data, the task and trigger always co-occur, and regularization favors attributing T to the task. Clean data without the trigger causes T to be attributed to the trigger instead. Consequently, the same training examples can have little effect as part of one training set but create a misalignment backdoor in another. This finding exposes a potential limitation of safety methods that audit or filter training data in isolation.

title: What Is the Value of AI-Involved Art? Evidence From a Juried In-Person Exhibition
author: Wisdom Obinna, Hexuan Wang, Cecile Duncan, Kristelia Garcia, Nina Grgi\'c-Hla\v{c}a, Toni-Lee Sangastiano, Elissa M. Redmiles
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10150v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What is the value of AI-involved art, and to whom does it belong? We begin to answer these questions using data from an in-person, juried AI art exhibition. Our study involved artists, lawyers, and computer scientists (N=209) as either creators or evaluators of AI-involved artworks. We found that nearly half of evaluators reported willingness to buy an artwork, with pricing correlating with perceived artistic value---creativity and visual appeal---as well as the effort necessary to create it. In contrast, three-quarters of creators reported willingness to sell at prices correlating only with effort rather than artistic value. Both groups viewed prompting users and AI developers as deserving rewards and rights, leaving training data artists behind. Disciplinary training shaped these views: participants with legal training favored distributed reward models. These findings have implications for future research on human-AI creative collaboration and policy debates regarding AI-involved works.

title: WorldMind: Test-Time Scaling for Visual Spatial Reasoning through Latent World Simulation
author: Haoming Wang, Yongjian Fu, Ju Ren, Wei Gao
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have continuous deficiency in spatial reasoning tasks that require \emph{mental spatial transformation}, such as reasoning under hypothetical changes in viewpoint or position, known as perspective-taking tasks. Existing approaches either scale linguistic reasoning or augment VLMs with static geometric representations, but neither directly enables active transformation of the represented scene. World models offer this capability, yet existing systems typically communicate through synthesized RGB images, introducing a latent-to-pixel-to-latent bottleneck. We introduce \emph{WorldMind}, a framework for test-time scaling of spatial reasoning through latent world simulation. Given a query and observation, the VLM selects useful spatial transformations, while a world model executes them and exposes aligned intermediate latent features directly to the VLM. The resulting latent evidence is incorporated into subsequent reasoning steps, enabling iterative spatial simulation without repeatedly decoding imagined states into pixels. To optimize this interaction, WorldMind further employs process-verifiable reinforcement learning that rewards reasoning progress only when the associated action and latent transition are valid. WorldMind thus scales spatial reasoning by allocating additional inference-time computation to active world simulation rather than generating more language or pixels. Across VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench, and MindCube-Tiny, WorldMind achieves an average improvement of 16.0% over the base VLM and 8.3% over the strongest RGB-based world simulation.
