title: DisMUSE: An Efficient Distributed Singular-Spectrum-Based Optimization Approach with Theoretical Convergence Guarantee
author: Zhen Qin, Zhiyao Zhang, Yingbin Liang, Jia Liu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10212v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years, singular-spectrum-based optimizers have attracted increasing attention due to their ability to preserve the matrix structure of neural network gradients, thereby enabling geometry-aware optimization. However, most singular-spectrum-based (SSB) approaches remain centralized, limiting their use in distributed learning infrastructures that exploit massive parallelism. Distributed SSB optimization is still at an early stage, with open questions about convergence guarantees and communication efficiency. To fill this gap, we propose the Distributed Momentum-based Spectral Estimator (DisMUSE), an efficient distributed SSB optimization framework for both data-center and federated settings. Using Muon-style exact orthogonalized momentum as the spectral update, DisMUSE integrates a recursive variance-reduced momentum estimator and achieves an $O((KT)^{-1/3})$ convergence rate, where $K$ and $T$ denote the number of nodes and local iterations per node, respectively. This rate matches the best-known rates for variance-reduced nonconvex distributed optimization. Building on this variance-reduced framework, we study two extensions. First, our DisMUSE method with finite Newton-Schulz (NS) iterations preserves the same convergence order under a uniform normalized support-spectrum condition, up to a multiplicative factor. Second, we develop a communication-efficient variant based on low-rank (LR) momentum transmission and quantify the error it introduces to the stationarity bound, characterizing the trade-off between accuracy and communication cost.

title: Rethinking How to Leverage Cheap Physics for Data-Efficient Neural Operators
author: Shuo Zhang, Senwei Liang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10217v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural operators learn mappings from PDE inputs, such as initial conditions and coefficient fields, to the corresponding solutions. Once trained, they can rapidly predict solutions for new inputs. However, obtaining input-solution pairs for supervised training often requires expensive numerical simulations, whereas PDE inputs and governing equations provide inexpensive physical information. This raises a question: how can cheap physical information reduce the need for labeled solutions? A natural approach is to use physics to select inputs for labeling, but our acquisition experiments show no consistent advantage over random sampling. This observation motivates exploring an alternative: using cheap physics to improve neural operator initialization before supervised training. We propose Physics-Informed Initialization (PI-Init), a simple yet effective method that pretrains neural operators on unlabeled inputs using physics-informed losses and retains the learned parameters for supervised fine-tuning on the labeled dataset. A linearized analysis shows that pretraining can improve downstream prediction accuracy by reducing initialization errors that limited labeled data cannot effectively correct. Experiments across diverse PDE benchmarks and neural operator architectures demonstrate improvements in predictive accuracy, out-of-distribution generalization, and label efficiency. Representative results show error reductions of up to 62.7% at the same label budget and comparable or better accuracy with 90% fewer labels, relative to supervised-only training.

title: Lower-Level Agnostic Bilevel Optimization
author: Peiwen Qiu, Prashant Khanduri, Jia Liu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.10223v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bilevel optimization is a fundamental framework for machine learning problems, where an upper-level (UL) objective depends on the solution of a nested lower-level (LL) problem. Existing bilevel algorithms typically assume that the LL objective is available for evaluation, differentiation, or unrolling. However, this assumption can fail when the LL response is produced by a black-box solver, simulator, adversary, or learned predictor. In this paper, we study LL agnostic bilevel optimization, where the UL learner has access only to an approximate LL solution $\bar{\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{x})$ and cannot query the LL objective, its gradients, Hessian/Jacobian information, or the procedure that generates the LL response. We propose LeGo-BiO, a coordinate-wise pseudo-hypergradient method that estimates the missing Jacobian $\nabla _{\mathbf{x}}\bar{\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{x})$ using finite differences of $\bar{\mathbf{y}}(\cdot)$. For each UL coordinate, LeGo-BiO constructs a decision vector subject to 1-sparse updates, thereby isolating the corresponding Jacobian column needed in the UL gradient computation. This avoids the directional-projection limitation of full-parameter response differences and, unlike derivative-free/zeroth-order approximations of the entire UL gradient, preserves the available first-order gradient information with respect to the UL variables for more accurate UL gradient evaluation. We establish convergence guarantees for LeGo-BiO in both deterministic and stochastic settings under an LL error-bound/Polyak-Lojasiewicz-type condition, without requiring LL strong convexity. Our bounds yield an $O(T^{-1})$ rate in the deterministic setting and an $O(T^{-1/2})$ rate in the stochastic setting when the LL approximation error decreases geometrically. Experiments demonstrate competitive performance of LeGo-BiO despite being agnostic to the LL objective.

title: Yonkers Rises
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: Tool: Yonkers Rises I realized I didn't know where Yonkers was, so I looked it up on Google Maps and then, to help embed its location and shape in my head (and to try out Claude Fable 5.2's 3D modeling and animation skills), I prompted Fable 5.2 Medium to: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and átomos around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data It correctly deduced that "átomos" was a mobile keyboard typo for "stomps": Tags: three-js , llms , ai , generative-ai , claude-mythos-fable

summary.tldr:
Simon Willison has demonstrated the 3D modeling and animation capabilities of the Claude Fable 5.2 Medium model through a project titled 'Yonkers Rises.' The project features an animated 3D diorama of New York City where a giant mech, shaped from the Yonkers boundary, rises from the ground and traverses Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, and the Bronx. The animation utilizes OpenStreetMap data to render the geography and includes a dynamic stomp counter and mech height readout.

The implementation uses Three.js to render the scene, which begins with a stand-up sequence followed by a looping walking tour. The model successfully interpreted the user's typo 'átomos' as 'stomps' and generated the necessary code to simulate building destruction upon footfall and status updates based on whether the mech is traversing land or water.
takeaways: **Model Capability:** Claude Fable 5.2 Medium demonstrated the ability to generate functional Three.js animation code from natural language prompts.
**Data Integration:** The project utilizes OpenStreetMap mapping data to define the geographical boundaries and layout of the New York City boroughs.
**Dynamic Features:** The animation includes real-time tracking elements such as a stomp counter, a mech height readout, and state-dependent status lines for land versus water movement.
**Error Correction:** The model correctly inferred the user's intent despite a mobile keyboard typo, interpreting 'átomos' as 'stomps' within the context of the prompt.

title: Meta introduces Muse Ember to power cost-efficient AI agents
author: Maria Deutscher
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 20:38 EST / NOVEMBER 09 2026

Meta introduces Muse Ember to power cost-efficient AI agents

Meta Platforms Inc. today introduced Muse Ember, an entry-level artificial intelligence model that costs significantly less than the competition.

Notably, it’s the first AI that the company trained using Muse Wonder. The latter algorithm is the Facebook parent’s flagship large language model. Meta didn’t specify which part of the workflow it automated with Muse Wonder.

One possibility is that the company used it to perform post-training, the task of honing a model’s capabilities by training it on additional data. Thinking Machines Labs Inc. recently demonstrated that even a relatively small LLM can run post-training runs end-to-end. Anthropic PBC, for its part, last week revealed that its AI models could soon gain the ability to significantly accelerate machine learning research.

Applications often use frontier LLMs such as Muse Wonder as part of AI ensembles. When a user enters a request, the frontier LLM splits it into smaller tasks and assigns them to agents powered by a lower-cost model. Meta says Muse Ember is specifically optimized to play the latter role.

The company evaluated the model using the Artificial Analysis Index, which aggregates nine AI benchmarks spanning use cases such as coding and financial analysis. Meta says that Muse Ember matched the score of Anthropic’s entry-level Claude Haiku 5.5 model at about a third the price. It also outperformed OpenAI Group PBC’s comparable GPT-6 Luna algorithm.

The same internal evaluation saw Meta test Muse Ember and the two rival models across nine other benchmarks. All three algorithms were in “max” mode, which means they used the maximum amount of hardware at their disposal instead of prioritizing cost-efficiency. Muse Ember outperformed Haiku and Luna across seven of the benchmarks.

The area where the model appears to have the biggest edge is business task automation. Whereas most of Muse Ember’s benchmark results were only a few percentage points better than those of Haiku and Luna, it clocked a 17% lead on AutomationBench-AA. It’s a collection of 657 tasks that span popular cloud applications such as Gmail and Salesforce.

Muse Ember has a context window of 1 million tokens, which enables it to ingest lengthy business documents. Users can also include images, audio and video in their prompts. Th

summary.tldr:
Meta Platforms Inc. has launched Muse Ember, an entry-level AI model designed for cost-efficient agentic workflows. It is the first model developed using Meta’s flagship LLM, Muse Wonder, as a training foundation. Positioned as a specialized component for AI ensembles, Muse Ember is optimized to handle sub-tasks delegated by larger frontier models, specifically targeting business automation and high-volume processing tasks.

Technically, Muse Ember features a 1-million-token context window and supports multimodal inputs, including audio, video, and images, with a maximum output generation capacity of 512,000 tokens. In internal evaluations using the Artificial Analysis Index, Meta reports that Muse Ember matches the performance of Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 at approximately one-third the cost, while outperforming OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna. Notably, in "max" hardware utilization mode, Muse Ember outperformed both competitors in seven out of nine benchmarks, including a 17% lead on the AutomationBench-AA suite, which tests integration across platforms like Gmail and Salesforce.

Access to Muse Ember is provided via Meta’s Model API. Pricing is set at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens. Meta also includes a prompt caching feature that reduces input costs to $0.004 per million tokens for frequently reused prompts.
takeaways: **Performance Benchmarking:** Muse Ember outperformed Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna in 7 out of 9 benchmarks when running in maximum hardware utilization mode.
**Automation Specialization:** The model achieved a 17% performance lead over competitors on AutomationBench-AA, a dataset comprising 657 tasks across cloud applications like Salesforce and Gmail.
**API Pricing:** Standard API pricing is $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output tokens, with a cached prompt rate of $0.004/million input tokens.
**Model Architecture:** Muse Ember supports a 1-million-token context window, multimodal input (text, image, audio, video), and generates responses up to 512,000 tokens in length.
**Training Methodology:** Muse Ember is the first model to be trained using Meta’s flagship Muse Wonder LLM, likely utilizing it for post-training optimization.

title: Anthropic reportedly plans to move forward with IPO plans
author: Marina Temkin
contentSnippet: Posted: 5:27 PM PST · November 9, 2026 Image Credits: Ruhani Kaur/Bloomberg / Getty Images Marina Temkin Anthropic reportedly plans to move forward with IPO plans Launching a major tech IPO would seem risky right now, shortly after one of Nasdaq’s biggest sell-offs and amid revelations that a CEO central to the AI boom had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. But that isn’t deterring Anthropic, which is moving ahead with its listing plans, according to The Wall Street Journal . Anthropic plans to set a valuation range this week and begin trading on Thursday or Friday of next week, the Journal reported. Investors will look to Anthropic’s valuation to gauge the strength of the AI boom. Some institutional investors are now pushing for a valuation below the $1.5 trillion target discussed as recently as last week, a figure that was itself considerably below the $2 trillion floated a few months ago, the report said. OpenAI, Anthropic’s main rival, was reportedly valued at $1.25 trillion last week after the ChatGPT maker raised $11 billion in fresh capital, short of the $20 billion it had initially sought. title: David Ellison says AI could be the ‘biggest creative unlock in modern history’
author: Stevie Bonifield
contentSnippet: During Paramount Skydance’s latest earnings call, CEO David Ellison said “it’s hard to imagine” AI won’t have a bigger impact on the film industry than CGI. In response to a question about the company’s outlook for AI, Ellison said: > “I think when you zoom out and look at production, AI really has the potential to be the biggest creative unlock in modern history. The last time we saw anything close to this was really the, you know, advent of CGI and digital composites in the early 90s. That technology gave birth to amazing stories like Jurassic Park and Terminator 2, and it’s hard to imagine that AI is not going to have a more significant impact than that. And I personally believe that’s going to be an incredible unlock on creativity.” Ellison gave Terminator as an example, describing how it cost $4 million to make, but “if you wanted to make that picture today, shot for shot, it’s $60 to 70 million.” He went on to suggest AI might be able to help with that: “We think these tools will help unlock more original storytelling by being able to make the budgets more digestible to be able to take that amount of risk.” Ellison said AI will “significantly” reshape Paramount Skydance’s business, saying the company has been developing its own AI tools. As a result of those tools, Ellison claims, “content will be easier to produce, projects across the organization will speed up, and how we work will transform.” He emphasized that “all of this makes the value of premium IP and live events more valuable, not less.” Ellison also noted that “in a world of AI slop, we think there will always be a premium for truly hand-crafted storytelling.” He added, “We also continue to believe that artificial intelligence is a tool for artists and will never be a replacement for them.”

summary.tldr:
Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison stated during the company's latest earnings call that artificial intelligence represents the 'biggest creative unlock in modern history,' projecting an impact on the film industry that will exceed the introduction of CGI and digital composites in the 1990s. Ellison framed the technology as a mechanism to reduce production costs and mitigate financial risk, citing the original 1984 'Terminator' film—which cost $4 million to produce—as an example of a project that would require $60 to $70 million to replicate today. By leveraging proprietary AI tools currently under development, the company aims to make production budgets more 'digestible' to facilitate more original storytelling.

Ellison emphasized that while AI will fundamentally transform internal workflows and accelerate project timelines, the company maintains a strategy that positions AI as a tool for artists rather than a replacement. He argued that the proliferation of AI-generated content will increase the market value of 'premium IP' and 'hand-crafted storytelling,' suggesting that high-quality, human-led creative work will command a premium in an environment saturated with automated content.
takeaways: **Cost Benchmarking:** Ellison noted that the original 'Terminator' film cost $4 million to produce, estimating a modern equivalent cost of $60 to $70 million for a shot-for-shot remake.
**Internal Development:** Paramount Skydance is actively developing its own proprietary AI tools to streamline production and accelerate organizational workflows.
**Strategic Positioning:** The company plans to use AI to lower production costs and risk, while simultaneously marketing 'hand-crafted' content as a premium product to differentiate from 'AI slop.'
**Industry Comparison:** Ellison explicitly compared the potential impact of AI to the advent of CGI in the early 1990s, which enabled films like 'Jurassic Park' and 'Terminator 2'.

title: How skills and agents work in AWS Quick
author: Jed Lechner
contentSnippet: If you use AI agents, you’ve probably explained the same task more than once. You might describe how to build your weekly status update, write release notes, manage a project, or create tickets. These are all repeatable tasks that you can encode using AWS Quick through agents and skills. AWS Quick is an AI-powered service for automating tasks, analyzing data, building web applications, and conducting research. You work with it in natural language, and Quick uses AI agents to process your requests against your connected data sources and applications. In this post, we cover how agents, skills, and your data fit together in AWS Quick, and how to build and share skills that work for your team. We also show how the official catalog and custom agents help you put those skills to use. Understanding foundational concepts In this section, we explain the foundational concepts that help you understand AWS Quick in relation to agents, skills, and your data. Figure 1: How a Quick agent follows its instructions, loads the skills a task needs, acts through connectors, and grounds its answers in your data The agent sits at the center of Figure 1. It follows its instructions, loads the skills that a task calls for, takes action through connectors, and grounds its answers in your data: spaces, knowledge bases, datasets, and dashboards. Working with agents An agent in AWS Quick is a configurable AI with its own instructions, knowledge sources (spaces), and connectors, which it uses to answer questions and get work done for you. You can work with an agent in chat, or let it run on its own using a routine . Agents can only reach the resources and services that you can, and you decide what each agent is allowed to do. Quick is the default built-in agent that every user has access to. It has no fixed scope, so in each conversation it works with whatever resources you have access to, such as your spaces, knowledge bases, dashboards, connectors, and skills. You don’t need to decide in advance which data or tools a request needs, so you can start most work with Quick. A custom agent is one that you or someone on your team configures for a specific job. An example is a human resources (HR) onboarding assistant that answers new-hire questions from the HR team’s space. You give it its own instructions and limit it to the spaces, connectors, and skills that your use case requires. After

summary.tldr:
AWS Quick is an AI-powered service designed for automating tasks, analyzing data, building web applications, and conducting research through natural language interactions. The platform utilizes AI agents to process user requests by integrating connected data sources, applications, and specific functional capabilities known as skills.

The system relies on core architectural components including agents, skills, connectors, and data sources such as spaces, knowledge bases, datasets, and dashboards. The default built-in agent, Quick, has no fixed scope and operates across any resources the user can access. Alternatively, users can configure custom agents—such as an HR onboarding assistant—tailored to specific jobs with restricted instructions, spaces, connectors, and skills. Agents can execute tasks directly via chat interfaces or run autonomously using routines, while remaining strictly bounded by the user's permission limits.
takeaways: **Core Service Functionality:** AWS Quick automates tasks, analyzes data, builds web applications, and conducts research using natural language prompts processed by AI agents.

**Built-in Agent Capabilities:** The default Quick agent has no fixed scope, automatically utilizing all user-accessible spaces, knowledge bases, dashboards, connectors, and skills without requiring upfront tool selection.

**Custom Agent Configuration:** Users can build custom agents for specialized tasks—such as HR onboarding—by assigning dedicated instructions and limiting access to specific spaces, connectors, and skills.
**Execution Methods:** Agents operate either interactively through chat conversations or independently via automated routines, acting exclusively within the permission boundaries of the user.

title: Anthropic launches Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 with science, coding upgrades
author: Maria Deutscher
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 19:08 EST / NOVEMBER 09 2026

Anthropic launches Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 with science, coding upgrades

Anthropic PBC today pulled back the curtains on Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, its two most capable large language models to date.

The LLMs are identical as far as their core capabilities are concerned. The difference is that Fable 5.2 blocks certain biology and cybersecurity use cases, while Mythos 5.2 includes more relaxed guardrails. The latter model is only available to trusted researchers through a pair of limited-access programs.

Anthropic tested Fable 5.2 against its predecessor across 14 artificial intelligence benchmarks. The model beat Fable 5.1’s score by more than 10% across most of the tests. It’s particularly adept at scientific research: Fable 5.2 scored 74.6% on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, a 22% improvement over Fable 5.1.

Earlier this year, Anthropic used an unreleased LLM to generate a computer-verifiable version of a famous mathematical proof. The project took 11 days. According to Anthropic, Fable 5.2 reduced the workflow to 30 hours by spinning up 1,000 agents to parallelize calculations. In a separate project, it answered two open questions about a theoretical physics concept related to black holes.

The company also tested Mythos 5.2, the invite-only version of Fable 5.2. It asked the model to study the protective shells of harmless viruses called AAVs. AAV shells, or capsids as they’re known in scientific parlance, are used by some therapies to deliver drugs.

Mythos 5.2 accurately modeled the structure of 28 out of the 34 AAV capsids it studied. The result is notable because capsids comprise dozens of different proteins. Other cutting-edge models that are optimized for biology research, notably Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold2, can only model the structure of individual proteins. The creators of the latter model won one half of the 2024 Nobel Prize in chemistry.

Fable 5.2 includes guardrails that block most research biology questions and many cybersecurity-related prompts. If users enter a request that falls into either of those categories, the model sends it to Opus 4.8 or Opus 5. Anthropic says Fable 5.2 is 55% less likely to erroneously block safe prompts than Fable 5.1.

The model outperforms its predecessor by more than 13% across two coding benchmarks called FrontierCode 2.0 FrontierSWE 2.0. According to Ant

summary.tldr:
Anthropic has released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, its most advanced large language models to date. While both models share identical core capabilities, they differ in safety guardrails: Fable 5.2 restricts specific biology and cybersecurity queries, while Mythos 5.2 features relaxed constraints and is restricted to trusted researchers via limited-access programs. Anthropic reports that Fable 5.2 outperforms its predecessor, Fable 5.1, by over 10% across 14 benchmarks, with a 22% improvement on the Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 test (scoring 74.6%) and a 13% gain on the FrontierCode 2.0 and FrontierSWE 2.0 coding benchmarks.

The models leverage a multi-agent architecture to handle complex, open-ended tasks. In internal testing, Fable 5.2 utilized 1,000 parallel agents to complete a mathematical proof in 30 hours—a task that previously required 11 days—and successfully built a functional operating system in eight days. Mythos 5.2 demonstrated significant biological research capabilities by accurately modeling 28 out of 34 AAV (adeno-associated virus) capsids, a feat Anthropic notes exceeds the capabilities of models like AlphaFold2, which are typically limited to individual protein structures. Fable 5.2 also features improved safety filtering, with a 55% reduction in false-positive blocks compared to Fable 5.1.

Pricing for both models is set at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, representing a 20% cost reduction over previous generations. A high-performance mode is available for double the standard price, offering 2.5x faster response generation. For standard workflows, Anthropic recommends integrating these models with Opus 5.5, which was released in July.
takeaways: **Performance Metrics:** Fable 5.2 achieved a 74.6% score on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 and a 13% improvement over Fable 5.1 on FrontierCode 2.0 and FrontierSWE 2.0 benchmarks.
**Agentic Workflow:** Fable 5.2 can deploy up to 1,000 parallel agents to accelerate complex tasks, such as reducing a mathematical proof workflow from 11 days to 30 hours.
**Biological Modeling:** Mythos 5.2 successfully modeled 28 of 34 AAV capsids, demonstrating an ability to handle multi-protein structures beyond the scope of AlphaFold2.
**Pricing Structure:** The models are priced at $8/million input tokens and $40/million output tokens, with a high-performance tier available at 2x cost for 2.5x speed.
**Safety Guardrails:** Fable 5.2 is 55% less likely to erroneously block safe prompts than Fable 5.1; restricted queries are automatically routed to Opus 4.8 or Opus 5.

title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep! I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such. Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map. The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced. How it works When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices , a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract: We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a

summary.tldr:
A developer utilized Claude Code to build 'Beep Locator,' a software system designed to triangulate the source of intermittent noises using multiple consumer devices. The system functions by running a Python web server that coordinates various listener devices—including iPads, a MacBook Pro, and a Surface Ultra—connected via QR code or URL. To overcome initial localization challenges, the system incorporates a 'Rough mode' for manual device placement, which is then refined through acoustic ranging. A 'clapping mode' allows for system validation by mapping test sounds as diamonds on a UI, while confirmed mystery beeps are marked with an 'X' after the user verifies the audio playback from each device.

Once the system identifies the specific frequency and interval of the target beep, it uses the triangulated device positions to calculate the most likely source location. In a practical test, the software successfully localized a dying carbon monoxide detector within a 40cm margin of error. The underlying architecture is based on the 2007 research paper 'BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices' by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan, which details the methodology for high-accuracy acoustic ranging using off-the-shelf hardware.
takeaways: **System Architecture:** Uses a Python-based web server to coordinate multiple listener devices for acoustic triangulation.
**Calibration Method:** Employs a 'Rough mode' for manual device positioning and a 'clapping mode' to verify spatial accuracy before tracking the target sound.
**Performance Metric:** Successfully localized a target sound source within a 40cm radius in a cluttered environment.
**Research Foundation:** The implementation is derived from the 2007 paper 'BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices'.

title: What could China get from Jensen Huang?
author: Hayden Field
contentSnippet: It’s difficult to overstate Nvidia’s power in today’s AI landscape. The company’s chips are the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built, and demand has consistently outpaced supply for years. Nvidia has also been an influential investor in a wide range of up-and-coming AI companies in recent years, with about $99 billion worth of equity investments in frontier AI labs, neoclouds, infrastructure companies, and more. Its chief executive has even become close with President Donald Trump. This is why, as both cofounder and longtime CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry. Huang is in hot water after news broke of his extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen) is an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud provider and a top Nvidia customer. Questions are swirling around how the affair may have influenced Huang’s reported push to sell advanced chips to China — and potentially even influenced President Trump’s own decisions surrounding AI export controls. US officials believe the Megaspeed executive is a foreign intelligence asset that has funneled information straight to the Chinese government, per The New York Times — in particular, officials reportedly believe that Megaspeed is related to a convoluted web of Chinese companies working together to access chips in bulk and perhaps even illegally get some of those chips into China. Alibaba is reportedly one of Megaspeed’s top customers. “It’s not entirely surprising that the CEO of arguably one of the most important, if not the most important, AI chip companies is the target of some sort of intelligence-gathering from countries like China,” Hanna Dohmen, a senior research analyst at CSET, said in an interview with The Verge, adding that an alleged spy would potentially be interested in “better understanding what the US government is thinking on export controls,” as well as gathering information on Huang’s conversations with the Trump administration, attempting to influence policy, and gathering information on trade secrets like “who’s buying Nvidia’s chips, who’s getting them first, what’s coming next in terms of AI chips.” Megaspeed’s sister company, headquartered in Malaysia, spent $4.8 billion or more on Nvidia chips and technology between June 2024 and Februa

summary.tldr:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing severe scrutiny following reports of an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based cloud provider Megaspeed whom US officials allege is a Chinese intelligence operative. Megaspeed and its Malaysian sister company reportedly spent $4.8 billion or more on Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, with Alibaba listed as a top customer. US intelligence suspects the relationship was leveraged to gather trade secrets, monitor US export control policy, and facilitate bulk chip access for Chinese entities.

The situation intersects directly with Huang's high-level lobbying efforts targeting the Trump administration to loosen advanced semiconductor export controls to China. According to reports cited by The New York Times and Culper Research, Huang interacted with Alice Huang in Taipei in June 2024 and May 2025, around the same periods key policy shifts regarding Nvidia's China-specific H20 chips were unfolding. Huang subsequently met with President Donald Trump in the Oval Office in July 2025 to advocate for broader sales, aligning with advocacy from then-White House AI czar David Sacks. By December 2025, the administration permitted H20 sales to an approved list of Chinese customers with a 25 percent US government cut.

A classified memo overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned officials of the Megaspeed executive's alleged ties to China's Ministry of State Security prior to a presidential trip to China. Despite these intelligence warnings and the ongoing investigation, President Trump has publicly defended Huang as an "honorable guy," and Nvidia's board has retained him as CEO. Huang issued an internal memo apologizing to his family, employees, and board for his infidelity.
takeaways: **Financial and Investment Scale:** Nvidia maintains about $99 billion in equity investments across frontier AI labs, neoclods, and infrastructure companies, while boasting a market cap of approximately $4.25 trillion.

**Massive Hardware Purchases:** Megaspeed's Malaysian sister company spent $4.8 billion or more on Nvidia chips and technology between June 2024 and February 2026, with Alibaba identified as a top customer.

**Lobbying and Policy Milestones:** Jensen Huang lobbied the Trump administration throughout 2025—aided by White House AI czar David Sacks—culminating in a December 2025 policy allowing H20 chip sales to approved Chinese customers under a 25 percent US government revenue cut.

**Classified Intelligence Warnings:** A classified memo overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated among Trump administration officials warning that the Megaspeed executive was an alleged intelligence operative for China's Ministry of State Security seeking advanced AI chip access.

title: Here’s what Trump said he knew about Jensen Huang
author: Jay Peters

title: Jensen Huang reportedly engaged a PR firm with a history of handling  high-profile sex scandals a year ago
author: Marina Temkin
contentSnippet:
Posted: 3:28 PM PST · November 9, 2026 Image Credits: Jose Sarmento Matos/Bloomberg / Getty Images Marina Temkin Jensen Huang reportedly engaged a PR firm with a history of handling high-profile sex scandals a year ago Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang hired Heller Inc., a crisis communications firm known for handling sex scandals, at least a year before he publicly acknowledged an extramarital affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, Wired reported .

Heller Inc. founder Risa Heller has advised prominent men through personal scandals and sexual misconduct accusations, according to a 2023 New York Magazine profile. Her reported clients include former congressman Anthony Weiner , celebrity chef Mario Batali , and former New Yorker writer Jeffrey Toobin.

Wired also reported that Nvidia’s internal communications team was told to copy Heller Inc. on press inquiries about Huang shortly after an October 2025 New York Times report about whether Nvidia was helping Chinese companies evade U.S. chip export restrictions.

The Times reported that Megaspeed, a then little-known Singapore-based data center company with ties to China, had acquired nearly $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips. It described Megaspeed CEO Alice Huang, the woman later linked to Jensen Huang, standing next to him at a Taipei gathering of Nvidia customers.

Heller and Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

On Sunday, Nvidia published a statement from Huang acknowledging an affair with a former Megaspeed executive, though he didn’t name Alice Huang. Nvidia’s board separately announced an independent investigation, citing reports that Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

title: IBM builds on hybrid cloud and governance to advance its enterprise AI operating model
author: Manny Veiga
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 18:20 EST / NOVEMBER 09 2026

IBM builds on hybrid cloud and governance to advance its enterprise AI operating model

Enterprises are moving beyond AI pilots, putting greater emphasis on governance, production readiness and measurable business outcomes.

Research from Deloitte highlights a significant gap between enterprise AI ambition and execution: 54% of organizations plan to move at least 40% of their AI initiatives into production within six months. Yet only 25% have done so today. IBM is betting on its strengths — mainframe hardware, hybrid computing assets and a legacy of strong governance — to gain a leg up on the rest of the market, according to theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante .

“In our opinion, IBM has found a differentiated path in enterprise AI by productizing workflow-level outcomes across a stack that, while sometimes confusing, customers generally trust,” he said. “Client Zero proof, a workload-first hybrid design, durable platforms reimagined for agents and a pragmatic quantum roadmap create a credible basis for sustained advantage.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of how enterprise AI has moved beyond the race for model supremacy, with major technology players now focused on enabling governed enterprise AI that delivers trust, reliability and predictable business outcomes. (* Disclosure below.)

Building toward an enterprise AI operating model

IBM already has a substantial book of business around generative AI, with AI-related software sales and consulting engagements totaling more than $12.5 billion as of Q4 2025 , up from $9.5 billion the previous quarter.

Through a series of investments, acquisitions and product launches, IBM is gathering assets for an enterprise AI operating model with four pillars: agent orchestration, trusted data, intelligent operations and governance.

Many of these capabilities were rolled out as part of a steady drumbeat of announcements leading up to IBM Think 2026 in May. In February, the company announced a partnership with Deepgram Inc. to integrate voice capabilities into watsonx Orchestrate, its enterprise platform for building, deploying and managing agents. Two months later, it made IBM Bob — an AI-assisted coding tool that helps developers plan, write, test, modernize and deploy code — globally available .

In May 2026, IBM completed its acquisition of Confluent , the

summary.tldr:
IBM is positioning itself as the primary infrastructure provider for enterprise AI by focusing on a four-pillar operating model: agent orchestration, trusted data, intelligent operations, and governance. As of Q4 2025, IBM reported $12.5 billion in AI-related software sales and consulting engagements, up from $9.5 billion in the previous quarter. The company is leveraging its legacy in mainframe hardware and hybrid cloud to address the 70% of enterprise data currently locked in on-premises systems, emphasizing "sovereignty" as a core competitive advantage for clients concerned with data control and regulatory compliance.

Key product developments include the launch of the Sovereign Core platform for embedded governance, the repositioning of Concert as an agentic IT operations platform, and the acquisition of Confluent to bolster real-time data streaming within watsonx.data. IBM is also utilizing its own internal operations as "Client Zero," reporting that over 80,000 employees use the "IBM Bob" AI-assisted coding tool, which the company claims has driven a 45% increase in productivity. Furthermore, IBM Consulting has deployed over 4,000 digital workers across 450 projects, utilizing models from watsonx, Anthropic, and OpenAI.
takeaways: **Financial Growth:** IBM's AI-related software and consulting revenue reached $12.5 billion in Q4 2025, a $3 billion increase from the prior quarter.
**Infrastructure Performance:** IBM Z mainframe revenue grew 51% year-over-year, while Red Hat OpenShift revenue increased 13% year-over-year.
**Productivity Metrics:** IBM reports that 80,000 employees using the "IBM Bob" coding assistant have achieved a 45% productivity gain.

**Agent Deployment:** IBM Consulting has deployed more than 4,000 digital workers across 450 active projects, incorporating models from IBM, Anthropic, and OpenAI.

title: A short seller flagged Nvidia CEO’s ties to a suspected Chinese spy six months before the scandal
author: Sarah Perez
contentSnippet:
Six months before the Nvidia spy scandal emerged , the New York-based short seller firm Culper Research had already raised questions about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unusually close relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that buys Nvidia chips. She is now suspected to be a Chinese spy.

The Nvidia CEO admitted to an extramarital affair over the weekend, and the company has now opened a formal investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang (who shares his last name but is not related). U.S. intelligence officials believe she was recruited by the Chinese government to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang and influence his position regarding U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips.

Culper’s May 13 report is resurfacing because it picked up on the connection between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang while investigating Megaspeed’s ties to Nvidia.

NEW: We are short Nvidia $NVDA . We believe Nvidia has a significant China problem. Please see our full report and disclosures now available on our website, link in bio. pic.twitter.com/oTaJyL7S2R

In particular, the report called the relationship between the two executives “uncomfortably close,” noting that the Nvidia CEO was spotted partying and socializing with Alice Huang on multiple occasions. The report even claimed that some Nvidia employees wondered whether they had a “special relationship.”

Culper Research also theorized the China business that Nvidia lost to export controls had been rerouted through Southeast Asia, and that Megaspeed, a major chip buyer in the region, was secretly financed by Chinese tech giant Alibaba through shell companies. It pointed to financial records that showed Megaspeed’s total liabilities and equity had grown from $33 million at the end of 2023 to around $3 billion by the end of 2024, much of it in the form of refundable deposits from an unidentified source.

Financial Times reported Monday that documents show Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed through subsidiaries.

Culper is a short seller, so it stood to financially benefit from making these allegations, and those about possible illegal chip diversion have not been independently verified. Its report is available on the web and was posted to X back in May .

title: The race is on to sue Nvidia
author: Connie Loizos
contentSnippet:
Nvidia’s stock slid more than 4% on Monday, the first trading day after its board said it would investigate CEO Jensen Huang over his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive U.S. intelligence believes was spying for China.

Securities lawyers were already moving. Several firms, including Schall, Brown & Schwartz, Levi & Korsinsky, Bronstein, Gewirtz & Grossman, and The Law Offices of Frank R. Cruz, announced investigations Monday into whether Nvidia made false or misleading statements or failed to disclose information that’s pertinent to investors. Robert Bartlett, a Stanford Law professor and securities law expert, expects them to have plenty of company.

“I would definitely wager that there’ll be a filing,” Bartlett said in an interview Monday morning, adding that he wouldn’t be surprised if a case had been filed by the end of day. Plaintiffs’ lawyers have good reasons to be first in line; under federal securities law, the first complaint triggers a public notice, and investors then have 60 days to ask the court to be named lead plaintiff. A firm that files early gets a head start on signing up investors with large losses, as well as on shaping the story of the case. Nvidia is headquartered in Santa Clara, and indeed, that’s where one of the first cases surfaced Monday afternoon.

Rosen Law Firm, a New York-based plaintiffs’ firm that specializes in securities class actions, filed the case Monday in federal court in the Northern District of California. (The firm was lead counsel in a $250 million settlement with Alibaba and ranks among the most active filers of such cases.) The suit was brought on behalf of Mark Kistenmacher, who’s described as an individual investor. According to the complaint, Kistenmacher made seven purchases totaling roughly $20,500 between February and November of this year. The proposed class covers anyone who bought Nvidia securities between Oct. 9, 2025, and Nov. 8, 2026, and the suit names both Nvidia and Huang.

The complaint accuses them of misleading investors about Huang’s ties to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data center outfit where Alice Huang was considered a top executive. It points to three statements: Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo’s claim that Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected,” the company’s claim that it found “ no evidence of diversion ” of its chips, and Jensen Huang’s Oct.

summary.tldr:
Nvidia is facing a wave of securities litigation following the company's announcement that its board is investigating CEO Jensen Huang regarding his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive allegedly monitored by U.S. intelligence for espionage ties to China. Nvidia stock fell 4.27% ($7.97 per share) on Monday following the disclosure. Multiple law firms, including Schall, Brown & Schwartz and Levi & Korsinsky, have initiated investigations into whether the company misled investors regarding the nature of the relationship and its business dealings with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center firm where Alice Huang held a top executive role.

The first formal class-action lawsuit was filed in the Northern District of California by Rosen Law Firm on behalf of investor Mark Kistenmacher, who claims losses from purchases made between February and November 2025. The complaint alleges that Nvidia and Jensen Huang made false statements by characterizing the CEO's interactions with Alice Huang as "not unusual" and claiming no evidence of chip diversion to Megaspeed. Legal experts, including Stanford Law professor Robert Bartlett, characterize this as a "fraud on the market" claim, where investors argue that stock prices were artificially inflated by incomplete or misleading public disclosures. The suit seeks unspecified damages, interest, and a jury trial.

While the board has stated it has no evidence that Nvidia secrets were compromised, the legal exposure centers on whether the company's public denials constituted material misrepresentations. Under federal securities law, Jensen Huang's knowledge is imputed to the company, creating potential liability regardless of the board's internal findings on his private life. While the SEC has the theoretical authority to seek an officer-and-director bar, experts suggest such action is unlikely under current political conditions. The litigation is expected to proceed as a long-term civil matter, typically resulting in settlements funded by the company and its insurers.
takeaways: **Market Impact:** Nvidia shares dropped 4.27% ($7.97) on the first trading day following the board's announcement of the investigation.
**Legal Basis:** The lawsuit filed by Rosen Law Firm alleges "fraud on the market," claiming Nvidia misled investors about the CEO's relationship with Alice Huang and its business ties to Megaspeed.

**Specific Allegations:** The complaint cites three specific statements as misleading: a spokesperson's claim that interactions were "not unusual," the company's assertion of "no evidence of diversion," and Jensen Huang's October 30 comment to Bloomberg describing dealings as "normal."
**Class Period:** The proposed class action covers investors who purchased Nvidia securities between October 9, 2025, and November 8, 2026.

**Governance Risk:** Beyond securities fraud, the company faces potential board-level liability if directors failed to implement adequate reporting lines for critical risks once the relationship became public knowledge.

title: Exploring the world's languages with Language Explorer
author: Google AI Research Blog
contentSnippet:
November 9, 2026 Daan van Esch, Senior Technical Program Manager, Google DeepMind and Uche Okonkwo, Senior Program Manager, Google Research

Language Explorer, featured in an exhibition at the Museum of Communication in Berlin, Germany, lets you explore the world's linguistic diversity online through visualizations and data.

Our world has a fascinating wealth of languages, and for over two decades, Google has been building language technologies that cover as many languages as possible. In 2006, we started a small experiment with Google Translate, supporting just two languages (English and Arabic) at the time. Fast forward to today: nearly 250 languages are supported, with around a trillion words translated every month . Our commitment to linguistic diversity runs across products, all in service of our mission to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible and useful. Building products that reflect the world's linguistic diversity takes far more than software engineering; it requires close collaboration with the communities we aim to serve, building in a way that's deeply aligned and respectful of local communities, heritage, history, values and context. This is why we've been working on grassroots initiatives like Project Vaani in India and Project Waxal in Africa, partnering with local organizations to collect thousands of hours of open speech data across underserved languages.

But gathering this data is only one part of the journey. Preserving language vitality requires working closely with native speakers, academic institutions, and cultural organizations. Partnerships, such as our coalition with the Gates Foundation , ensure that modern digital tools reflect the nuances and authentic voices of their communities. Expanding language coverage responsibly also requires deeply understanding linguistic diversity on a global scale. This approach enables products like Gboard , our Android keyboard, to support 900+ language varieties.

To better appreciate the breadth and complexity of this speech diversity, we've been working on a tool to help visualize the world's linguistic diversity, inspired by earlier visualization initiatives like Google Earth . The Language Explorer is an interactive web platform designed to let researchers, educators, and language enthusiasts discover and visualize linguistic diversity around the world. Develope

summary.tldr:
Google DeepMind and Google Research have launched 'Language Explorer,' an interactive web platform designed to visualize global linguistic diversity. Developed under the company's '1,000 Languages Initiative,' the tool aggregates data from the open-source LinguaMeta dataset to provide researchers and educators with a comprehensive view of language distribution and complexity. The platform serves as a digital extension of Google's long-term efforts to expand language support across its product suite, which currently includes nearly 250 languages in Google Translate and over 900 language varieties in Gboard.

The initiative emphasizes a community-centric approach to data collection, highlighting grassroots efforts such as Project Vaani in India and Project Waxal in Africa, which focus on gathering open speech data for underserved languages. These efforts are supported by partnerships with organizations like the Gates Foundation to ensure digital tools accurately reflect local cultural nuances and heritage. The Language Explorer is currently featured as an interactive installation in the 'Real Talk! Language. Power. World.' exhibition at the Museum of Communication in Berlin, which runs through February 2028, with a subsequent run in Frankfurt through September 2029.
takeaways: **Platform Scope:** Language Explorer is an interactive web-based visualization tool built on the open-source LinguaMeta dataset.
**Product Integration:** Google Translate now supports nearly 250 languages with a volume of approximately one trillion words translated monthly.
**Gboard Capability:** The Gboard Android keyboard currently supports over 900 distinct language varieties.
**Exhibition Timeline:** The 'Real Talk!' exhibition featuring the tool is scheduled to run in Berlin until February 2028 and in Frankfurt until September 2029.
**Data Initiatives:** Google is actively collecting open speech data for underserved languages through Project Vaani (India) and Project Waxal (Africa).

title: Single-shot and agentic retrieval with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
author: Siddhant Sahu
contentSnippet: A banking operations employee starts the morning by asking an internal AI assistant which documents are needed to open a business account. The answer is in a single checklist. A few hours later, the same employee asks how those requirements differ across sole proprietorships, LLCs, and partnerships with multiple owners. That answer is spread across several policy guides. One assistant has to handle both questions, quickly and cheaply for the first and thoroughly for the second. Applications need a way to match retrieval effort to each request without building separate systems for simple and complex questions. Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports single-shot Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and retrieval-only requests through AgenticRetrieveStream . With single-shot RAG, the service searches your knowledge bases once and uses a foundation model (FM) to generate an answer from the passages it finds. With retrieval-only requests, the service returns the matching passages without generating an answer, so your application or the user can work with the source text directly. These modes join the existing agentic retrieval, where the service plans and runs multiple searches before answering. You can now use the same API for both of the employee’s questions: single-shot RAG for the checklist lookup and agentic retrieval for the cross-policy comparison. In this post, we explain how the new settings work and when to use each mode. We use an illustrative internal banking policy assistant to show how single-shot RAG handles direct questions and how agentic retrieval supports comparisons across policy documents. We also show how to configure retrieval-only requests when an employee needs to review source passages rather than a generated answer. Key benefits Agentic retrieval helps an assistant answer questions that require more than one search. A foundation model breaks the question into sub-queries, searches the relevant knowledge bases, and evaluates whether the results provide enough information to answer the original question. If it identifies gaps, it can refine the search and retrieve additional evidence, within the configured iteration limit. For application builders, this provides several benefits: Better support for multi-part questions –  Targeted searches can find evidence for each part of a question instead of relying on one search to cover e

summary.tldr:
Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base has expanded its retrieval capabilities by introducing single-shot Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and retrieval-only request modes, accessible via the AgenticRetrieveStream API. These additions allow developers to match retrieval complexity to specific user queries within a single system, moving beyond the previous requirement of using agentic retrieval for all tasks. Single-shot RAG performs a single search against knowledge bases and uses a foundation model to synthesize an answer, while retrieval-only mode returns raw source passages without triggering a generation step.

These new modes complement the existing agentic retrieval workflow, where the foundation model autonomously decomposes complex queries into sub-queries, executes multiple iterative searches, and evaluates the sufficiency of retrieved evidence against configured iteration limits. By integrating these options into one API, Amazon Bedrock enables applications to handle simple, direct lookups—such as checklist requirements—using single-shot RAG, while reserving agentic retrieval for multi-part or comparative policy analysis that requires cross-document synthesis.
takeaways: **API Integration:** New retrieval modes are implemented through the AgenticRetrieveStream API within Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base.
**Single-shot RAG:** Executes a single search and uses a foundation model to generate an answer, optimized for direct, simple queries.
**Retrieval-only Mode:** Returns source passages directly to the application or user without invoking a foundation model for text generation.
**Agentic Retrieval:** Maintains the ability to decompose complex questions into sub-queries and perform iterative searches until sufficient information is gathered or iteration limits are reached.

title: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 on AWS
author: Dani Mitchell
contentSnippet: Today, we are announcing the availability of Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on Amazon Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS. Claude Fable 5.2 is Anthropic’s most capable generally available model for technical work that raises the bar in coding and the sciences. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available through Anthropic’s verification programs for advanced work in cyber security and life sciences. In this post, we cover what’s new in both models, why Fable 5.2 matters for your technical workloads, and how to get started building with the model on Amazon Bedrock. Why Claude Fable 5.2 Fable 5.2 raises the bar on the hardest problems in coding, math, and science. It takes on ambiguous, multi-step work, verifies its own output, and can run unattended for hours to days. It interprets prompts, iterates, catches its own errors, and optimizes as it goes. In Anthropic’s alignment testing, Mythos 5.2 hallucinates less, completes tasks more reliably, surfaces important information more consistently, and self-reports issues more honestly than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1. Anthropic expects Fable 5.2 to behave similarly. If a cyber security query is declined, you can retry it on Opus 4.8, and if a biology query is declined, you can retry it on Opus 5. On Amazon Bedrock, the retry is your code’s job, not an automatic switch. If the declined request hit the prompt cache, the refusal also includes a fallback credit token. Send that token with the retry and it’s billed as cache reads, so you don’t pay to write the same cache twice. Check the documentation for more information on fallback credit. For authorized work in cyber security and life sciences, Claude Mythos 5.2 is available through Anthropic’s verification programs . Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 use cases Where Fable 5.2 fits: Agentic coding across large, multi-repository codebases. Long-running agents for coordinating many subagents on multi-day work. Scientific research from new analytical methods to formal mathematical proofs. Financial analysis for quantitative research and forecasting. Design for 3D, hardware, and motion for generating environments, components, and simulations in code. Mythos 5.2 covers two high-risk domains, available only through the verification programs noted earlier: Cyber security , for security engineering, red teaming, and penetration testing. Life sciences research , especially bi

summary.tldr:
Anthropic has announced the availability of Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on Amazon Bedrock and the Claude Platform on AWS. Claude Fable 5.2 is positioned as Anthropic's most capable generally available model for technical workloads, targeting coding, mathematics, and scientific research. It is designed to handle ambiguous, multi-step operations, verify its own outputs, self-correct errors, and execute unattended tasks running from hours to days. Meanwhile, Claude Mythos 5.2 is restricted to authorized verification programs for high-risk domains including advanced cybersecurity and life sciences.

In alignment testing, Mythos 5.2 demonstrates lower hallucination rates, higher task reliability, more consistent information surfacing, and more honest self-reporting of issues compared to Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1, with Fable 5.2 expected to exhibit similar behavioral improvements. Fable 5.2 use cases include agentic coding across multi-repository codebases, long-running multi-day agent coordination, formal mathematical proofs, quantitative financial analysis, and code-based 3D, hardware, and motion design. Mythos 5.2 focuses on security engineering, red teaming, penetration testing, and life sciences research.

For deployment mechanics on Amazon Bedrock, declined security or biology queries require manual code-level retries on fallback models such as Opus 4.8 or Opus 5, rather than automatic routing. When a declined request impacts prompt caching, the refusal generates a fallback credit token that bills the retry as a cache read to prevent duplicate cache-writing costs.
takeaways: **New Model Availability:** Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are now available on Amazon Bedrock and the Claude Platform on AWS.

**Target Workloads for Fable 5.2:** Built for agentic coding across multi-repository codebases, long-running multi-day subagent coordination, scientific research and formal proofs, quantitative financial forecasting, and 3D/hardware/motion design in code.
**Mythos 5.2 Access Restrictions:** Claude Mythos 5.2 is restricted to specialized verification programs for cybersecurity (red teaming, penetration testing) and life sciences research.
**Alignment and Performance Improvements:** Mythos 5.2 hallucinates less, completes tasks more reliably, and self-reports issues more honestly than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1.
**Bedrock Fallback Caching Mechanism:** Declined prompt-cached requests on Bedrock return a fallback credit token, allowing retries on models like Opus 4.8 or Opus 5 to be billed at cache-read rates.

title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
author: Venu Kanamatareddy
contentSnippet: Today, we’re announcing that NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. You can deploy it with a few steps in SageMaker Studio or with a few lines of the SageMaker Python SDK. Super VL is the vision-language model (VLM) in the NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 family. It accepts images, video, and text as input and generates text. The model pairs a 120B-parameter hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language backbone with 12B active parameters and a C-RADIO vision encoder. It supports context lengths of up to 1 million tokens and includes a built-in Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head that supports speculative decoding. You can configure reasoning per request. NVIDIA built Super VL for document intelligence, GUI understanding for computer-use agents, video question answering, and multimodal agentic applications. JumpStart offers two variants: NVFP4, quantized from BF16 with quantization-aware distillation for optimized inference, and the BF16 full-precision reference weights. In this post, we walk through the model’s capabilities and the JumpStart deployment configurations. We then show the measured inference performance and demonstrate text, image, and video inference. Model overview Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a 120B-parameter model with 12B active parameters per token. It combines a hybrid language backbone with a dedicated vision encoder. Language backbone : 88 layers that interleave Mamba-2 and MoE layers (512 routed experts, 22 active per token) with 8 attention layers, plus a shared MTP head. The backbone is initialized from Nemotron 3 Super Base and distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra Base. Vision encoder : A C-RADIO vision encoder encodes images and sampled video frames, and a vision-language connector maps them into the language backbone’s embedding space. The encoder and connector stay in BF16 in both variants. Training : The model first goes through continued pre-training, long-context and software-engineering mid-training, and vision-language training. It then goes through two-stage multimodal supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on vision, reasoning, code, tool, chat, safety, and long-context data. Next come reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards and human feedback in NeMo RL and NeMo Gym, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and a final stage that further trains the MTP head. The NVFP4 checkpoint is produced from BF16 with NVIDIA Model

summary.tldr:
NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super VL vision-language model is now available for deployment in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart via SageMaker Studio or the SageMaker Python SDK. The model processes images, video, and text inputs to generate text, featuring support for context lengths up to 1 million tokens and a built-in Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head for speculative decoding with configurable per-request reasoning. Amazon SageMaker JumpStart provides two variants for deployment: an optimized NVFP4 quantized checkpoint derived from BF16 using quantization-aware distillation, and the full-precision BF16 reference weights.

Architecturally, Super VL is a 120B-parameter hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 12 active parameters per token, pairing its language backbone with a C-RADIO vision encoder and a vision-language connector. The 88-layer language backbone interleaves Mamba-2 and MoE layers—utilizing 512 routed experts with 22 active per token—alongside 8 attention layers and a shared MTP head. The model was trained through continued pre-training, mid-training for long context and software engineering, vision-language training, two-stage multimodal supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning using NeMo RL and NeMo Gym, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and final MTP head training.

Designed for enterprise applications such as document intelligence, GUI understanding for computer-use agents, video question answering, and multimodal agentic workflows, the model's language backbone is initialized from Nemotron 3 Super Base and distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra Base. In both the NVFP4 and BF16 deployment variants, the vision encoder and connector remain in BF16.
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a 120B-parameter model with 12B active parameters per token, combining an 88-layer hybrid language backbone (interleaving Mamba-2 and MoE layers with 512 routed experts and 8 attention layers) with a C-RADIO vision encoder.

**Deployment Variants:** Amazon SageMaker JumpStart offers two versions of the model: NVFP4 (quantized from BF16 via quantization-aware distillation for optimized inference) and full-precision BF16 reference weights.

**Context and Decoding:** The model supports context lengths up to 1 million tokens, includes a built-in Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head for speculative decoding, and permits per-request reasoning configuration.
**Target Use Cases:** NVIDIA built Super VL specifically for document intelligence, GUI understanding for computer-use agents, video question answering, and multimodal agentic applications.

**Training Pipeline:** Training included continued pre-training, mid-training, vision-language training, two-stage multimodal supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning via NeMo RL and NeMo Gym, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation.

title: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
author: Dan Goodin
contentSnippet: Hackers are actively exploiting a recently discovered critical vulnerability that allows them to log in to privileged accounts on many Linux systems, multiple researchers are reporting. The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole became publicly known last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real. Attackers conducting "mature intrusions" Security firm Greynoise said Monday that honeypots it maintains in Southeast Asia have come under attack by a group it’s tracking as GT10. The group conducted “mature intrusions" into the systems, which Greynoise uses to detect attempted or successful attacks in real time. Greynoise subsequently gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims and some of the tools used in the campaign. A backdoor the group is using in the attacks contains Chinese language comments and appears to be generated with the use of AI. Read full article Comments

title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
author: James O'Donnell
contentSnippet: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.  One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport .  Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg,

title: Pluggable Agentic AI Framework: A seven-layer composable enterprise agentic AI reference architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
author: Sindhura Palakodety
contentSnippet: “How do we run our AI agents in production at scale?” is the question every customer eventually asks. It comes bundled with several questions. How do we handle thousands of concurrent user requests securely and confidently? How do we make sure the agents stay reliable under real traffic instead of failing silently? How do we know if an agent still meets the quality and safety standards it passed during testing? What are agent security best practices? Should that be deterministic or non-deterministic? And many more. A proof-of-concept answers none of these, because it is built to show the agent model can do the task, not to survive production traffic, cost pressure, and security review. That gap between a working prototype and a system that runs reliably, securely, frugally and responsibly at scale, is where most agentic AI initiatives stall, and it is rarely the model’s fault. Every team building an agent tends to rebuild the same scaffolding from scratch: its own routing logic, its own guardrails, its own observability, all applied after the fact rather than built in from the start. The teams need a shared, production-ready architecture that every agent can build on. This post walks through a seven-layer composable reference architecture designed to take multi-agent AI applications from prototype to production scale. Composable architecture The Pluggable Agentic AI Framework is a reference architecture for multi-agent applications organized into seven layers , each with a distinct responsibility and a stable contract. The services and technologies shown in each layer reflect the reference implementation, not mandatory choices. Organizations can substitute alternatives that align with their existing infrastructure and requirements. Together, these layers offer a blueprint for building, securing, and operating agentic AI applications at production scale. Whether an agent is checking out a healthcare formulary, tracking inventory, or interpreting a compliance rule, it needs relevant, up-to-date information to answer correctly. title: Anthropic launches new Claude Fable and Mythos 5.2 models

title: How CrossnoKaye grounds physical AI with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
author: Raphael Simon
contentSnippet: Industrial operations present AI challenges that don’t show up in typical enterprise software. In most facilities, plant data and control logic are spread across separate systems from different vendors: programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and distributed control systems (DCS) run the equipment logic, historians record time-series tags under site-specific naming schemes, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems drive operator screens, and standalone optimization tools or alarm loggers sit on the side. Bolting an external AI agent onto that stack rarely works well in practice. Each system uses its own naming conventions. The logic that actually governs how equipment behaves (the control sequences, state machines, and safety interlocks) is locked inside proprietary controller code that an external tool can’t inspect. Giving a bolt-on agent access across multiple operational technology (OT) systems also means distributing credentials across the plant network. CrossnoKaye took a different approach to bring physical AI to heavy industry using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . Its software-defined automation platform, ATLAS, connects live plant data and AI reasoning to closed-loop control of the equipment running food and beverage plants, industrial refrigeration facilities, aggregates quarries, and manufacturing sites. Across more than 100 industrial facilities and 13,000 controlled assets, CrossnoKaye stores over 22 trillion machine data points, ingests more than 50 billion new readings every day, and runs over 1,000 live advanced process control (APC) applications; CrossnoKaye reports that these applications improve production throughput by 11–17 percent while reducing total facility energy costs by an average of 21 percent. Because ATLAS already manages the facility model, the base control software, the historian, and the optimization applications in one platform on AWS, CrossnoKaye’s agentic intelligence system, AURA, has native access to the full operational state of the plant within a single security boundary. Having the plant context is only half the problem, though. Large language models (LLMs) are good at interpreting engineering context and planning an investigation, but they cannot reliably compute statistics or physical balances over millions of sensor readings in a prompt.
