title: Agentic-OPD: Recovering Forgotten Agent Capabilities via On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Tasks
author: Tingcheng Bian
contentSnippet: Reinforcement learning is now the mainstream paradigm for training LLMs on agentic tasks, yet standard practice keeps only the best-validation checkpoint and discards the rest. We show that this is lossy: in GRPO training of LLM agents, the best-validation checkpoint fails on problems that earlier checkpoints from the same run had already solved, and the union of problems solved across checkpoints far exceeds any single one. The discarded checkpoints thus form a teacher pool obtained at no additional training cost, which on-policy distillation (OPD) can mine to recover the lost coverage. Mining this pool raises two challenges: i) which checkpoint to distill from, as no checkpoint dominates the others and complementarity to the student is problem-specific; ii) where to trust it, as even a well-chosen teacher is only locally superior, so indiscriminate distillation overwrites behavior the student has already mastered. We propose Agentic-OPD, which treats the best-validation checkpoint as the student and all saved checkpoints as frozen teacher candidates, using the student's evolving capability gaps to guide both teacher selection and supervision filtering: the HCN policy (Highest Coverage Next) dynamically selects teachers by weighted coverage of the student's unsolved problems, while the LAD module (Locality-Aware Distillation) confines transfer to failed student rollouts on problems where the teacher performs better. Across five agentic task domains and 24 benchmarks and task subsets, Agentic-OPD improves over its initialization checkpoint by up to 7.4 points, with a 4B student surpassing the latest frontier models GPT-5.6 and DeepSeek-V4.1 on deep search. Agentic-OPD recasts a finished RL run as a reusable pool of policies and establishes post-RL capability recovery as a stage orthogonal to improvements in the RL algorithm itself.

title: On theCUBE Pod: Blue wave sends AI stock plunging
author: Devony Hof
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 12:13 EST / NOVEMBER 09 2026

On theCUBE Pod: Blue wave sends AI stock plunging

The very blue results of last week’s midterms have sent technology investors into a tailspin.

With many successful candidates running on platforms opposing data centers and calling for greater restrictions on artificial intelligence, investors anticipate a slowdown in AI spending. Tech stocks fell, with a collective loss of $2.5 trillion in market cap , and the Nasdaq dropped more than 5.5%.

“Yesterday was a bloodbath,” said John Furrier (pictured), executive analyst for theCUBE Research. “It was brutal here and the tech stocks got pounded. 41 states had data centers on the ballot. They all lost or won, depending how you look at it. Now it’s so mainstream, it’s a political football. So you’re starting to see the reality of AI. It’s hitting everybody. Everyone is impacted.”

On the latest episode of theCUBE Pod , Furrier and Dave Vellante (pictured, right), chief analyst for theCUBE Research, discussed the fallout from the midterms and whether or not AI companies will really suffer in the long term. They also explored who will own the “system of intelligence” that will govern enterprise AI.

Midterms puts AI investors on shaky ground

After the “bloodbath” last week, the question remains: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom? Despite the shockwaves from the midterms, theCUBE’s researchers are predicting a longer path toward monetization. A recent analysis identified 2029 as the highest-risk year for the AI bubble.

“There’s a clock in terms of the data center monetization and financing and how long it takes to build data centers,” Vellante said. “We know anybody who can sell GPUs is making money but the enterprises aren’t yet self-funding. I had said that by 2026, this year, you’re going to start to see clear evidence of monetization in the enterprise. I think you see it, but you’re seeing it within tech companies.”

Tech companies are applying AI more effectively, according to Vellante, which should not come as a surprise. He thinks the tech titans are in a solid position while neoclouds are taking on a greater share of risk by pioneering a new software model, although not all of them will make it in the long term.

A GPU-based AI economy will shift in the next several years, Furrier believes, which could lead to surprising winners and losers.

“Supermicro [Inc.], good n

summary.tldr:
Following recent U.S. midterm election results, technology markets experienced a significant downturn, with a collective loss of $2.5 trillion in market capitalization and a 5.5% drop in the Nasdaq. Analysts John Furrier and Dave Vellante of theCUBE Research attribute this volatility to a "blue wave" of candidates campaigning on platforms that oppose data center expansion and advocate for stricter AI regulation. With 41 states having data center-related issues on the ballot, AI has transitioned into a contentious political issue, leading investors to anticipate a potential slowdown in enterprise AI spending.

Despite the market "bloodbath," researchers suggest a long-term path toward monetization, identifying 2029 as the peak risk year for the current AI bubble. While tech titans and hyperscalers remain resilient, enterprise-level self-funding remains elusive. The infrastructure landscape is shifting beyond GPU-centric computing toward a broader focus on networking, optics, memory, storage, and power efficiency. Notable industry activity includes Marvell Technology Inc.’s $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum, signaling a strategic pivot toward system-level architecture as a competitive advantage.

The race to define the "system of intelligence"—the layer bridging intelligent agents and data systems—remains open. Analysts highlight Databricks Inc. CEO Ali Ghodsi’s strategy as particularly strong, citing his focus on client surface, governance catalogs, and agent action layers. While frontier models are viewed as a "wild card," the consensus is that the ultimate control point in the AI-native enterprise will be data, context, and agentic workflows rather than the models themselves.
takeaways: **Market Impact:** The tech sector lost $2.5 trillion in market cap, with the Nasdaq falling over 5.5% following midterm election results.
**Strategic Acquisition:** Marvell Technology Inc. closed a $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum to address infrastructure bottlenecks.
**System of Intelligence:** Analysts identify Databricks as having a leading strategy for the "system of intelligence" layer, focusing on governance, agent action, and client-facing surfaces.
**Market Outlook:** 2029 is projected as the highest-risk year for the AI bubble, with enterprise monetization still lagging behind tech-sector internal applications.
**Infrastructure Shift:** The industry is moving toward a system-level architecture approach, prioritizing power efficiency, networking, and storage over pure GPU-centric computing.

title: Google Unveils TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx: A Dual-Chip TPU and a Confidential TPU
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Google has added two new systems to its eighth-generation TPU lineup. TPU 8i Max targets massive context windows and rack density. TPU 8tx targets secure, confidential inference. Google TPU 8i Max is a dual-chip package built from 2 TPU 8i chips. Both arrive alongside TPU 8t and TPU 8i, announced in April . TL;DR Size: TPU 8i Max = 2 TPU 8i chips in 1 package. TPU 8tx = TPU 8t silicon plus 5th Gen AMD EPYC hosts. Runs on: Google Cloud TPU systems. Performance: 8i Max doubles TPU 8i compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth. 8tx cuts latency up to 2x versus TPU 8t. Best: 2x the silicon in the existing rack footprint (TPU 8i Max). Worst: No absolute specs, benchmarks, prices or regions published for either system. What did Google announce? Google announced both systems today. These are new system configurations, not new chips. Google reuses its existing eighth-generation silicon and changes packaging, hosts, memory and networking around it. How does TPU 8i Max work? TPU 8i Max attacks the memory wall. Google team combines 2 low-latency TPU 8i chips onto 1 package. The result doubles compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth compared with TPU 8i. Each TPU 8i chip is rated at 10.1 PFLOPS of FP4, 288 GB of HBM and 8,601 GB/s . It also carries 384 MB of on-chip SRAM. Doubling those figures implies about 20.2 PFLOPS FP4, 768 MB SRAM and 17.2 TB/s per package. Google did not publish these absolute figures. It also did not state HBM capacity for TPU 8i Max. TPU 8i Max fits twice the silicon in the existing rack footprint. Google positions it for agents working across whole codebases or hours of video. What makes TPU 8tx different? TPU 8tx is built for regulated enterprises and governments. It keeps data and model weights protected even while in active use. Normally, data must be decrypted in memory during processing. TPU 8tx uses the same silicon as TPU 8t . It pairs that silicon with 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPU hosts. It also adopts the Boardfly network from TPU 8i. Google claims up to 2x lower latency than TPU 8t, with a near-zero security penalty. Teams can fine-tune, distill and run reinforcement learning on 1 system. That avoids moving sensitive data between separate clusters. What changed in the TPU software stack? title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
author: Grace Huckins
contentSnippet: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.  I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation.  Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth.  “Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big

summary.tldr:
California State Senator Scott Wiener, recently elected to succeed Nancy Pelosi in San Francisco’s congressional seat, is positioning himself as a central figure in federal AI regulation. Wiener’s legislative track record includes authoring California’s SB 1047, which aimed to establish safety standards for frontier AI models before being vetoed by Governor Gavin Newsom, and the subsequent SB 53, which was signed into law. He advocates for a precautionary approach to AI development, frequently citing the risk of "recursive self-improvement"—a concept recently highlighted in a report by the nonprofit METR regarding Anthropic’s model capabilities—as evidence that current regulatory efforts are insufficient.

Wiener’s congressional campaign faced scrutiny over a $3 million contribution from Public First Action, a nonprofit funded in part by Anthropic. Critics suggested this funding indicated a conflict of interest, but Wiener maintains that the support was based on his established history of introducing and implementing AI safety legislation despite opposition from major technology companies. He has expressed frustration with the current pace of federal action, stating that he had hoped for decisive congressional intervention by the end of 2024, a timeline he now views as unlikely.
takeaways: **Legislative Record:** Wiener authored California's SB 1047 (vetoed) and SB 53 (signed), both of which served as templates for proposed federal AI legislation.
**Campaign Funding:** Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit organization that receives significant funding from Anthropic.

**Regulatory Stance:** Wiener explicitly advocates for slowing down AI development to prevent "recursive self-improvement," citing recent METR research as a primary justification for urgent federal oversight.
**Policy Timeline:** Wiener expressed that he does not expect Congress to pass significant AI regulation before the end of 2024, despite his stated preference for immediate action.

title: Anthropic joins AI’s natural gas frenzy, buys $3.4B worth of turbines
author: Tim De Chant
contentSnippet: Anthropic bought billions of dollars' worth of natural gas turbines in a deal that could give it buyer's remorse.

summary.tldr:
Anthropic has moved to secure 1.7 gigawatts of electricity generation capacity by purchasing $3.4 billion worth of natural gas turbines directly from manufacturer Caterpillar. This move marks a significant departure from the company's historical strategy of renting infrastructure, as evidenced by its existing $1.25 billion monthly commitment to xAI for computing power through May 2029. The acquisition was reportedly finalized after the original purchaser, equipment supplier OnePWR, failed to secure financing for the order.

The purchase highlights the intensifying "power crunch" facing AI labs, where backlogs for natural gas turbines and electrical grid connection queues now extend into the early 2030s. By bypassing intermediaries and securing the hardware directly, Anthropic aims to mitigate the risk of losing critical energy capacity to competitors. This trend mirrors broader industry shifts, with Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta also pursuing on-site natural gas power generation to support data center operations, potentially leading to U.S. data center gas consumption exceeding the combined usage of Germany and Japan by 2035.
takeaways: **Investment Scale:** Anthropic is spending $3.4 billion on natural gas turbines capable of generating 1.7 gigawatts of power.
**Strategic Shift:** The company is moving from a pure "rent-only" infrastructure model—exemplified by its $1.25 billion/month xAI compute contract—to direct ownership of power generation assets.
**Supply Chain Constraints:** The acquisition was prompted by multi-year backlogs for turbine manufacturing and grid connection, with the equipment originally intended for supplier OnePWR.
**Market Context:** Analysts project that natural gas prices in some markets could triple by 2030, posing a long-term financial risk to hyperscalers relying on this energy source.

title: Baidu’s ERNIE Evolve Automated Research System Beats NanoChat and NanoGPT Records
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Baidu has just released ERNIE Evolve , an automated research system that improves AI training and inference code. Given a repository, an objective and evaluation criteria, it picks research directions, edits code and runs experiments. Only changes that pass a hidden evaluator and a separate reviewer are kept. Baidu team tested the ERNIE Evolve automated research system on three public benchmarks. It then optimized inference for ERNIE-5.5-Flash, still in development. TL;DR Size: It is an agent system; Baidu has not disclosed which LLMs power its agents. Runs on: Benchmarks used 1 NVIDIA B200 (NanoChat, SOL-ExecBench) and 8×H100 (Speedrun Track 1). Production tests ran on Kunlunxin P800 and GPUs (GPU model not disclosed). Performance: Beat the best public result on 3 of 4 public metrics, and cleared production checks on ERNIE-5.5-Flash. Best: Generation speed on Kunlunxin P800 reached 623.6% of baseline after 4 research rounds. Worst: SOL-ExecBench mean SOL of 0.819, behind the 0.827 leaderboard best. Bottom line (best): Real production inference gains: +33.7% deterministic throughput, +14.9% decode speed. Bottom line (worst): Self-reported, system not released, and public-benchmark margins are small. What is ERNIE Evolve? ERNIE Evolve is an automated research system from Baidu that optimizes code against a fixed, measurable objective. Baidu announced it on X as a practical step toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). In RSI, AI systems improve the software that builds and serves AI. How does ERNIE Evolve work? The system runs 2 nested loops. The outer loop decides what to investigate. The inner loop develops and tests improvements inside each direction. Director: picks the next research direction and a starting code version. It reads an Experience Bank of past results and a Knowledge Base of papers and code. Selector: chooses a candidate from a lane’s tree and names the next hypothesis to test. Executor: implements that plan in an isolated environment. Evaluator: a fixed program kept outside the repository. No agent can see it. Gains must exceed the noise threshold. Reviewer: checks whether a change follows the intended direction or exploits an evaluation loophole. Several research lanes run in parallel, each with its own tree of code versions. Given a repository, an objective and evaluation criteria, it picks research directions, edits code and runs experiments. Only changes that pass a hidden evaluator and a separate reviewer are kept.

Baidu team tested the ERNIE Evolve automated research system on three public benchmarks. It then optimized inference for ERNIE-5.5-Flash, still in development. TL;DR Size: It is an agent system; Baidu has not disclosed which LLMs power its agents.
takeaways: Runs on: Benchmarks used 1 NVIDIA B200 (NanoChat, SOL-ExecBench) and 8×H100 (Speedrun Track 1).
Production tests ran on Kunlunxin P800 and GPUs (GPU model not disclosed).
Performance: Beat the best public result on 3 of 4 public metrics, and cleared production checks on ERNIE-5.5-Flash.
Best: Generation speed on Kunlunxin P800 reached 623.6% of baseline after 4 research rounds.

title: AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security
author: Vishal Sharma
contentSnippet: This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast . Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance. However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof? There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP? Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of fa

summary.tldr:
Researchers at Queen’s University Belfast are highlighting critical security vulnerabilities in multi-agent AI systems, specifically focusing on the risks associated with context recovery attacks and the limitations of current zero-trust architectures (ZTA). As organizations deploy task forces of agents managed by orchestrators for functions like risk assessment and client profiling, they face the challenge of ensuring data hygiene. While systems may implement checkpoints to delete historic logs to prevent decision-making bias, these agents remain susceptible to prompt-injection attacks that can force the recovery of supposedly deleted information.

The article critiques the application of ZTA in agentic workflows, noting that the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) itself becomes a single point of failure that requires implicit trust, contradicting the "never trust, always verify" principle. Furthermore, the rise of "vibe coding"—the practice of using AI models to generate software—poses a significant threat to organizational security. By exposing entire codebases to external, untrusted AI entities, developers risk widespread vulnerability exposure, which complicates the implementation of secure, trusted execution environments for agentic queries.
takeaways: **Context Recovery Risk:** AI agents tasked with deleting historic logs remain vulnerable to future prompts that can force the retrieval of deleted data.

**ZTA Paradox:** Implementing zero-trust architectures for AI agents creates a dependency on the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP), which must be inherently trusted, undermining the core zero-trust philosophy.
**Vibe Coding Vulnerability:** Using external AI models for software development risks leaking proprietary codebases to untrusted entities, creating broad attack surfaces.
**Operational Integrity:** The reliance on autonomous webs of agents requires strict guardrails to prevent systemic failures when operating under low-tolerance conditions.

title: Medium’s new TK app brings AI assistance directly into the writing process
author: Sarah Perez
contentSnippet:
Online publishing platform Medium on Monday launched a new app, called TK, which aims to bring AI technology deeper into the writing process. The idea behind TK is to make it easier to turn ideas into written words by incorporating an AI assistant into the editor itself, allowing users to ask for help by typing “@TK” followed by their request or prompt.

In publishing and journalism, the term “TK” serves as a placeholder used to mark where missing information can be added later. The “TK” stands for “to come,” but uses a “K” instead of “C” as there are few English words where the “tk” letter combination exists, making it stand out more easily in written text where it could be caught by proofreaders.

In Medium’s app , TK takes on a new role as it tries to help users fill in the blanks.

The company suggests the AI assistant could help answer questions that you might normally have to switch to another tab to quickly look up, like how many days are in a particular month. The app could also pull in bits of writing you had previously saved to the app when you were still fleshing out your ideas.

In addition, Medium says TK will ship with particular skills for editorial feedback, headline feedback, and others that could match your draft to the style guide for Medium publications.

Medium’s move to embrace AI in the early stages of writing could prove controversial at a time when the publishing and literary worlds have been reckoning with the role that artificial intelligence has played in the creation of new long-form prose. Multiple authors have lost book deals over suspicions that they used AI technology to help them write, while other literary awards have come under scrutiny after winners were suspected of writing with AI assistance .

While writers have long used automated tools for proofreading and light grammatical edits, there is growing concern across the publishing industry that an AI assistant’s editorial “suggestions” can become the writing itself, instead of being reflective of the thoughts in the writer’s own mind.

But because AI models were trained on human writing, there are also questions around the reliability of AI detection tools in terms of their ability to properly determine when something was written with AI, rather than with its assistance, versus not at all.

TK leans into this debate, taking the side that these nuances will ultimately no

summary.tldr:
Medium has launched "TK," an AI-integrated writing application designed to assist authors throughout the drafting process. Named after the traditional editorial placeholder for "to come," the tool is accessible via the web for all Medium account holders at no cost. Users invoke the AI assistant directly within the editor by typing "@TK," allowing for real-time queries, editorial feedback, headline suggestions, and alignment with specific publication style guides. The platform also serves as a repository for saved ideas and previous drafts, aiming to streamline the transition from conceptualization to finished prose.

Technically, TK functions as a collaborative writing environment that supports Markdown import and export, though it is not a native Markdown editor. To address concerns regarding AI-generated content, Medium has implemented a transparency feature allowing authors to publish notes detailing their use of AI, including specific prompts and source materials. The app supports integration with personal AI agents via an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server or Claude skill, enabling the AI to reference a user's specific project history and stated positions. While the current iteration is web-based, a dedicated desktop application is on the company's development roadmap.
takeaways: **Integration Mechanism:** Users trigger AI assistance within the editor by typing "@TK" to request help, research, or editorial feedback.
**Transparency Features:** The platform includes a disclosure system for authors to document the provenance of their writing, including specific prompts and source materials used.
**Agent Connectivity:** TK supports connections to personal AI agents through an MCP server or Claude skill to access user-specific project memory and context.
**Platform Availability:** The tool is currently available on the web for all Medium account holders, with a desktop application planned for future release.
**Data Security:** The app is designed for collaboration and does not feature end-to-end encryption, though it provides granular access control permissions for shared work.

title: Trump’s 60 Minutes interview touched on AI safety, threat to arrest an AI exec
author: Stevie Bonifield
contentSnippet: Asked about AI executives’ warnings about their models’ safety on 60 Minutes, Trump said, “I think that the risk is not nearly as real as it– as they talk, and I think the risk can be managed, and it’s managed.” He claimed the DOJ is managing that risk, saying, “We had a situation where somebody was reported to us to be doing something bad with AI. We called them very strongly and said, ‘Get ready to go to jail. Please give your wife a kiss good night.’” Trump refused to name the person or company he was referring to, but said it was the leader of an AI company, “One of the big ones.” He claimed that after the threat of arrest, “this person totally changed everything.” Despite previously claiming that “artificial intelligence” is a term used by people he considers the enemy, Trump said AI rather than SI or super intelligence multiple times during the interview. Eventually he said China’s Xi is “…all in to SI, as I call it, because it really is super intelligence. It’s a much better name, I think, because it’s not artificial.” 60 Minutes’s Ross Douthat went on to ask if Trump would work with Democrats on AI safety, and Trump said he “absolutely would,” adding, “I don’t mind guardrails, but I don’t want to put us in a deep second position. We’re leading number one. And China has no guardrails, by the way. [...] They have the guardrails that whatever President Xi says goes. With me, it’s pretty strong, but it’s not quite that strong.”

summary.tldr:
In a recent 60 Minutes interview, Donald Trump addressed AI safety, dismissing the severity of existential risks while asserting that the Department of Justice has already intervened in at least one instance of AI misuse. Trump claimed he personally threatened the leader of a major AI company with imprisonment, stating he told the executive to "get ready to go to jail" and "give your wife a kiss good night," which he alleged resulted in the executive immediately changing their company's practices. He declined to identify the specific individual or organization involved.

Trump also discussed his preferred terminology for the technology, favoring "super intelligence" (SI) over "artificial intelligence," arguing that the latter is a misnomer. He specifically linked the development of SI to geopolitical competition with China, noting that President Xi Jinping is "all in" on the technology. Regarding domestic policy, Trump expressed a willingness to collaborate with Democrats on AI safety guardrails, provided that such regulations do not compromise the United States' lead in the sector. He contrasted the U.S. regulatory environment with China's, characterizing the latter as having no external guardrails other than the absolute authority of President Xi.
takeaways: **Executive Threat:** Trump claimed to have threatened an unnamed leader of a "big" AI company with arrest to force a change in their operational practices.
**Terminology Shift:** Trump explicitly rejected the term "artificial intelligence," preferring "super intelligence" (SI) because he believes the technology is not artificial.
**Geopolitical Stance:** Trump identified China as the primary competitor in SI development, asserting that the U.S. currently holds the lead.
**Regulatory Philosophy:** Trump stated he is open to bipartisan cooperation on AI guardrails, provided they do not hinder U.S. technological dominance.

title: Double Blind Evals: Resolving the Dual Confidentiality Dilemma in AI Safety Auditing
author: Andrew Trask
contentSnippet: AI safety evaluations often involve sensitive prompts and proprietary models. Evaluators want to keep their evaluation prompts secret from model owners to prevent purposeful or incidental data leakage, ensuring longer usefulness of their benchmark. Model owners in turn wish to keep their proprietary model weights and inference code within their own secure infrastructure to protect their IP. We present a way forward for "double-blind evals", which provide cryptographic guarantees that an evaluator's prompts are not shared with the model owner, while simultaneously maintaining the confidentiality of the model weights and inference code. To accomplish this, we use secure enclaves that encrypt data in RAM at the hardware level. In a world-first pilot, we test this approach by evaluating a proprietary Google DeepMind model (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite) against a selection of the private AILuminate benchmark corpus, using an NVIDIA H100 secure enclave on Google Cloud Platform, and using OpenMined's PySyft to maintain data and model privacy. We believe this effort marks the first use of this technology to provide mutual secrecy for one organization's frontier-class proprietary model weights and another organization's closed benchmark.

We present a way forward for "double-blind evals", which provide cryptographic guarantees that an evaluator's prompts are not shared with the model owner, while simultaneously maintaining the confidentiality of the model weights and inference code. title: Disney and Adobe are building generative AI tools together
author: Jess Weatherbed
contentSnippet: The Walt Disney Company has teamed up with Adobe to develop proprietary “artist-led” generative AI models to support Disney’s production pipeline. The multiyear partnership was announced today at Adobe’s MAX conference, and it will see Adobe providing Disney with early access to its latest technologies for everything from Disney’s theme parks and cruise line to ESPN content. Disney and Adobe will also collaborate “to explore emerging technologies, including responsibly developed AI,” according to Adobe’s press release: > With Adobe Firefly Foundry, Disney will work directly with Adobe on generative AI models tailored to Disney’s properties that are human-centered and artist-led. Customized on Disney properties, these proprietary models are trained on unique world knowledge (character attributes, environments, visual styles) to generate commercially safe and production-ready outputs, while accelerating work and enabling the development of more creative projects. The announcement builds on the existing relationship between the two companies, with Adobe noting that Disney’s Imagineering R&D division is already using the Firefly AI platform for theme park development. Adobe will contribute to “expand internal creative workflows” at Walt Disney Studios and identify how AI can be used to shape ESPN content and “enhance the engagement with sports fans.” This is the latest example of Disney embracing generative AI tools, following a previous deal with OpenAI and involvement with Character.AI’s bankruptcy. Bloomberg reported last week that Disney is gearing up to lay off thousands of staffers and targeting 20 percent annual cost savings, in what’s expected to be its fourth round of job cuts in 2026.

summary.tldr:
The Walt Disney Company has entered a multiyear partnership with Adobe to develop proprietary, "artist-led" generative AI models tailored specifically for Disney’s production pipelines. Announced at Adobe’s MAX conference, the collaboration leverages Adobe Firefly Foundry to train models on Disney’s internal intellectual property, including character attributes, specific visual styles, and environmental assets. The initiative aims to produce commercially safe, production-ready outputs across Disney’s diverse business units, ranging from theme park development and cruise line operations to content creation for ESPN.

This partnership expands an existing relationship where Disney’s Imagineering R&D division has already integrated the Adobe Firefly platform into its theme park design workflows. Beyond creative production, the companies intend to explore how these AI tools can enhance fan engagement for ESPN and streamline internal workflows at Walt Disney Studios. This move follows Disney’s previous engagements with OpenAI and Character.AI, occurring alongside broader corporate efforts to achieve 20 percent annual cost savings and ongoing workforce restructuring.
takeaways: **Technology Platform:** Utilization of Adobe Firefly Foundry to build custom, proprietary generative AI models trained on Disney-specific world knowledge.
**Operational Scope:** Integration across Walt Disney Studios, Disney Imagineering R&D, ESPN content production, and theme park/cruise line operations.
**Strategic Objective:** Development of "human-centered" and "artist-led" AI tools designed to ensure commercially safe, production-ready assets while reducing operational costs.
**Corporate Context:** The partnership aligns with Disney’s broader 2026 financial strategy, which targets 20 percent annual cost savings and includes significant workforce reductions.

title: Hold up — I had a great time talking to the RIAA guy
author: Nilay Patel
contentSnippet: Today, I’m talking with Mitch Glazier, who is CEO and chairman of the RIAA. This conversation was a real full-circle moment for me: I was in college when Napster hit, and the RIAA became everyone’s villain for suing kids for downloading music. My entire career got on track when I was in college. Napster came out, my university banned Napster from the school network, and I decided right then I was going to go b

summary.tldr:
Nilay Patel of The Verge interviews Mitch Glazier, CEO and Chairman of the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA), regarding the organization's current stance on generative AI. The discussion centers on the RIAA's opposition to AI companies training models on copyrighted music without authorization, a position that aligns the record labels with broader public sentiment against AI-generated content.

The conversation explores the legal complexities surrounding AI-driven deepfakes, the potential for legislative intervention, and the practical challenges of implementing AI detection and labeling systems. Glazier and Patel examine the necessity of cooperation from major distribution platforms like Spotify and YouTube to make such detection frameworks effective, while also addressing the tension between protecting intellectual property and preserving freedom of expression.
takeaways: **RIAA Stance:** The organization is actively lobbying for legal changes and filing lawsuits against AI companies for unauthorized training on copyrighted works.
**Core Conflict:** The RIAA identifies AI-generated content as a threat to artists and labels, specifically citing the unauthorized use of creative works and the proliferation of AI-generated 'slop'.
**Implementation Challenges:** Effective AI detection and labeling systems are contingent upon the participation of major streaming platforms, including Spotify and YouTube.
**Legal Scope:** The discussion highlights the difficulty of regulating AI deepfakes without inadvertently infringing upon other forms of protected expression.

title: Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context
author: Hugging Face Blog
contentSnippet:
A compound AI approach to Japanese personas grounded in real-world distributions

Open Data Breaking Down Privacy Barriers to Pave the Way for AI in Finance

In the financial sector, the utilization of real-world data faces significant constraints due to strict privacy regulations, compliance requirements, and the need for advanced domain expertise. In this context, the development of agentic AI in the financial domain requires synthetic data capable of avoiding the risks of using real data while reflecting demographics, household structures, and asset statuses to reproduce diverse, realistic financial scenarios.

To address these challenges, Elith and NVIDIA have released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan , a financial domain extension of the open-source persona dataset " Nemotron-Personas-Japan ." To our knowledge, it is the first open persona dataset at million-record scale that pairs Japan’s official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. Built upon official government statistics, this dataset was developed using NeMo SDG-PGMs , a probabilistic graphical model framework for synthetic data generation (SDG), and NeMo Data Designer , an enterprise synthetic data generation system. Furthermore, to enhance the practical utility of the dataset in financial use cases, it was designed by incorporating insights and feedback provided by leading domestic financial institutions and industry associations, including Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association (FDUA).

This dataset expands the environment where Japanese developers and enterprises can develop and evaluate AI tailored to local and industry requirements, without using real customer data. Released under the CC BY 4.0 license, it is available for commercial use. From building conversational agents to customer simulation and model evaluation, it supports practical financial AI development . The Nemotron-Personas collection , including Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, is designed to seamlessly integrate with the user simulation framework NeMo User Sim , enabling instant execution of simulations drawn from diverse distributions consistent with the real world.

What’s in the Dataset?

9M personas total (1M records x 9 personas each), written in natural Japanese

50 fields per record

summary.tldr:
Elith and NVIDIA have released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, a synthetic dataset containing 9 million personas designed to support financial AI development within the Japanese market. As an extension of the Nemotron-Personas-Japan collection, this dataset is the first of its scale to integrate official Japanese government demographic and labor statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. It is released under a CC BY 4.0 license, enabling commercial use for training conversational agents, simulating customer interactions, and evaluating model performance without the privacy risks associated with real-world customer data.

The dataset was constructed using NVIDIA’s NeMo Data Designer and the NeMo SDG-PGMs (Probabilistic Graphical Model) framework, with text generation powered by the Gemma-4-31B-it model. Each of the 9 million records includes 50 fields—comprising 9 persona fields, 11 attributes, and 30 contextual fields—totaling approximately 1.5 billion tokens. The data covers over 1,600 occupation categories and incorporates granular details on education, life stages, household assets, and digital literacy to ensure realistic representation. The release is designed to integrate directly with the NeMo User Sim framework for immediate execution of user simulations.

This initiative aims to lower barriers for Japanese financial institutions, startups, and developers by providing high-quality, culturally grounded data that avoids Western-centric biases. The release coincides with the launch of Nemotron-PII-Japan, a companion dataset of 100,000 synthetic business documents containing labeled personal information, intended for testing data redaction and privacy protection pipelines. Key industry partners involved in the development include Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association (FDUA).
takeaways: **Dataset Scale:** Contains 9 million total personas (1 million records with 9 personas each) across 50 fields, totaling approximately 1.5 billion tokens.
**Technical Stack:** Built using NVIDIA’s NeMo Data Designer, NeMo SDG-PGMs (Apache-2.0), and the Gemma-4-31B-it (Apache-2.0) model for Japanese text generation.

**Data Composition:** Includes 1,600+ occupation categories and 30 contextual fields based on official Japanese government statistics, covering demographics, household finances, and financial literacy.
**Licensing and Availability:** Released under the CC BY 4.0 license for both commercial and non-commercial use, designed for integration with the NeMo User Sim framework.
**Companion Release:** Launched alongside Nemotron-PII-Japan, which provides 100,000 synthetic business documents with labeled PII for training and testing data protection models.

title: Jonathan Kanter is using AI to take on Big Tech
author: Lauren Feiner
contentSnippet: When Jonathan Kanter stepped down as head of the Justice Department’s Antitrust Division in 2024, he set out to keep fighting to dismantle illegal monopolies. But this time, he’s continuing the fight in the private sector, and with a perhaps unexpected tool: AI. Alongside former acting Antitrust Division chief Doha Mekki, Kanter recently launched a new tech startup, FluxCap. The team is stacked with former DOJ staffers and former Palantir engineers, and it’s selling an AI-based legal research and analysis tool that helps plaintiffs build and strengthen cases against the kinds of well-heeled companies Kanter and Mekki took on at the Antitrust Division. FluxCap is launching with a focus on antitrust cases, but it plans to expand into other practice areas as well. Kanter imagines FluxCap as a “force multiplier” for antitrust watchdogs taking on powerful opponents in Big Tech and elsewhere. “This, to me, it’s existential,” he tells The Verge in an interview. “Because it’s the only way that enforcement is going to work in the long term, is if technology and other tools are able to help scarce resources go significantly further than they can today.” FluxCap’s platform, built off proprietary technology and existing large language models, is primarily intended for research and analysis. It’s trained to pick up the facts and legal framework that will determine whether a case succeeds, then find potential holes in attorneys’ logic. To help attorneys prepare for trial, FluxCap can also help sift through vast piles of discovery materials, searching for signals that a company acted in anticompetitive ways. It’s part of a wave of legal tech tools that are using AI to try to help lawyers do more with less and make the legal process more efficient. Getting the tool to find relevant evidence was one of the hardest parts, Kanter says. Executives are unlikely to come out and say they’re monopolists, but surrounding context can give a very specific meaning to certain messages. In the antitrust trial against Live Nation-Ticketmaster, for example, the government played a recorded phone call between the Live Nation CEO and a customer who decided to switch to a different ticketing platform. In response, the CEO reminded the customer that a new arena in town could make it harder to deliver as many concerts to his venue. The customer testified he took it as a “not-so-veiled” threat t

summary.tldr: Former DOJ Antitrust Division head Jonathan Kanter and former acting chief Doha Mekki have launched FluxCap, a legal technology startup designed to assist plaintiffs in antitrust litigation. The company, which employs a team of former DOJ staffers and Palantir engineers, provides an AI-powered platform for legal research, evidence analysis, and case strategy. By leveraging proprietary technology alongside existing large language models, the tool is specifically engineered to identify anticompetitive signals within massive discovery datasets and evaluate the strength of legal arguments, aiming to serve as a 'force multiplier' for under-resourced antitrust enforcers and private plaintiffs.
takeaways: **Core Functionality:** FluxCap is designed to parse complex discovery materials to identify anticompetitive behavior, specifically training models to detect nuanced threats or coercive language that standard legal research tools often overlook.

**Resource Scaling:** Kanter claims the platform provides the effective manpower of '20-plus people working around the clock,' allowing smaller legal teams to compete with the massive document review capabilities of trillion-dollar corporations.

**Market Context:** The startup addresses a significant resource gap; the DOJ Antitrust Division’s FY2026 budget is $245 million with roughly 400 attorneys, a figure Kanter notes is dwarfed by the legal budgets of the Big Tech firms they target.
**Early Adoption:** The firm has already secured antitrust boutique Kressin Powers as an initial customer and is currently in discussions with both public and private sector enforcement entities.

**Development Origins:** The project builds upon internal efforts Kanter led at the DOJ to modernize case management, including a $45.5 million Tech Modernization Fund grant that the agency secured but did not fully implement during his tenure.

title: Exclusive: FormAssembly overhauls its platform to expand into AI-powered process automation
author: Paul Gillin
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 09:00 EST / NOVEMBER 09 2026

Exclusive: FormAssembly overhauls its platform to expand into AI-powered process automation

FormAssembly Inc. , a provider of online data collection and workflow automation software, today announced a complete platform overhaul that expands its capabilities beyond building forms to automating complex business processes using artificial intelligence.

The new platform, which the company said took seven months to develop, combines form creation, workflow automation, integrations and compliance management in a single no-code environment.

It also introduces conversational AI agents that can collect information through natural language interactions and support for the Model Context Protocol, enabling external AI agents to interact with FormAssembly’s software.

The launch marks a significant expansion for the 20-year-old company, which has traditionally focused on helping organizations collect structured information securely and integrate it into business applications. “We’re about how people share information with organizations and what happens after that,” said founder and Chief Executive Cedric Savarese.

The new platform builds on the AI assistant FormAssembly introduced last October , which enabled users to generate forms and configure workflows using natural language instructions. The latest release extends those capabilities to entire business processes, including approvals, document generation, electronic signatures and payments.

For example, a municipal government could describe an application process for obtaining a permit to hold an event in a public park. The platform’s assistant, called Fai, could then generate the necessary forms, approval workflows and documentation requirements.

“You can explain what you need in plain English to your agent, and the agent will build the entire process in a couple of minutes,” Savarese said.

FormAssembly claims the AI-assisted builder can reduce development time from days or weeks to minutes. Savarese said the company based those estimates on recreating existing customer workflows using the new platform.

A second major addition is conversational intake agents that replace traditional forms with interactive voice or text conversations. The agents use predefined data structures to guide conversations, answer questions and convert unstructured responses into information suita

summary.tldr:
FormAssembly, a 20-year-old data collection and workflow automation firm, has launched a comprehensive platform overhaul that shifts its focus from simple form building to AI-powered business process automation. Developed over seven months, the new no-code environment integrates form creation, workflow management, and compliance tools. The platform features 'Fai,' an AI assistant capable of generating complex workflows—including approvals, document generation, and payments—from natural language prompts, which the company claims reduces development timelines from weeks to minutes.

The platform introduces conversational intake agents that replace static forms with interactive voice or text interfaces, utilizing predefined data structures to guide users and convert unstructured responses into structured data. To ensure security, FormAssembly utilizes frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI under zero-retention agreements. The system also incorporates Model Context Protocol (MCP) support, allowing external AI agents to interact with FormAssembly workflows, and includes a governance layer that flags potential compliance violations for human review rather than blocking them automatically.
takeaways: **AI Integration:** The platform uses frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI with zero-retention agreements to ensure customer data privacy.
**Development Efficiency:** FormAssembly claims its AI-assisted builder can reduce the time required to create complex business workflows from days or weeks to minutes.
**Interoperability:** The platform supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling external AI agents to manage and execute workflows directly within the software.
**Governance Features:** New compliance tools evaluate workflows against predefined or custom policies, flagging potential violations for human oversight before publication.
**Migration Timeline:** Existing customers are not required to migrate until January 2027, with pricing for the new automation features yet to be finalized.

title: Practice Makes Precise: At CoRL, NVIDIA and Partners Reveal How Robots Rehearse Delicate Work in Simulation
author: Sasa Docca
contentSnippet: Simulation, which has long been the proving ground for robots learning to walk, roll and hop, is now helping researchers teach robots tasks that require a finer touch: aligning gears, connecting cables and assembling small components. The shift from locomotion to manipulation is taking center stage at this week’s Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in Austin, Texas, alongside the rise of agentic robotics — a new paradigm that integrates frontier agents to create interpretable code for physical robotics systems. At CoRL, NVIDIA is introducing new open robotics technologies, including world action models , simulation tools, benchmarks and agentic workflows. title: Innovating with AI in the special chemicals industry
author: MIT Technology Review Insights
contentSnippet: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance. Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.” Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust. “Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers. title: Evolving Infra: Agent-Adaptive LLM Serving at Scale
author: Hao Kang
contentSnippet: Agentic workloads are a major source of LLM inference demand. Existing prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated serving systems offer limited flexibility for runtime adaptation of compute allocation and KV cache management, and rely on coarse signals that only partly capture the diverse and dynamic agent workload. These limitations lead to load imbalance between prefill and decode nodes and eviction of KV caches that agents will reuse. We present Evolving Infra, an agent-adaptive serving framework that adapts compute allocation to agent workloads and KV cache management to agent context management at runtime. We decouple compute allocation from key--value (KV) cache management, allowing nodes to switch efficiently between prefill and decode. Building on this design, an online planner matches the PD split to workload composition, while an agent-aware distributed KV manager guides cache eviction and transfer with signals from agent context management. Across coding, math, and computer-use tasks with GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 on up to 256 GB300 GPUs, Evolving Infra reduces mean end-to-end request latency and P95 TTFT by up to 4.1x and 14x over Dynamo, NVIDIA's production framework.

title: Reconfigurable Action Theories: A Formal Foundation for Dynamically Composable Agent Harnesses
author: Jianmin Ji
contentSnippet: Action theories typically fix their vocabulary and causal laws, whereas agent harnesses can change their tools, providers, and policies during execution. We introduce Reconfigurable Action Theories (RAT), in which actions can change the action theory itself. A theory module in RAT contains a vocabulary, causal laws, and an initializer. A RAT configuration records the active modules and the world state. Module loading and unloading are represented by actions governed by ordinary causal laws. RAT retains the standard causal action semantics of its language fragment when the active module set is fixed. We give sufficient conditions for at most one next configuration, preservation of existing behavior when a module is added, and equal results when modules are loaded in either order. We establish the computational complexity of reasoning tasks in RAT and translate finite RAT systems into nonmonotonic causal theories and Answer Set Programming (ASP), preserving bounded executions. Experiments compare finite RAT models with executions of official DeepSeek Harness, Pi, and OpenHands implementations. RAT provides a formal basis for checking how component changes affect a harness's available actions, behavior, and reachable goals.

title: Let the Fixer Decide: Training a Code Localizer from the Fixer's Likelihood
author: Khalil Hennara
contentSnippet: Code localizers are usually trained to predict the files a reference patch edits, but the code a fixer needs to read is not the same as the code it changes. We propose Fixer-Guided Localization (FGL): the localizer proposes several localizations, a frozen fixer scores each by how likely it makes a verified patch, and the localizer is trained on these scores with weighted supervised fine-tuning, without running tests and without reinforcement learning. We build the full pipeline on Gemma 4 E4B for the Kaggle Gemma-4 Developer Agent competition, from 1,629 test-verified Kimi K3 trajectories. The FGL target helps the fixer find the bug as often as the teacher's localization while using 27.5% less code. On the development set, one EM round moves the agent in the expected direction compared with a matched control: more tasks reach a patch (53 vs. 46), fewer tasks get stuck reading files that do not exist (43 vs. 54), and more tasks are solved (8 vs. 6). Training also changes how the agent works: trained agents explore about three times more than the base model and write far fewer wrong patches, and the single agent solves up to 11 of 78 tasks, against 8 for the base model. An analysis of 13 evaluation runs identifies what limits a 4B agent under an 8-minute budget (time, repetition loops and edit quality) and gives practical lessons for training small coding agents. All data, code and adapters are publicly available.

title: Translating KV Caches Between Hybrid-Attention Language Models: MLA Latents, Linear-Attention States and Sparse-Attention Indexers
author: Povilas Kvedaras
contentSnippet: A model that takes over another model's conversation must normally re-read the whole history; a text hand-off shortens the re-read only by dropping content. KV-cache translation instead maps the source's cache into the target's own format, so the target continues from the full context without re-reading it. It works for grouped-query attention (GQA), but open-weights frontier models now cache compressed latents (MLA), sparse-attention indexer keys and fixed-size linear-attention states. We replicate KV-Lingo on a GQA pair and then give, for each of these objects, where to capture and inject it and a mechanism that reaches native quality. We study two hybrid pairs at 16-48B scale in both directions, Kimi-VL-A3B - Kimi-Linear-48B (MLA - MLA + Kimi Delta Attention) and Qwen3.5-27B - Qwen3.8-27B (Gated DeltaNet hybrids), plus a sparse-attention target (Qwen3.8-27B - Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). MLA latents translate with token-wise linear maps; recurrent states are copied with a closed-form correction or synthesised by replaying the target's own recurrence. Exact long-range recall needs token identity: decoding token ids from the source's layer-0 MLA latent raises needle recall from 0.09 to 0.99 at 2-32K and to 0.83-1.00 at 64K, eight times the longest training prompt. The hybrid full-MLA direction is within the paired confidence interval of native quality on every task metric, and same-shape GDN hybrids reach the native level in both directions (apart from 6% refusals inherited from the source), with time to first token 18.7 and 46.8 times shorter than a re-read at 64K tokens. Segment-wise multi-turn transfer stays at the re-prefill level; naive re-translation collapses. On the sparse-attention target, predicted indexer keys recall the needle as well as the target's own keys (one seed). We state as a hypothesis how the recipes transfer to 300B+ hybrid flagships.

title: Reason Machines Open-Sources Aspen, a Git Server Built for AI Agents
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Reason Machines has released Aspen , an open-source Git server for AI agent traffic. It targets repositories that hundreds of agents push to at once. Aspen independently implements the design OpenAI described for Pando. TL;DR Size: One Rust binary. Branches live in PostgreSQL (or SQLite), packs live in object storage. Runs on: A laptop ( aspen dev ), one host via Docker Compose, or Helm and Terraform clouds. Performance: Pushes to different branches never wait on each other, and fetches reuse stored packs. Best: 567 pushes per second sustained for 5 minutes on one 8-core server (self-reported). Worst: Landing on main runs at about 4 per second, and the project is pre-alpha. Bottom line: Best: per-branch writes remove the per-repository push ceiling. Worst: no releases, no web UI, and the 24-hour durability gate is not met. What is Aspen? Aspen is a self-hostable Git server from Reason Machines that scales writes per branch, not per repository. It speaks plain Git over HTTPS and SSH. Packs go to S3-compatible object storage; branch history goes to PostgreSQL. Why do classic Git servers struggle with AI agents? An agent pushes every few minutes, and CI fetches after each push. Per Reason Machines , a classic server queues every push to a repository together. It also builds a fresh pack for every fetch. Server work grows with clients, not with new code. OpenAI hit this wall and built Pando. It cut median push latency by nearly 5x and serves nearly a petabyte daily. How does Aspen work? Aspen follows Pando and drops 2 claims most Git servers keep. Per-branch compare-and-swap Each branch is a chain of versions in one Postgres row. A push uploads its pack, then moves the branch with one compare-and-swap. Pushes to different branches never wait for each other. If 2 pushes race on one branch, one wins. The other gets Git’s usual “fetch first” error. The cost: branches may be read at slightly different moments. Stored packs instead of per-client packs Aspen never unpacks a push. It checks the pack, completes missing bases and stores it as-is. A fetch streams stored packs the client lacks, recompressing nothing. Signed URLs can serve packs from a CDN. Trunk-only advertisement and compaction A push sees only the trunk branch, so negotiation stays small with a million branches. Background compaction merges packs 16 at a time, in levels like a log-structured merge tree.

summary.tldr:
Reason Machines has released Aspen , an open-source Git server for AI agent traffic. It targets repositories that hundreds of agents push to at once. Aspen independently implements the design OpenAI described for Pando.

TL;DR Size: One Rust binary. Branches live in PostgreSQL (or SQLite), packs live in object storage. Runs on: A laptop ( aspen dev ), one host via Docker Compose, or Helm and Terraform clouds.
takeaways: Performance: Pushes to different branches never wait on each other, and fetches reuse stored packs.
Best: 567 pushes per second sustained for 5 minutes on one 8-core server (self-reported).
Worst: Landing on main runs at about 4 per second, and the project is pre-alpha.
Bottom line: Best: per-branch writes remove the per-repository push ceiling.

title: NVIDIA Announces New Planned Investments in Korean Startups at the MSIT-NVIDIA AI Startup Partnership Forum
author: NVIDIA Writers
contentSnippet: Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT and NVIDIA hosted the MSIT -NVIDIA AI Startup Partnership Forum at COEX. Representatives from the Ministry of Science and ICT and NVIDIA met with over 20 Korean startups across foundation models, physical AI, AI infrastructure and AI semiconductors. NVIDIA also announced an investment in Korean startup Point2 , with additional investments planned in Motif Technologies , RLWRLD and Upstage. Point2 Technology, an AI interconnect company, builds scalable, radio frequency-based interconnects that move data between chips and racks in AI factories, offering an innovative alternative to conventional copper and optical interconnect solutions for AI cluster scale-up, delivering the reach, performance and efficiency needed for next-generation AI infrastructure. Motif Technologies , a Seoul-based AI lab, develops foundation models for building AI agents that carry out complex tasks, including Motif-3, a large language model released with open weights. RLWRLD, a physical AI startup based in San Francisco, Seoul and Tokyo, develops robotics foundation models that enable humanoid and industrial robots to perform complex real-world tasks that require five-finger dexterity, such as precisely inserting components, threading nuts onto bolts and kitting parts from moving conveyors. Upstage , a Korean enterprise AI company, develops Solar language models and document AI tools that help businesses extract information from complex documents, streamline workflows and build AI applications for everyday operations. The companies represent work across the full AI stack , from infrastructure to models to robotics applications. The planned investments build on NVIDIA’s work with Korea’s startup and venture community, including more than 1,000 Korea-based members of NVIDIA Inception , a program that helps startups grow with access to preferred pricing, technical expertise and opportunities for investor introductions.

title: 0sec Labs Open-Sources 0, an AI Security Harness With Web UI, CLI and MCP
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Zurich-based 0sec Labs has released 0 , an open-source AI security harness. It runs vulnerability investigations, code review, pentesting, reverse engineering and fix generation. Developers drive it from a local browser console, a headless CLI or an MCP server . The 0sec Labs open-source AI security harness is licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0 and ships as a research preview. TL;DR Wrapper: It is a software harness. Bring your own LLM from 14 listed providers . Runs on: Apple Silicon macOS, x64 or ARM64 Linux, or the ghcr.io/0sec-labs/0 container. No GPU needed. Model inference runs at your provider. Performance: Strong self-reported CTF scores, plus a public record of upstream Linux kernel fixes. Best: 93/95 (97.9%) on XBOW web CTFs, gpt-5.4 cohort, any-success grouping. Worst: Black-box-only XBOW union of 81/104 (77.9%) . A 2026 cold run scored 45/104 (43.3%) . Bottom line: Best: one harness spans web, source, packages, binaries and kernels. Worst: headline scores are self-reported and not pass@1. What is 0 from 0sec Labs? 0 is a control plane around LLMs and security tools. It is not a model. You plug in a provider, and 0 runs scoped workflows against authorized targets. The research team describes it as a self-evolving, multi-model harness . 0sec Labs is backed by Y Combinator . How does the 0 harness work? The architecture docs state one rule: reproduce before trusting. Agentic scans follow a conceptual pipeline: Plan, Discover, Attack: a research agent picks vulnerability classes, maps endpoints and tests hypotheses. Triage: filters remove weak findings and check evidence completeness. Verify: a separate session re-exercises each candidate, with 5 turns per finding. Report: outputs include HTML, PDF, SARIF, Markdown and JSON. Web pentesting is shell-first. The agent uses bash with curl, python3 and sqlmap, not a fixed HTTP tool set. Evidence carries a proof grade from candidate to impact-proven . Compiled targets go through 0verse , a separate in-repo engine. It wraps Ghidra, angr and AFL++. Its local MCP server exposes 9 tools for scanning, triage, PoVs and reports. How do developers use it? Installation is one script. Running 0 opens the local browser console without an account.
