title: Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching
author: Chuangtao Ma, Sriom Chakrabarti, Arijit Khan, Bálint Molnár
contentSnippet: Traditional similarity-based schema matching methods fail to resolve semantic ambiguities and conflicts in complex, domain-specific mappings due to a lack of commonsense and domain-specific knowledge. In parallel, large language models (LLMs) without sufficient background knowledge tend to hallucinate, further complicating schema matching. To overcome these limitations, we introduce KG-RAG4SM, a Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching. This method integrates novel retrieval mechanisms, including LLM-based, vector-based, graph traversal-based, and hybrid techniques with advanced reranking schemes to extract the most relevant subgraphs from large external KGs. Our approach achieves superior results without requiring re-training, as evidenced by improvements of 39.79% in precision and 30.56% in F1 score over LLM-based state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods (e.g., Jellyfish-8B) on the MIMIC dataset, and enhancements of 69.20% in precision and 21.99% in F1 score over pre-trained language model (PLM)-based SOTA methods (e.g., SMAT) on the Synthea dataset. Additionally, KG-RAG4SM scales effectively across KGs from commonsense KGs to domain-specific ones, while its instruction-tuning knowledge exclusion component ensures truthful performance in end-to-end schema matching tasks despite the suboptimal relevance of KG context. Our empirical analysis and case studies from real-world scenarios show that the hallucination problem in LLMs for schema matching is well mitigated by our solution.

title: SkinMind: Equipping Agentic RAG with Human-Inspired Graph Probing for Reliable Dermatology AI
author: Jing Hao, Weinan Zhou, Zhihong Lu, Yaling Shen
contentSnippet: Reliable dermatology AI requires access to verifiable evidence distributed across heterogeneous textual and visual sources. However, conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically relies on one-shot retrieval from flat corpora, limiting its ability to adapt retrieval granularity, explore multi-hop relations, and integrate multimodal clinical evidence. We introduce SkinMind, a multimodal agentic RAG framework that equips policy models with human-inspired graph probing for autonomous evidence seeking. SkinMind organizes retrieval as an iterative interaction between an orchestrator and a graph environment. Through eight hierarchical graph-probing tools, the orchestrator progressively identifies relevant entities, inspects node-level information, traverses relations and paths, and retrieves source-text and visual evidence. This progressive-disclosure design allows the model to adaptively determine the retrieval modality, exploration direction, and evidence granularity while constructing a query-specific evidence subgraph. To support autonomous graph probing, we construct SkinMind-KG from a 62M-token corpus of dermatology guidelines and textbooks and 423K images, guided by a dermatologist-informed schema and a conflict-resolution mechanism. The resulting graph contains over 1.0M nodes and 2.0M edges, unifying textual, relational, and visual evidence for retrieval. Across six dermatology VQA benchmarks and two policy-model settings, SkinMind improves the average score over direct answering by 8.70 and 8.89 points with GPT-5.4-mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash, respectively, while consistently outperforming competing RAG methods. Together, SkinMind and SkinMind-KG provide an effective foundation for evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning in dermatology.

title: Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices
author: Dan Goodin
contentSnippet:
Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password.

The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations.

One connection, works every time, needs no retries

There are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a “*” in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts.

When all the conditions are met, the consequences are high.

“An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password,” Alpine maintainers said Thursday . “It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries.”

When logging into a passwordless account, the attacker can gain access by inputting more than 256 characters in the password field.

Security firm Checkpoint said that the use of the SHA256 or SHA512 functions “matters because sshd borrows that account’s salt. Without it, the attack fails.” Company researchers said their testing also showed that the account must be active, not just hold a hash. Checkpoint further reported that root accounts are safe under the default PermitRootLogin prohibit password setting, though reachable accounts with doas or sudo rights can still become root.

Despite the prerequisites, *sshole —the vulnerability name given by the person who discovered it—likely threatens large numbers of systems. The Docker Hub base image for Alpine has more than 1 billion downloads. Alpine has long been popular in

summary.tldr:
A critical vulnerability, dubbed '*sshole', allows unauthorized remote access to Linux systems running specific configurations of OpenSSH and the musl libc library. The flaw enables attackers to log into systems without a password by inputting more than 256 characters into the password field. Successful exploitation requires three specific conditions: the system must use musl instead of glibc, OpenSSH must be configured without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM), and the target account must be passwordless (indicated by a '*' in the /etc/shadow file) while utilizing SHA256 or SHA512 hashing functions.

While Alpine Linux is the primary distribution identified, the vulnerability potentially impacts any system using the musl/OpenSSH stack, including embedded devices, routers, and containerized environments. Checkpoint researchers confirmed that while root accounts are generally protected by default 'PermitRootLogin prohibit-password' settings, accounts with sudo or doas privileges remain high-value targets. The vulnerability is highly reliable, requiring only a single connection attempt with no retries. Both Alpine and OpenSSH have released patches to mitigate the issue, though the root cause remains a point of contention between OpenSSH maintainers and musl developers regarding responsibility for the implementation error.
takeaways: **Exploitation Mechanism:** Attackers gain access by entering a password string exceeding 256 characters on systems where the target account is configured as passwordless in /etc/shadow.
**System Requirements:** Vulnerability requires the combination of musl libc, OpenSSH without PAM, and the use of SHA256 or SHA512 password hashing.
**Scope of Risk:** Alpine Linux, which has over 1 billion downloads on Docker Hub and is widely used in embedded systems and containers, is the primary affected platform.
**Mitigation Status:** Patches have been issued by both Alpine Linux and OpenSSH; users are advised to update immediately despite the lack of an official CVE designation.
**Security Impact:** While default root logins are typically safe, accounts with administrative privileges (sudo/doas) are susceptible to full system compromise.

title: Google Releases Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: 15-Second AI Video at $0.07 per Second
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Google has released Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash , the newest version of its video generation and editing model. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates and edits clips up to 15 seconds natively. It also cuts the price by 30% compared with Omni 1.1 Flash. The model is generally available on Google Cloud and the Gemini API . For developers, the takeaways are longer clips, fewer re-renders and a lower bill per second. TL;DR Runs on: Google-hosted only (Gemini API, Google Cloud). No open weights, no local deployment. Performance: Google reports better reference adherence and less drift. No 1.2 benchmark scores are published. Best: Native 15-second clips at $0.07 per second of 720p video, about $1.05 per 15-second clip. Worst: Google says fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics still need work. What is Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash? Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is a multimodal video model from Google DeepMind. It takes text, images, short video clips and audio as input. It outputs video with audio. Google’s developer docs describe the Omni line as natively multimodal, with editing handled through the Interactions API. What changed from Omni 1.1 Flash? The launch lists 6 upgrades: Longer clips: Generation and editing now reach 15 seconds, up from 10 seconds in Omni 1.1. Duration control: You set length in 1-second steps from 3 to 15 seconds. Reference adherence: You can combine character, product or style images with motion clips up to 3 seconds. Consistency: Faces, garments, packaging text and brand colors hold across camera angles with less morphing. Speech: Dialogue sounds more natural, with clearer lip-sync and distinct multi-speaker conditioning. Camera control: FPV flythroughs, zoom-outs and orbits show fewer unwanted jump cuts. How does the draft, edit, upscale workflow work? Google frames cost control as a workflow, not just a price. You draft at 360p or 720p. You fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of regenerating the whole clip. Then you upscale the best result to 1080p or 4K. Multi-turn conversational editing now works across full 15-second clips. In practice, you can swap a product, background, lighting or aspect ratio turn by turn. The docs show this through a previous_interaction_id , so the prior video is not re-uploaded. How much does Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash cost? Google prices Omni 1.2 Flash at $0.07 per second of 720p video . Savings are similar at

summary.tldr:
Google has released Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, a multimodal video generation and editing model developed by Google DeepMind. The model accepts text, images, short video clips, and audio as inputs, outputting video with synchronized audio. It natively generates and edits clips up to 15 seconds long—a 50% increase from the 10-second limit in Omni 1.1 Flash—while cutting prices by 30% to $0.07 per second of 720p video, translating to approximately $1.05 per 15-second clip. The model is hosted exclusively on Google Cloud and accessible via the Gemini API, with no open weights or local deployment options available.

Technically, Omni 1.2 Flash introduces 1-second duration controls ranging from 3 to 15 seconds, improved reference adherence combining character, product, or style images with motion clips up to 3 seconds, and enhanced consistency that preserves faces, garments, packaging text, and brand colors across camera angles with reduced morphing. Audio features include more natural dialogue with clearer lip-sync and multi-speaker conditioning, while camera controls show fewer unwanted jump cuts for FPV flythroughs, zoom-outs, and orbits. The workflow utilizes a draft, edit, and upscale methodology where users draft at 360p or 720p, execute multi-turn conversational edits using a previous_interaction_id to avoid re-uploading prior videos, and finally upscale to 1080p or 4K.

Google reports that despite these upgrades, fast sports action, rapid script changes, and complex physics still require improvement. No formal 1.2 benchmark scores were published alongside the release.
takeaways: **Model Specifications:** Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash natively generates and edits 720p video clips up to 15 seconds long, upgraded from the 10-second limit of Omni 1.1 Flash.

**Pricing & Availability:** Priced at $0.07 per second of 720p video (roughly $1.05 per 15-second clip), representing a 30% price cut over Omni 1.1 Flash. Available exclusively via Google Cloud and the Gemini API with no open weights.
**Workflow & Architecture:** Supports multi-turn conversational editing across full 15-second clips using a previous_interaction_id parameter to avoid re-uploading prior source video.
**Known Limitations:** Google acknowledges that fast sports action, rapid script changes, and complex physics remain challenging for the model, and no quantitative benchmark scores were published.

title: Airbnb says it’s launching an AI travel agent in the first half of 2027
author: Sarah Perez
contentSnippet:
Airbnb has teased its plans to build its own AI travel agent before, but on Thursday the company announced that the new AI feature will launch in the first half of 2027. In the company’s Q3 shareholder letter on Thursday , Airbnb also provided more detail about how the agent will work, what it will actually do, and how it’s different from a typical AI chatbot.

In prior interviews, CEO Brian Chesky sketched out the travel company’s approach to AI, describing a plan to build an AI agent that has a richer interface than a conventional chatbot. He also expressed his opinions about how chatbots aren’t the right interface for travel, noting that people take pleasure in the planning process and in anticipating a trip. Any agent that it built, then, shouldn’t take away from the inspiration and the browsing, he told TechCrunch in an interview last month.

Chesky today reiterated that belief, telling analysts on the earnings call that people won’t use one AI agent for everything.

“Today’s AI agents like Muse and Instinct are good at simple routine tasks like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment. But planning a trip is different,” he said. “Travel is aspirational. Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience. In fact, 80% of travelers say they enjoy spending time researching trips. People want to look at photos. They want to compare homes. They want to make decisions with people they’re traveling with,” he continued. “And I don’t think the general-purpose agents are the best to do that. So that is why we are building our own AI agent,” Chesky said.

Airbnb described its agent as having a personalized interface that’s designed specifically for travel, where it will “build an interface” around a user’s question instead of simply responding as a chatbot would.

“What we are doing is developing a custom-designed AI-native experience that responds to what guests are looking for,” Chesky said. “So instead of relying on traditional chat alone, which is very text-heavy—which, again, is definitely not the way you should plan travel, our agent draws from a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface components—maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries—and composes them in real time to match what they’re looking for.”

The exec said the agent will feel “a little bit like generative UI” as it’s designed to offer up “the

summary.tldr:
Airbnb has officially scheduled the launch of its proprietary AI travel agent for the first half of 2027. Announced during the company's Q3 earnings call, the agent is positioned as a departure from standard text-based chatbots, which CEO Brian Chesky argues are ill-suited for the aspirational and visual nature of travel planning. Airbnb cites internal data suggesting 80% of travelers enjoy the research process, necessitating an interface that prioritizes discovery over simple task automation.

The agent will utilize a "generative UI" architecture, drawing from a library of hundreds of travel-specific components—including maps, photos, comparison tools, calendars, and itineraries—to compose real-time, dynamic interfaces tailored to specific user queries. Beyond discovery and booking, the agent is designed to handle post-booking logistics, such as reservation changes, payment disputes, refunds, and 24-hour safety support, leveraging Airbnb’s proprietary data on host-guest interactions. The company intends to eventually expand the agent's scope to include services and experiences beyond home and hotel bookings.

This announcement accompanied strong Q3 financial results, with revenue reaching $4.87 billion, a 19% year-over-year increase that exceeded analyst expectations. Consequently, Airbnb has raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast from the mid-teens to the high teens, signaling a reacceleration of growth for the platform.
takeaways: **Launch Timeline:** The AI travel agent is scheduled for consumer release in the first half of 2027.
**Architectural Approach:** The agent uses a generative UI model that dynamically assembles travel-specific components (maps, photos, itineraries) rather than relying on text-heavy chatbot responses.
**Functional Scope:** The tool will support end-to-end trip management, including reservation modifications, payment resolution, refunds, and 24-hour safety support.
**Financial Performance:** Airbnb reported Q3 revenue of $4.87 billion, representing 19% growth, and increased its 2026 revenue growth outlook to the high teens.

title: StarLoc: A Practical Approach to Encoding Geographic Locators in IPv6 for Starlink
author: Vanya Singla
contentSnippet: LEO satellite networks such as Starlink provide Internet connectivity across continents, oceans, and airspace. IP geolocation providers map Starlink's IPv6 prefixes to locations mainly through its self-published GeoFeed. However, users may be far away from their assigned Points of Presence (PoPs), one label covers an entire prefix, and labels and PoP mappings can change while addresses stay the same. We characterize Starlink's IPv6 addressing using 925 historical GeoFeed snapshots (2024--2026), one year of PoP mappings, and over 7.9 million observed IPv6 addresses. Our findings reveal that customer prefixes lack clear geographic structure, prefix labels lie a median of 540km from their PoPs, and relabeling a single /40 can affect the reported locations of up to 65,536 possible /56 delegations. To address these challenges, we propose StarLoc, a geographic Locator--Identifier separation scheme that embeds terminal location into IPv6 addresses using a resolution-adaptive H3 Locator while preserving existing Starlink prefixes, /56 delegations, and stable Endpoint Identifiers. To balance accuracy and privacy, StarLoc reveals only cells with at least a certain number of terminals, and operators can cap resolution in sensitive regions or withhold location entirely. Unlike topology-based schemes, StarLoc encodes physical location and lets Locators follow moving users.

title: Perplexity launches its own take on AI agents for work
author: Emma Roth
contentSnippet: Perplexity is taking on OpenAI and Anthropic with its own work-focused AI agents. The startup’s new always-on “Teammates” can take on multiple roles within a workspace, while pulling existing projects, skills, and memory from the Perplexity tools you already use. Teammates integrate with Perplexity Computer, an AI system that can deploy agents on your device to complete tasks. But Perplexity says Teammates “build on top” of Computer by offering the ability to collaborate and complete “ongoing, large-scale work.” You can assign each Teammate different jobs that they can perform simultaneously — much like OpenAI’s Dots and Claude Duet. Perplexity’s take on the feature is much more expensive, however, as it requires a subscription to its $200 / month Max plan. [Image: Each Teammate gets their own thread. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/perplexity-teammates.png?quality=90&strip=all] Perplexity notes that you can keep tabs on Teammates’ progress through individual threads in the Perplexity app, as well as interact with them in Slack. “Over time, we envision every org having hundreds of teammates working for each person,” Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas says on X.

summary.tldr:
Perplexity has launched 'Teammates,' a suite of AI agents designed for enterprise workflows that function as persistent, role-based collaborators within a workspace. These agents leverage the company's existing 'Perplexity Computer' system—which enables agents to execute tasks directly on a user's device—to manage ongoing, large-scale projects. Unlike standard chatbot interfaces, Teammates are designed to operate simultaneously, allowing users to assign distinct responsibilities to multiple agents that maintain memory and skill sets derived from the user's existing Perplexity data.

The service is positioned as a direct competitor to OpenAI’s 'Operator' (referred to as 'Dots' in the text) and Anthropic’s 'Claude Duet.' Users can monitor agent progress through dedicated threads within the Perplexity application or via Slack integration. Access to the Teammates feature is gated behind the company’s 'Max' subscription plan, which is priced at $200 per month. CEO Aravind Srinivas has stated that the long-term vision for the platform involves organizations deploying hundreds of these agents to support individual employees.
takeaways: **Product Architecture:** Teammates are built on top of the Perplexity Computer system, enabling agents to perform tasks locally on user devices while maintaining persistent memory of projects and skills.
**Pricing Model:** Access to the Teammates feature requires a Perplexity Max subscription, priced at $200 per month.
**Integration Capabilities:** Agents provide status updates and interaction capabilities through individual threads in the Perplexity app and via Slack.
**Competitive Positioning:** The feature is designed to compete with OpenAI's 'Dots' and Anthropic's 'Claude Duet' by enabling simultaneous, multi-agent collaboration on large-scale work.

title: Baidu Releases ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base: A 280B MoE Base Model With 14B Active Parameters
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Baidu has released ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base , the raw pre-training checkpoint of its new sparse Mixture-of-Experts language model. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base is a 280B-parameter text model from Baidu that activates 14B parameters per token. The weights stop at the end of pre-training, with no mid- or post-training applied. This as a clean starting point for teams that want to compare fine-tuning, instruction tuning or RL methods from one checkpoint. TL;DR Size: 280B total, 14B active per token; 128K training context, 1M for fine-tuning and inference. Runs on: Multi-GPU servers. Baidu’s reference configs use 4-way parallelism in SGLang and vLLM. GPU model and VRAM not disclosed. FP8 and BF16 weights. Performance: Best score on 24 of 30 base-model benchmarks in Baidu’s unified pipeline (self-reported). Best: MMLU-Pro 78.4, ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base at 69.2. Worst: HELMET-Rerank 56.2, behind DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base at 60.0. What is ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base? It is a text-only MoE base model with 43 layers and a 4096 hidden size . It was pre-trained from scratch on 33.5T tokens with the Muon optimizer. The tokenizer has 201,216 entries and groups numbers right-to-left in chunks of up to 3 digits. Activated compute, KV cache and long-context cost were treated as one budget. Pre-training data leaned on repository-scale code and long-context material, since those are hard to add later. How does the ERNIE 5.5 Flash architecture work? Hybrid attention : 37 layers use Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA), which caches 1 entry per 128 tokens. The other 6 layers use Multi-head Latent Attention with sparse attention (MLA + DSA). That means 1 in 7 layers keeps full-context access. HCA layers use 512-dim heads; MLA layers use 256-dim heads. Gated and mixed heads : The attention output gate comes from the low-rank query latent, cutting gate-projection parameters by 75%. Virtual Head Attention adds a lightweight low-rank mix across heads. Multi-Router Latent MoE. Each MoE layer has 512 routed experts (top-10) plus 1 shared expert. Several independent sigmoid routers replace a single router, per Baidu’s Multi-Router paper . Expert FLOPs and communication volume stay unchanged. Experts run in a 2048-d latent space, half the hidden width. ECHO instead of MTP. : ECHO reuses the backbone’s final layer to predict future tokens. The same layer doubles as a built-in draft model for speculative

summary.tldr:
Baidu has released ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base, a 280B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model that activates 14B parameters per token. The release consists of raw pre-training weights without mid- or post-training, intended as a baseline for research into fine-tuning, instruction tuning, and RL methods. The model features a 128K training context window, extendable to 1M tokens for inference and fine-tuning, and supports both FP8 and BF16 precision. It was trained from scratch on 33.5T tokens using the Muon optimizer, with a tokenizer containing 201,216 entries that utilizes right-to-left chunking for numerical data.

Architecturally, the model utilizes 43 layers with a 4096 hidden size, employing a hybrid attention mechanism: 37 layers use Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) with 1:128 token caching, while 6 layers use Multi-head Latent Attention with sparse attention (MLA + DSA). The MoE layers feature 512 routed experts (top-10 selection) plus one shared expert, managed by independent sigmoid routers. Instead of Multi-Token Prediction (MTP), the model uses ECHO, which repurposes the final backbone layer to predict future tokens, serving as a built-in draft model for speculative decoding. Baidu reports the model outperforms DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base on 24 of 30 internal benchmarks, including an MMLU-Pro score of 78.4 compared to 69.2, though it trails on the HELMET-Rerank benchmark.
takeaways: **Architecture Specs:** 280B total parameters, 14B active per token, 43 layers, 4096 hidden size, and 512 routed experts per MoE layer.
**Attention Mechanism:** Hybrid approach using 37 layers of Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) and 6 layers of Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with sparse attention.
**Training Details:** Pre-trained on 33.5T tokens using the Muon optimizer; features a 201,216-entry tokenizer.
**Performance Benchmarks:** Achieved 78.4 on MMLU-Pro (vs. 69.2 for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base) and 56.2 on HELMET-Rerank (vs. 60.0 for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base).
**Deployment:** Supports 4-way parallelism in SGLang and vLLM; utilizes ECHO for speculative decoding instead of MTP.

title: Getting started with Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
author: Adrianna Chudy
contentSnippet: Today, we are announcing the general availability of Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With Web Answer, agent builders get a synthesized, source-cited answer to a natural-language question with a single tool call. They no longer build a search, retrieve, synthesize, and citation pipeline themselves. If you have built agents that need to answer questions from current web sources, you know the pattern: call a search API, decide which results to trust, retrieve and clean page content, prompt a model to synthesize, and engineer citation extraction so the output traces back to a source. Every step is code you maintain, and every step is another place things can go wrong: hallucination when evidence is insufficient, stale content when the index moves, and broken attribution when a claim and its source drift apart. The Web Answer collapses that entire pipeline into one request. You send a question. You get back a cited answer in seconds. In this post, we explain what Web Answer does, compare it with Web Search on AgentCore, show how it works and what it returns, and walk through adding Web Answer to a gateway and calling it from an agent. What Web Answer does Figure 1: Request flow from an agent through the Gateway to Web Answer and back Your agent sends a question to your AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The Gateway authenticates the call with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) or a JSON Web Token (JWT). The Gateway calls Web Answer, a managed connector that AWS owns, using its own service role. Web Answer plans its searches, runs several in parallel, and reads key pages to check the facts. When the evidence is insufficient, it searches again. It then writes an answer that ties each claim to its source URL. The Gateway returns the answer and its citations to your agent as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool result. Web Answer is a managed AgentCore Gateway tool that takes a natural-language question and returns a synthesized answer in seconds grounded in current web sources. Here is what you get back: A grounded, cited answer, where each grounded claim maps to a citation, with a source URL where one is available. Current sources. Web Answer runs new searches for every question, and its model is given today’s date so it can search for up-to-date information. Agentic search: Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several

summary.tldr:
Amazon has announced the general availability of Web Answer, a managed tool within Amazon Bedrock AgentCore designed to automate the retrieval, synthesis, and citation of web-based information. By integrating this capability, developers can replace custom-built search pipelines—which typically involve manual search API calls, content cleaning, and citation engineering—with a single tool call. The service is designed to mitigate common issues in agentic workflows, such as hallucinations due to insufficient evidence, stale data, and broken attribution links.

When an agent sends a natural-language query to the AgentCore Gateway, Web Answer executes a multi-step process: it plans parallel searches, verifies facts by reading key pages, and performs iterative searching if initial evidence is insufficient. The final output is a synthesized response where every claim is mapped to a specific source URL. The service authenticates via AWS IAM or JWT and returns results to the agent as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool result, ensuring the model is provided with the current date to maintain temporal relevance for all queries.
takeaways: **Core Functionality:** Web Answer collapses search, retrieval, synthesis, and citation extraction into a single managed tool call within Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
**Authentication:** The AgentCore Gateway supports authentication via AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) or JSON Web Tokens (JWT).
**Output Format:** Returns a grounded, synthesized answer where each claim is explicitly mapped to a source URL via the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
**Search Methodology:** The tool performs parallel searches and iterative fact-checking, automatically re-searching if the initial evidence is deemed insufficient.

title: Vera Delivers the Best of Both Worlds: Highest Throughput and Fastest Agents
author: Hannah Coutand
contentSnippet: AI agents do more than generate answers. They search for information, query databases, write and test code and take action. Each of those steps relies on a CPU, with agents moving between GPU reasoning and CPU execution throughout a task. As businesses put more agents to work, AI factories need CPUs that can execute those steps quickly and support many agents at once, all within the limits of available power. What this means: AI infrastructure providers need to support more agents without making each one wait longer to get work done. And critically, AI factories are power limited. This means operators need to choose infrastructure that maximizes the work done for every watt. Why it matters: NVIDIA Vera delivers both fast agent performance and high capacity per watt within a single CPU. That gives providers one CPU for a range of agent workloads, rather than having to mix and match fast and dense x86 parts to balance speed and capacity. The data that proves it: In a 100-megawatt data center comparison, NVIDIA found that a single Vera CPU performs better than the fastest x86 CPU and the most energy-efficient x86 CPU. Vera delivers industry-leading agent speed while enabling 1.6x more agents per watt versus the fastest x86 CPU. Vera delivers 2x faster agent speed with leading energy efficiency compared with the most energy-efficient x86 CPU. Partners are already putting Vera to work. Early adopters see the same exceptional performance in production-style tests: Perplexity : Ran agentic coding tasks 1.5x faster with Vera than on traditional CPUs. Perplexity plans to deploy Vera in an upcoming production system. DeepInfra : Delivered up to 2.2x speed of the best x86 processor on agentic orchestration for its production agent workload, achieving the fastest of the four architectures tested. ClickHouse : Its standard binary, with no Vera-specific tuning, scaled near-linearly across 176 cores and topped the ClickBench hardware leaderboard. DuckLabs : Achieved about 1.5x the median TPC-H SF1000 performance of an Intel Xeon 6 baseline. Daytona : Brought 1,000 agent sandboxes online in 10.8 seconds, and achieved 12.7 completed jobs per second at 2,000 concurrent sandboxes, using Vera versus 88.4 seconds with x86. Modal : Achieved up to 2x sandbox throughput per core versus comparable x86 hardware, with gains that grow under heavy load. Learn more about the NVIDIA Vera

summary.tldr:
NVIDIA has introduced Vera, a CPU architecture designed to optimize AI agent workflows that require frequent switching between GPU-based reasoning and CPU-based execution. By consolidating high-speed performance and energy efficiency into a single processor, Vera aims to eliminate the need for data centers to mix and match specialized x86 hardware for different agent tasks. NVIDIA claims that in a 100-megawatt data center simulation, Vera outperforms both the fastest and the most energy-efficient x86 CPUs currently available.

Technical benchmarks indicate that Vera provides 1.6x more agents per watt compared to the fastest x86 CPU and delivers 2x faster agent speed than the most energy-efficient x86 alternative. Early production-style testing by partners demonstrates significant gains: Perplexity reported 1.5x faster agentic coding tasks, while DeepInfra achieved 2.2x the speed of the best x86 processor for agentic orchestration. Additionally, Daytona demonstrated a reduction in sandbox deployment time from 88.4 seconds on x86 to 10.8 seconds on Vera, while Modal observed up to 2x higher sandbox throughput per core under heavy load.
takeaways: **Agent Throughput:** Daytona achieved 12.7 completed jobs per second at 2,000 concurrent sandboxes using Vera.
**Database Performance:** ClickHouse scaled near-linearly across 176 cores on Vera, topping the ClickBench hardware leaderboard without specific tuning.
**Energy Efficiency:** Vera provides 1.6x more agents per watt than the fastest x86 CPU and 2x faster agent speed than the most energy-efficient x86 CPU.
**Benchmark Comparison:** DuckLabs recorded 1.5x the median TPC-H SF1000 performance compared to an Intel Xeon 6 baseline.
**Deployment Speed:** Daytona brought 1,000 agent sandboxes online in 10.8 seconds on Vera, compared to 88.4 seconds on x86 hardware.

title: Meta says US users can now video chat with their Muse AI avatar
author: Sarah Perez
contentSnippet:
Muse Voice, a feature that lets users call and video chat with Meta’s consumer AI agent, Muse, is now available to everyone in the U.S., the company announced on Thursday.

First introduced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September, the video-chatting feature involves new AI models, Muse Realtime Avatar and Muse Realtime Voice technology, which help power the digital avatar that chats with the user.

While other AI competitors offer voice chat features, Meta’s Muse offers a cute, animated avatar (nicknamed Jolly), which users interact with as they ask questions or request tasks to be handled on their behalf. Users can also customize the avatar as they choose, changing it to something that looks more like a person, animal, or some other character.

The company believes that anthropomorphizing Muse in this way could make consumers feel more connected to their AI agent — a connection that could grow even stronger as they begin to engage in live conversations with it.

As the Muse avatar speaks, Meta says it will use “subtle expressions and gestures” that match the tone of the conversation. (Muse doesn’t actually “see” the user, but it hears them and reacts based on their conversations.)

The news of the rollout was announced via blog post and on X by Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, who shared a demo of his Muse in action. The video saw Wang joking around, referencing his love of posting memes on X, which he told his Muse may have gotten him in trouble with his boss. His Muse, a fluffy white dog, responds with a suggestion to add disclaimers to those memes that could be misinterpreted as Meta endorsing anything risqué. (Ha!)

The added support for video chats and calls comes just before Meta’s plan to launch a Tamagotchi-like wearable device for its Muse AI agent before year-end. When the device arrives, the digital avatar will appear on its small screen, letting users talk to the agent, which can then reply or carry out tasks for them.

Meta says the real-time conversations are supported on mobile, web, and Mac and will later come to its AI Glasses and the upcoming “Muse Charm” hardware device.

summary.tldr:
Meta has officially launched 'Muse Voice,' a video-chatting feature for its consumer AI agent, Muse, to all users in the United States. First unveiled at the September Connect developer conference, the feature utilizes proprietary 'Muse Realtime Avatar' and 'Muse Realtime Voice' technology to facilitate interactive, real-time conversations. The interface features an animated avatar, such as the default 'Jolly,' which users can customize to resemble humans, animals, or other characters. Meta intends for this anthropomorphization to foster deeper user engagement, with the avatar programmed to mirror conversational tone through subtle gestures and expressions.

Technically, the Muse avatar operates via audio input, as it does not possess visual perception of the user. The system is currently accessible across mobile, web, and Mac platforms. Meta plans to expand this functionality to its AI Glasses and a forthcoming wearable device, internally referred to as 'Muse Charm,' which is scheduled for release before the end of the year. This hardware is designed to function as a Tamagotchi-like device, displaying the digital avatar on a small screen to handle user requests and tasks.
takeaways: **Core Technology:** Muse Voice is powered by Muse Realtime Avatar and Muse Realtime Voice models.
**Platform Availability:** The feature is currently live for U.S. users on mobile, web, and Mac platforms.
**Hardware Roadmap:** Meta plans to launch a wearable device called 'Muse Charm' by the end of the year, featuring a screen for the AI avatar.
**Interaction Mechanics:** The avatar uses non-verbal cues like gestures and expressions to match conversational tone, though it does not have visual input capabilities.

title: New NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Open Models for Interactive World Simulation
author: Hugging Face Blog
contentSnippet:
NVIDIA Cosmos world model development platform adds four new open-weight checkpoints to its Cosmos 3 model family for generating interactive world simulation and multi-sensor multi-view driving scenes:

🌦️ Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto : Generate multi-view driving data with varied weather, lighting, and time of day.

🚗 Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto : Stream synchronized camera and LiDAR observations for driving simulation.

🎨 Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer : Turn simulator controls and a text prompt into photorealistic video.

🤖 Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual : Predict video from robot or camera actions.

All four models are post-trained examples of Cosmos 3 Nano and have 16B trainable parameters. The models use OpenMDW1.1, permitting commercial and non-commercial use under its terms.

Download the checkpoints · Read the technical report . Watch the demos

Why do you need these checkpoints?

🦾 Robotics needs environments that can answer this across changing scenes and viewpoints. These checkpoints offer complementary ways to build them: Sim-Bimanual predicts visual consequences from actions, while Sim-Transfer turns a physics simulator’s controls into generated observations.

🚦 For autonomous driving, appearance and geometry must agree. Synchronized camera and LiDAR generation connects visual observations with 3D sensing. Scene and traffic-signal controls let researchers vary road layouts and signal states, then study how a driving policy responds.

🔄 Each observation can shape the next action. Streaming generation connects video prediction to ongoing interaction, giving world-model researchers a way to explore how actions and observations unfold together.

🌐 An open foundation for others to build on. NVIDIA’s vision is to help researchers and developers create richer, more responsive simulated worlds. Open weights and post-training recipes provide a shared starting point for adapting models, comparing methods, and contributing improvements. These problems remain hard: the work ahead is to measure where the models faithfully support policy learning and evaluation, understand their limits, and improve where they fall short.

Build Autonomous Vehicle Worlds with Cosmos3-Nano

🌦️Transfer-Auto: driving scenarios → multi-sensor data

Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto is a bidirectional model for offline synthetic driving data generation. It generates synchronized video across up t

summary.tldr:
NVIDIA has released four new open-weight checkpoints for its Cosmos 3 world model platform, specifically designed for interactive simulation in robotics and autonomous driving. All four models—Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto, Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto, Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer, and Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual—are based on the Cosmos 3 Nano architecture, featuring 16 billion trainable parameters. These models are released under the OpenMDW1.1 license, permitting both commercial and non-commercial use, and are intended to serve as a foundation for researchers to build, adapt, and refine world models for specific sensor rigs and physical environments.

The models utilize a Mixture-of-Transformers backbone that integrates text-processing and visual-generation networks. The technical pipeline employs a four-stage training recipe: bidirectional adaptation, teacher forcing, consistency distillation (reducing generation to four denoising steps), and self-forcing to mitigate error compounding during long-horizon rollouts. The models operate on compressed video latents, where each latent time step represents four RGB frames. For autonomous driving, the models support synchronized multi-view camera generation (up to 11 views) and joint RGB–LiDAR generation using World Scenario Map (WSM) controls. For robotics, the Sim-Bimanual variant enables interactive two-arm simulation, supporting 59-value control schemas for YAM and AgiBot embodiments.
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** All four released checkpoints are 16B parameter models based on the Cosmos 3 Nano architecture.
**Driving Capabilities:** Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto supports offline synthetic data generation with up to 11 camera views and joint RGB-LiDAR output.
**Streaming Simulation:** Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto is a causally distilled variant designed for fast, interactive rollouts by generating successive video chunks in four denoising steps.
**Robotics Integration:** Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual supports bimanual robot simulation, accepting 59-value control sequences to predict visual consequences of actions for YAM and AgiBot platforms.

**Training Methodology:** The models undergo a four-stage process including bidirectional adaptation, teacher forcing, consistency distillation, and self-forcing to ensure temporal stability in generated history.

title: Meta warns that election backlash against data centers could make AI expansion harder
author: Sarah Perez
contentSnippet:
Meta president Dina Powell McCormick said that the Democratic wins in the midterm elections are going to make it a lot harder for companies to build data centers, adding that the industry has “not done as good a job as we needed to explain the benefits of these investments.”

Speaking at the WSJ Tech conference on Wednesday, the Meta exec pointed out that the backlash against data centers — which was very much on the ballot during this election season — was also tied to people’s feelings about AI technology overall.

“The visible sort of manifestation of AI is a data center, and it’s something that people can say, ‘I don’t want this in my community,’” she explained. “I think there’s an underlying bigger issue, which is how people feel about AI in general.”

Meta believes it could turn around the negative consumer sentiment around AI if it’s able to demonstrate the value, not only of the data centers coming to local communities, but also in the technology itself.

“The stakes of who builds the technology that cures cancer, that gives access to education, that is also a very fundamental difference … Mark [Zuckerberg, Meta CEO] is very ‘long human,’ and he’s betting on humans more than machines,” Powell McCormick explained. “And that’s what we mean when we say the future is for everyone. That people should not be left behind. But the way to ensure that is that this technology is democratized, that people have access to it in a very fair and transparent way,” she said.

The exec also touted Meta’s experience in building data centers, saying that the company has been doing so for 20 years, as it takes a lot of compute power to offer the products it does in the social networking space. Today, the company has data centers in 23 states, she said, and five of them, including one in Texas, are planned as projects of 1 gigawatt or more.

But Meta is now worried that it could lose some of its investments after politicians ran on anti-data-center platforms during the midterms.

“I think it’s going to be harder,” Powell McCormick said, describing what the future of building data centers looks like. “It has been hard, I should say, but I also think that it’s becoming clear what models work, and the states want those models that work.”

Specifically, communities only want data centers when it benefits them in some way, she explained, laying out the approach that Meta today

summary.tldr:
Meta President Dina Powell McCormick warned at the WSJ Tech conference that recent midterm election results signal increasing political resistance to data center construction, complicating the company's AI infrastructure expansion. Meta currently operates data centers across 23 U.S. states and is planning five new projects with capacities of 1 gigawatt or more, including a site in Texas. The company attributes the local backlash to a broader public apprehension regarding AI, noting that data centers serve as the primary physical manifestation of the technology for local communities.

To mitigate opposition, Meta is shifting its community engagement strategy to emphasize tangible local benefits, such as directing tax surpluses toward education and first responders, prioritizing local labor, and securing bipartisan political support. Despite potential regulatory hurdles, Meta maintains that its massive compute investments remain viable; the company reports daily inbound interest from third parties seeking to lease its excess compute capacity, providing a secondary monetization path should its internal consumer AI agent, Muse—which currently has 10 million users—fail to reach its target of billions of users.
takeaways: **Infrastructure Scale:** Meta currently operates data centers in 23 U.S. states, with five upcoming projects designed to reach 1 gigawatt or more in capacity.
**Monetization Strategy:** Meta is actively exploring leasing its compute capacity to third parties, citing daily inquiries as a hedge against potential underutilization of its AI infrastructure.

**Community Engagement Model:** Meta's current strategy for securing data center approval involves funding its own electricity, allocating tax surpluses to local teachers and first responders, and mandating local labor forces.
**User Metrics:** Meta's consumer AI agent, Muse, has reached 10 million users, with the company aiming to scale the platform to serve billions.

title: OpenAI released a new cybersecurity model. Is that enough?
author: Tim Fernholz
contentSnippet:
Max Justicz, the chief technology officer and co-founder of the startup Charge Robotics, used an OpenAI model to find a severe vulnerability that — if exploited — could allow hackers to take control of servers running Ubuntu, a widely used open source Linux-based operating system.

Justicz, who has a hobbyist’s interest in cybersecurity and previously found a vulnerability in the same codebase, told TechCrunch that he found this issue using GPT 5.6 Sol, released in July, through the AI maker’s Daybreak Blue, a program that gives cybersecurity defenders access to powerful frontier models.

“I literally just aimed ChatGPT at the same body of code and said ‘I found this bug previously that was fixed several years ago, please find bugs as bad or worse,’ and it came back in two hours with this,” Justicz said. “It’s extremely convoluted and hard for a human to find, but it works!”

He reported the issue to the Debian Project, which maintains the software in question and issued a patch to fix the vulnerability. There has been no known evidence of exploitation. Still, the ease with which he found it suggests that we’ve only seen the tip of the iceberg when it comes to potential exploits that even novice hackers can utilize with the help of AI models.

“I can only imagine what one could do with more time and access to less neutered models. We should expect some extremely crazy bugs to be found and exploited over the next few months,” Justicz wrote in a social media thread discussing his finding. “This might be obvious to most folks here, but there is currently huge alpha in taking some code or binary someone has not audited yet and just aiming a powerful AI model at it.”

OpenAI appears to have noticed. Today, the AI giant announced a new model focused on cybersecurity, ChatGPT Cyber, would be made available to the highest tier of users in the cybersecurity program, Daybreak Red, which allows offensive cybersecurity researchers tools for vulnerability hunting and development. Yesterday, OpenAI said that the same model had been used to scan and prepare patches for vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel, finding 948 potential issues. OpenAI also found 81 “novel” vulnerabilities in Firefox, the web browser.

“Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers,

summary.tldr: OpenAI has introduced 'ChatGPT Cyber,' a specialized model integrated into its 'Daybreak Red' program, designed to assist offensive cybersecurity researchers in vulnerability hunting and development. This follows the release of the 'GPT 5.6 Sol' model in July, which was utilized by Charge Robotics CTO Max Justicz to identify a severe, complex vulnerability in Ubuntu. OpenAI reports that its internal testing of these models successfully identified 948 potential issues in the Linux kernel and 81 'novel' vulnerabilities in the Firefox browser, marking a significant shift toward using frontier models for automated security auditing.
takeaways: **Model Capabilities:** OpenAI's internal testing with its cybersecurity-focused models identified 948 potential vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel and 81 novel vulnerabilities in Firefox.

**Program Structure:** OpenAI operates two tiers of cybersecurity access: 'Daybreak Blue' for defenders and 'Daybreak Red' for offensive researchers, with the latter receiving access to the new ChatGPT Cyber model.

**Financial Commitment:** OpenAI has launched a $1 billion initiative to support cybersecurity professionals working on critical infrastructure, though critics note the $1.2 million spent on the Linux bug hunt is significantly lower than the $6 million the company invested in fluid dynamics research.

**Security Concerns:** Researchers like Max Justicz report that while these models are highly effective at finding convoluted bugs, OpenAI has recently restricted ('nerfed') the capabilities of the Daybreak Blue tier, potentially hindering legitimate security research compared to unrestricted open-weight models.

title: Muse has a voice mode now
author: Jay Peters
contentSnippet: Meta now lets you have voice conversations with your Muse AI agent in real time, CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced today. The feature has been rolled out to me, and I gave it a spin on the iOS app while writing this article. As you chat with your Muse agent, the avatar at the top of your conversation animates in time with the words that it’s saying. You can also change the tone of the voice by just asking your agent about what you want and letting it decide or by browsing through a bunch of options in the avatar settings. [Media: https://www.threads.com/@muse/post/DfXsBBYCnf5] In my brief tests, my Muse agent responds quickly over voice, though it occasionally pauses while it’s looking up information or checking something for me (like it would with a text chat query). It also animates what it’s saying well, though for my particular avatar, it’s been a little uncanny. I set my Muse agent’s avatar to look like Mark Zuckerberg as a constant reminder that I’m chatting with a Meta service (I refuse to be charmed by a Jolly!), and seeing the digital Zuckerberg facsimile actually talk with me is quite weird. I also can’t get my Muse agent’s voice to sound exactly like Mark Zuckerberg. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/IMG_0227.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Muse’s voice mode and expressive avatars are rolling out now in the US for the app, Meta says. They’re coming “soon” for Meta’s AI glasses and will also be available for its forthcoming Muse Charm gadget, which is supposed to ship this year.

summary.tldr:
Meta has introduced a real-time voice mode for its Muse AI agent, enabling interactive spoken conversations within the iOS application. The feature includes animated avatars that synchronize lip movements with the agent's speech, and users can customize the voice tone either through direct requests or by selecting from a menu in the avatar settings. The system is designed to process queries similarly to text-based interactions, occasionally pausing during information retrieval or external lookups.

The update is currently rolling out to users in the United States. Meta has confirmed that the voice mode and expressive avatar functionality will be extended to the company's AI glasses in the near future and will be integrated into the upcoming Muse Charm hardware device, which is scheduled for release later this year.
takeaways: **Platform Availability:** The Muse voice mode is currently live on the iOS app for users in the United States.
**Hardware Roadmap:** Voice mode support is confirmed for Meta's AI glasses and the forthcoming Muse Charm gadget.
**Customization:** Users can modify the agent's voice tone via avatar settings or by providing natural language instructions to the agent.
**Visual Feedback:** The interface features animated avatars that provide real-time lip-syncing during voice interactions.

title: Unpacking the Compute Efficiency of Strong-to-Weak OPD against GRPO
author: Zeyu Leo Liu
contentSnippet: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher's per-token supervision. Does this dense signal reduce the training FLOPs needed to reach a target accuracy compared with reinforcement learning? We systematically compare vanilla reverse-KL OPD with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) across task difficulty, student and teacher size, domain, and optimization choices, measuring held-out accuracy against training FLOPs. With an external post-trained teacher, OPD generally loses to GRPO in accuracy per training FLOP at matched settings, even when the teacher is further trained with GRPO, and often suffers response-length inflation. Yet a different teacher changes the picture: when the teacher is the student's own GRPO checkpoint, OPD recovers that checkpoint's accuracy on math with $50\times$ fewer distillation FLOPs than GRPO needs to reach the same accuracy. Following the same teacher setting, we consistently observe this high efficiency with a larger student, on code, and in a second model family. On a single domain, however, the GRPO checkpoint is already the desired model, so distilling it adds to total compute. Across domains, separate GRPO checkpoints hold different capabilities, and no single checkpoint serves every domain. Multi-teacher OPD (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) consolidates per-domain GRPO experts into a single student that matches each expert's accuracy, with the distillation stage costing only 5.2% (on 2 domains) and 8.0% (on 4 domains) of the specialist training FLOPs. Counting specialist training and distillation together, this pipeline reaches joint GRPO's performance on the 2-domain mix with 42.0% fewer total FLOPs.

We systematically compare vanilla reverse-KL OPD with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) across task difficulty, student and teacher size, domain, and optimization choices, measuring held-out accuracy against training FLOPs.

With an external post-trained teacher, OPD generally loses to GRPO in accuracy per training FLOP at matched settings, even when the teacher is further trained with GRPO, and often suffers response-length inflation. Yet a different teacher changes the picture: when the teacher is the student's own GRPO checkpoint, OPD recovers that checkpoint's accuracy on math with $50\times$ fewer distillation FLOPs than GRPO needs to reach the same accuracy. Following the same teacher setting, we consistently observe this high efficiency with a larger student, on code, and in a second model family.
takeaways: On a single domain, however, the GRPO checkpoint is already the desired model, so distilling it adds to total compute.
Across domains, separate GRPO checkpoints hold different capabilities, and no single checkpoint serves every domain.

Multi-teacher OPD (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) consolidates per-domain GRPO experts into a single student that matches each expert's accuracy, with the distillation stage costing only 5.2% (on 2 domains) and 8.0% (on 4 domains) of the specialist training FLOPs.
Counting specialist training and distillation together, this pipeline reaches joint GRPO's performance on the 2-domain mix with 42.0% fewer total FLOPs.

title: ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts
author: Yubo Wang, Rui Meng, Jaehyun Nam, Tomas Pfister
contentSnippet: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.
